Every question from the four exam series was tallied by topic. Study these clusters first — they carry the highest probability of appearing again. Tags show every sitting that asked it.

PAPER I — WHAT REPEATS

1. NMES / electrical stimulation instrumentation — asked in EVERY sitting

Nov 23 Q8 ·May–Jun 24 Q2 & Q6 ·May 25 Q5 & Q10 ·Nov 25 Q8 & Q9 — 7 questions in 4 papers

The single most repeated topic in the series. Know the instrumentation chain (oscillator → timer → amplifier → charge-balanced output), motor parameters (35–50 Hz, 200–400 µs, duty 1:3–1:5), Russian current (2.5 kHz carrier, 50 bps), and the electrophysiological assessment devices (EMG/NCS: differential amplifier, CMRR, filters).

2. Statistics & research methods — every sitting, 3–4 questions

Sampling (Nov 23 Q4,May 25 Q3) · study designs (May 25 Q6,Nov 25 Q3) · hypothesis testing & p-value (May–Jun 24 Q7) · probability & normal distribution (May–Jun 24 Q5) · central tendency (Nov 25 Q4) · parametric vs non-parametric (May 25 Q7) · pilot study (Nov 23 Q3)

Expect at least two pure-methods questions per paper. The 68–95–99.7 rule, p-value interpretation, and sampling designs with Indian examples are the repeated core.

3. Ethics — ICMR 2017 and the four principles

Nov 23 Q2 ·May 25 Q4 ·Nov 25 Q2 (ICMR verbatim)

Beauchamp & Childress principles + ICMR's twelve principles: at least eight with one line each is the scorer.

4. Exercise physiology: adaptations, energy systems, obesity prescription

Energy transfer (Nov 23 Q6) · adaptations to exercise (May–Jun 24 Q3,Nov 25 Q6) · aerobic vs anaerobic (May 25 Q9) · obesity/weight control (Nov 23 Q7,May 25 Q8) · age & sex (Nov 25 Q7) · strength training methods (May–Jun 24 Q10)

ATP-PC 10 s → glycolysis 2 min → oxidative; 7.3 kcal/mol; MET 3.5 mL/kg/min; Indian waist 90/80 cm; FITT 150→300 min/week. These numbers recur across four questions.

5. SPADI psychometrics + Bloom's taxonomy — the "fixed" questions

SPADI:Nov 23 Q9,May–Jun 24 Q8 · Bloom:Nov 23 Q10,May–Jun 24 Q9 · ICF documentation:May 25 Q1,Nov 25 Q1

SPADI (5 pain + 8 disability items, 0–100, MCID 8–10) and Bloom's six verbs in order are near-guaranteed marks. ICF documentation with codes (b/s/d/e) is the newest repeat.

PAPER II — WHAT REPEATS

1. Pain theories and pain states

Nov 23 Q8 ·May 25 Q8 ·Nov 25 Q9 (specific pain states)

Gate control (Melzack & Wall 1965) → neuromatrix (1999) is asked every time; the 2025 sittings add specific syndromes — radicular vs nociceptive vs central sensitisation.

2. Biophysical effects of heat / thermal agents

Nov 23 Q9 ·May–Jun 24 Q10 ·Nov 25 Q10 (adhesive capsulitis)

Q₁₀ metabolic rise, collagen extensibility, depth of superficial vs deep agents (SWD 27.12 MHz, US 1 MHz) — repeated in three consecutive series.

3. Posture — control and deformities

Posture control after IVDP (Nov 23 Q6) · forward head posture (May–Jun 24 Q6) · thoracic abnormalities (May 25 Q6) · mechanism of postural control (Nov 25 Q8)

4. Gait — determinants, aging, pathology

Determinants (Nov 23 Q7) · foot-drop gait case (May–Jun 24 Q8) · ankle instability gait (May 25 Q7) · older adults (Nov 25 Q4)

The six determinants with examples and the 60/40 stance-swing split carry the marks; the 2024 paper dressed it as a clinical case (gluteal injection → sciatic palsy).

5. Joint mechanics + exercise metabolism + anthropometry

Knee (May 25 Q5) · hip (May 25 Q10) · elbow FFD (May–Jun 24 Q5) · ACL (Nov 25 Q7) · rotator cuff (Nov 23 Q5,May–Jun 24 Q3) · BMI/body fat (Nov 23 Q2,May 25 Q2,May–Jun 24 Q9) · oxygen supply/adaptations (Nov 23 Q4,May–Jun 24 Q4,May 25 Q4,Nov 25 Q5)

Scapulohumeral rhythm 2:1, Q-angle 13–18°, PFJ force 3–7× BW, GRF 1.2/3× BW — one mechanics question and one metabolism question per sitting is the norm.

PAPER III — WHAT REPEATS

1. Region screening — the core of the paper

Neck C3–C4 (Nov 23 Q2) · upper back/fibromyalgia (Nov 23 Q3) · head & neck in UCS (May 25 Q2) · SI & pelvis (May 25 Q10) · shoulder impingement (Nov 25 Q2) · lumbar disc herniation (Nov 25 Q3) · knee PCL (May–Jun 24 Q5) · ankle (Nov 23 Q5,May–Jun 24 Q9)

Two screening questions per sitting, always. Learn each region's dermatome-myotome-reflex trio, its two special tests with sensitivity/specificity, and its differentials.

2. Fracture neck of femur — pre & post-operative assessment

May 25 Q6 ·Nov 25 Q9 — the SAME question twice in one year

The only verbatim repeat inside a single calendar year: Garden classification, pre-op fitness, post-op precautions (posterior approach), Harris Hip Score, TUG ≤12 s, gait speed ≥1 m/s.

3. Assessment fundamentals + autonomous practice

Role of assessment (Nov 23 Q1) · demographic data & history (May–Jun 24 Q7) · basic assessment methods (Nov 25 Q1) · joint play (May 25 Q1) · decision making (May–Jun 24 Q2) · direct access (Nov 23 Q4) · autonomous practice (Nov 25 Q4)

4. Amputations, fractures and investigations

Below-knee (Nov 23 Q8) · Symes (May–Jun 24 Q6) · supracondylar (Nov 23 Q7) · both-bone forearm (May–Jun 24 Q3) · osteoporosis investigations (Nov 23 Q6) · SCI investigations (May–Jun 24 Q4)

5. Outcome measures & exercise testing

Shoulder (Nov 23 Q9) · knee (May–Jun 24 Q8) · ACL-R exercise testing (May 25 Q5) · exercise testing in MSK disease (Nov 25 Q6) · ICF in diagnosis (Nov 25 Q10)
PAPER IV — WHAT REPEATS

1. Electrotherapy — mechanism + evidence, every sitting

Pain-relief mechanisms (Nov 23 Q2) · soft-tissue evidence (Nov 23 Q7) · AK-amputation advances (May–Jun 24 Q2) · fibromyalgia (May 25 Q6) · LBP with evidence (Nov 25 Q8) · electromagnetic agents (Nov 25 Q9)

Conventional TENS 80–100 Hz/50–100 µs vs acupuncture-like 2–4 Hz/200–300 µs; IFT 4 kHz carrier; SWD 27.12 MHz; ultrasound 1 vs 3 MHz. Quote one negative trial to show examiner-level honesty.

2. Ergonomics & work — the Indian-workplace favourites

CROSS-PAPER TOPICS — ASKED IN TWO DIFFERENT PAPERS

The bridges RGUHS builds between papers

  • ICF — documentation in Paper I (May 25, Nov 25) AND diagnosis in Paper III (Nov 25).
  • Pain science — theories in Paper II, management/electrotherapy in Paper IV. Study them together.
  • Electrical currents — instrumentation in Paper I, clinical evidence-based use in Paper IV.
  • Exercise physiology — energy systems and adaptations in Paper I, oxygen supply and metabolism in Paper II.
  • Outcome measures — psychometric properties in Paper I (SPADI), regional scales in Paper III.
  • Ergonomics — risk assessment and return-to-work in Paper III, workplace interventions in Paper IV.
  • Posture — control and deformities in Paper II, corrective interventions in Paper IV.
  • Amputation — assessment in Paper III (BK, Symes), electrotherapy/recent advances in Paper IV.

Examiner's strategy note

Verbatim repeats are real: fracture neck of femur assessment appeared twice in 2025, McKenzie twice, SPADI psychometrics twice, wrist/software ergonomics twice. Of 160 questions, roughly 60% fall into the 25 clusters above — master these clusters and you have prepared for the majority of any future paper, whatever its surface wording. The last-hour sheet of each paper carries the numbers for its own clusters.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Definition of physiotherapy? Explain in detail the principles of evidence based practice in physiotherapy?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 1a, 1d — Definition & scope; Principles of Evidence Based Practice

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition of physiotherapy (World Physiotherapy)1.5
Definition & triad of EBP (Sackett)1.5
The five steps of EBP explained with example3
Hierarchy of evidence2
Application in physiotherapy practice + conclusion2
★ Memory hook — EBP = E′·E′·P′ — Evidence + Expertise + Patient values (three legs of one stool). The five steps are the five A’s in order: Ask → Acquire → Appraise → Apply → Assess.

aDefinition

Per World Physiotherapy: physiotherapy is the service provided only by, or under the direction and supervision of, physiotherapists to individuals and populations to develop, maintain and restore maximum movement and functional ability throughout the lifespan — including circumstances where movement and function are threatened by ageing, injury, disease or environmental factors. It is a primary-contact, autonomous profession within the ICF framework.

bEvidence-based practice — the triad

EBP (Sackett): the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best research evidence, integrated with the clinician's expertise and the patient's values and circumstances, in making decisions about the care of individual patients. Remove any one of the three and the practice is no longer evidence-based — evidence without expertise is cook-book medicine, expertise without evidence is opinion, and both without patient values are paternalism.

cThe five steps

  1. Ask — convert the clinical problem into a focused, answerable PICOT/PICO question (e.g., "In chronic low-back pain (P), is motor-control exercise (I) more effective than general exercise (C) for reducing disability (O) at 3 months (T)?").
  2. Acquire — search the literature systematically: PubMed/MEDLINE, Pedro (physiotherapy-specific), Cochrane Library; MeSH terms and Boolean operators.
  3. Appraise — critical appraisal for validity, magnitude and applicability using the hierarchy of evidence: systematic reviews & meta-analyses of RCTs at the top, then RCTs, cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, case series, and expert opinion at the bottom.
  4. Apply — integrate the appraised evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's preferences, culture and finances — critical in Indian practice (cost of, say, shockwave therapy in a daily-wage patient).
  5. Assess (audit) — evaluate the outcome of the decision and one's own performance; feeds the next cycle.
Fig 1 — the 5-step EBP cycle around the evidence-expertise-patient core. Reproduce this and the pyramid in any EBP answer.
Students write a lovely definition and stop — the five steps with a physiotherapy example are what carry 5 of the 10 marks. Naming PEDro as the physiotherapy-specific database earns a bonus smile.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 1 (a, d).
  2. Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM. Churchill Livingstone (syllabus Paper-I reference 5).
  3. Herbert R, Jamtvedt G, Hagen K, Mead J. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy. Churchill Livingstone (syllabus Paper-I reference 6).
  4. World Physiotherapy policy statement — description of physiotherapy.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Write the ethical issues faced in clinical practice of physiotherapy?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 2 — Core Professional Values; ethical issues in practice; ICMR guidelines

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Four cardinal principles of biomedical ethics2
Ethical issues in clinical practice (at least six, explained)4.5
Research/ICMR-relevant issues1.5
Resolution strategies + conclusion2

aFoundations

Beauchamp & Childress' four principles anchor all clinical ethics: autonomy (respect the patient's informed choices), beneficence (act in the patient's best interest), non-maleficence (do no harm) and justice (fair, equitable distribution of services). The syllabus adds the World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice and the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines as the profession's normative documents.

bCommon ethical issues in Indian physiotherapy clinics

  • Consent and autonomy: treating without adequate explanation; in India, families often decide for the patient — negotiating informed consent across language and literacy barriers is a daily issue.
  • Confidentiality: sensitive conditions (HIV status, occupational injury claims) shared casually in open treatment areas or with employers without consent.
  • Scope of practice & referral: treating beyond competence (e.g., manipulating the cervical spine without training), or handling red-flag cases that needed medical referral.
  • Overtreatment & commercial pressure: unnecessarily prolonged packages; outcome-driven billing exploits the imbalance of knowledge.
  • Dual relationships/boundaries: treating relatives/close acquaintances, gifts, or social-media friendships that cloud clinical judgement.
  • Documentation & record keeping: poor notes that fail medicolegal scrutiny; tele-rehabilitation consent and data privacy.
  • Equity: refusing treatment to patients with infectious disease; gender-related discomfort (female patients and male therapists in India and vice versa); access for the poor.
  • Advertising & misrepresentation: promising cures ("guaranteed back-pain relief") violates honesty.

cResearch ethics link

ICMR 2017 guidelines and RIPE 2020: institutional ethics-committee approval, voluntary participation, compensation for trial injury — directly relevant to any postgraduate dissertation involving patients.

dResolution

Institutional ethics committees, professional codes (World Physiotherapy/IAP), continuing education, peer review, honest documentation and transparent billing — the ethical clinician institutionalises these rather than relying on good intentions.

Fig 2 — The four-principles quadrant with patient welfare at the centre. Two minutes to draw, instantly shows the examiner you know the ethical scaffolding before you list the issues.
Marks come from explaining issues with an Indian clinical example each — not listing single words. An answer without the four principles and without ICMR mention rarely crosses 6.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 2 (a–d).
  2. ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research involving Human Participants, 2017 (syllabus Paper-I reference 9).
  3. World Physiotherapy (2011) Standards of Physical Therapy Practice (reference 8).
  4. Beauchamp TL, Childress JF. Principles of Biomedical Ethics. (standard ethics reference)
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Importance of pilot study in clinical research?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3a — Conceiving the research question & developing the study plan

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition of pilot study1
Purposes: feasibility, protocol, instruments, sample size, resources (1 each)5
Illustrative physiotherapy example2.5
Limitations & reporting1.5
★ Memory hook — Pilot study: tests the process, never the hypothesis — “P for Process, not Proof”.

aDefinition

A pilot study is a small-scale preliminary version of the main study, run on a handful of participants (often 10% of the intended sample), conducted to test whether the full study is feasible — NOT to test the hypothesis itself.

bWhy it matters — the five purposes

  1. Feasibility of recruitment: can we actually enrol 40 knee-OA patients in 3 months from one OPD? Are inclusion criteria workable?
  2. Protocol refinement: tests the intervention itself — dosage, session length, timing of outcomes; reveals impractical procedures (a 90-minute assessment no patient completes).
  3. Instrument testing: whether the outcome measures are understood — e.g., does the translated SPADI read naturally for Kannada-speaking patients? Missing-item rates, floor/ceiling effects.
  4. Sample-size estimation: provides pilot variance (SD) values to feed the power calculation for the main trial.
  5. Resources, cost & data management: estimated drop-out rate, staff time, budget, and whether the case-report form/eCRF actually captures the data.

cExample

Before an RCT of eccentric vs concentric quadriceps training in patellofemoral pain, a pilot with 8 patients showed that the VAS diary confused participants and that two dropped out due to travel cost — the main study switched to a numeric pain rating at weekly visits and offered transport reimbursement.

dLimitations

Small samples cannot confirm the main effect (estimates are unstable — the main study may still fail); pilot data must not be pooled into the main analysis; findings must be reported as feasibility outcomes (Lancet 2016 extension guidelines for pilot trials).

Fig 3 — Pilot-to-main-study flow. Any pilot-study answer with this flow and the five purpose-branches reads complete in one glance.
One sentence examiners hunt for: "a pilot study tests the research process, not the hypothesis." Follow with the five purposes and a dissertation-style example.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 3a (iii–vi).
  2. Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research. 4th ed. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins (syllabus Paper-I reference 11).
  3. Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics. 4th ed. CRC Press (reference 12).
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. How would you differentiate between simple random sampling and complex random sampling designs? Explain clearly by giving examples?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3a-iv — Choosing study subjects: specification, sampling and recruitment

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Simple random sampling: definition, methods, merits/demerits2.5
Stratified sampling (with example)2
Cluster sampling (with example)1.5
Systematic & multi-stage sampling (with example)2
Comparison summary table2
★ Memory hook — Sampling ladder: Systematic = every k-th from a list; Stratified = strata first, random inside each; Cluster = whole groups at random.

aSimple random sampling (SRS)

Every member of the sampling frame has an equal and independent chance of selection; done by lottery, random number tables or computer-generated random numbers. It is the only design that is purely probability-based, needs no knowledge of the population's structure, but demands a complete sampling frame and spreads samples thinly across wide areas. Example: drawing 60 of 400 registered low-back-pain patients from a hospital list using random numbers.

bComplex (restricted) random designs

  • Stratified — the population is first divided into homogeneous strata (by sex, disease severity, age band), then SRS is performed within each stratum, often proportionally. Guarantees representation of small subgroups and improves precision. Example: in a TKR study, sampling male and female patients separately in a 1:2 ratio because the clinic population is one-third women.
  • Cluster — natural groups (schools, villages, wards) are randomly selected and all members of the chosen clusters are studied. Cheapest for dispersed populations; less precise (intra-cluster correlation). Example: randomly picking 6 of Bengaluru's 40 physiotherapy colleges and surveying every final-year student in them.
  • Systematic — every kth person from a list after a random start (k = frame size ÷ sample size). Simple but risk of periodicity. Example: every 5th patient attending an OPD from a random Monday start.
  • Multi-stage — random selection in successive stages (state → district → hospital → patient), practical for large community surveys. Example: Karnataka → 4 districts → 2 PHCs each → all adults screened for knee OA.

cThe comparison an evaluator wants

FeatureSRSComplex designs
Frame neededComplete list of allList of strata/clusters only

The differentiator marks sit in the examples with numbers — "every 5th patient," "6 of 40 colleges." Also state that stratified samples within strata are still random — students often mistake stratification for quota sampling (non-probability).

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Write in detail the fundamentals of qualitative research methods?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3b-vi, 3c-iv — Fundamentals of qualitative research; designing qualitative studies

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Paradigm & when qualitative methods are appropriate1.5
Major designs (phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, narrative)2.5
Sampling & data collection2.5
Analysis approaches2
Trustworthiness criteria1.5

aParadigm

Qualitative research explores meanings, experiences and processes ("why" and "how") rather than measuring quantities ("how much"). It answers questions RCTs cannot: how do stroke survivors in rural Karnataka experience self-management? Data are words and observations; the researcher is the instrument.

bDesigns

  • Phenomenology — lived experience of a phenomenon (patients' experience of chronic low-back pain).
  • Grounded theory — builds a theory from data through constant comparison, to explain a process (how adherence to home programmes develops).
  • Ethnography — culture of a group (pain beliefs within a community).
  • Narrative inquiry / case study — stories of illness over time.

cSampling and data collection

Purposive sampling of information-rich cases, extended by snowball technique; enrolment continues until data saturation — no new themes emerging (often 10–15 in-depth interviews). Tools: semi-structured in-depth interviews, focus-group discussions, non-participant observation, document review; audio-recording with consent, verbatim transcription.

dAnalysis

Thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke: familiarisation → coding → themes → review → definition → report) or content analysis; framework approach for policy research; software (NVivo/ATLAS.ti) assists but does not replace the analyst. Analysis proceeds simultaneously with collection.

eTrustworthiness

Lincoln & Guba's criteria: credibility (triangulation, member-checking), transferability (thick description), dependability (audit trail), confirmability (reflexivity) — the qualitative counterparts of validity and reliability.

Fig 5 — The qualitative pipeline with the constant-comparison loop underneath and the four trustworthiness criteria on the side — the whole methodology in one sketch.
One viva-trap: qualitative research is NOT "research without numbers because it's easier" — it is a deliberate paradigm with its own rigour. Score by naming two designs AND two trustworthiness criteria with their quantitative equivalents.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 3b-vi and 3c-iv.
  2. Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research. 4th ed. (reference 11).
  3. Braun V, Clarke V. Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qual Res Psychol. 2006;3:77–101. (primary method reference)
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Write note on fundamentals of Human energy transfer?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4a — Fundamentals of Human Energy Transfer

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Laws of thermodynamics as applied to the body2
ATP — the energy currency; coupled reactions2.5
The three energy systems3
Efficiency & physiological application2.5
★ Memory hook — Energy systems run 10 : 2 : ∞ — ATP–PC about 10 seconds, glycolysis about 2 minutes, oxidative forever.

aLaws of thermodynamics

The first law (conservation): energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted — the human machine converts chemical energy of food into mechanical work, heat and stored energy. The second law: conversions are inefficient; much is lost as heat — which is why exercising bodies warm up. Biogenic molecules are reduced (energy-rich) and oxidised to CO₂ and H₂O to release free energy.

bATP — the universal currency

Cells cannot use food energy directly; all transfers pass through ATP, whose terminal phosphate bond releases ~7.3 kcal/mol on hydrolysis. ATP is regenerated by phosphorylation of ADP through coupled reactions: substrate-level (glycolysis, creatine phosphate) and oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondrial electron-transport chain. The CP shuttle provides the fastest regeneration: ADP + CP → ATP + creatine, catalysed by creatine kinase.

cThree energy systems

  • ATP-PC (phosphagen) — immediate, ~10 s of explosive power, anaerobic, no lactate.
  • Anaerobic glycolysis — 10 s to ~2 min of high-intensity effort; rapid ATP but limited by H⁺/lactate accumulation.
  • Oxidative (aerobic) system — carbohydrate and fat oxidation; unlimited duration at lower intensity, dominant after ~2 min; fat yields more ATP per gram but needs more oxygen.

dEfficiency and application

Whole-body mechanical efficiency is only ~20–25% (cycle ergometry); the rest is heat — the physiological basis of warm-up, of thermoregulation during exercise, and of caloric-expenditure calculations (1 L O₂ ≈ 5 kcal; MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min). Training shifts substrate use (fat oxidation at higher intensities in the trained) and raises the lactate threshold — the underpinning of every endurance prescription.

Fig 6 — The power–duration curve with the three energy systems fenced off along the time axis. One curve, three systems, full marks for Q6.
This is a physiology-of-exercise question in a research-paper wrapper — connect each system to a physiotherapy activity (phosphagen = a single hoist transfer in the gym; glycolytic = 2-min TUG repetitions; oxidative = a walking programme). Fick's equation can cameo for the aerobic system.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 4a, 4g.
  2. McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance. 8th ed. Lippincott (syllabus Paper-I reference 13).
  3. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Elsevier.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Briefly prescribe the exercise protocol for weight control?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4f — Body composition, evaluation, obesity and weight control

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Assessment & goal setting1.5
Energy balance & target deficit2
Aerobic FITT prescription2.5
Resistance + behavioural components2
Progression, precautions, Indian context2
★ Memory hook — Weight control numbers: deficit 500–750 kcal/day → 0.5–1 kg/week; goal 5–10% body weight in 3–6 months. FITT = Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.

aAssessment and goal

Baseline: BMI + waist circumference (Indian cutoffs: waist ≥90 cm men/≥80 cm women = abdominal obesity), body composition if available, PAR-Q+ screening, joint status (knees take the first brunt in the obese), resting BP and blood sugar. Goal: 0.5–1 kg/week — a 5–10% weight loss over 3–6 months is already clinically meaningful.

bThe energy-balance principle

Weight falls only in negative balance: target a deficit of 500–750 kcal/day (≈ 1200–1500 kcal diet for women / 1500–1800 for men) plus exercise. Exercise alone contributes 200–400 kcal/session — diet and activity act together.

cAerobic prescription (the core of the answer)

Follow the FITT principle: 150 min/week progressing to 250–300 min of moderate aerobic activity (brisk walking, cycling, aqua-jogging), 5–7 days/week, 45–60 min continuous or accumulated in 10-min bouts, at 60–75% HR reserve / RPE 11–14. Obese or knee-compromised starters: non-weight-bearing modes (cycling, swimming) initially.

dResistance and behaviour

Progressive resistance training 2–3 days/week (8–10 large-muscle exercises, 2–3 sets of 10–15 at 60–70% 1RM) preserves lean mass during dieting and raises resting metabolism. Add behavioural scaffolding: goal-setting, self-monitoring (steps: build to 8,000–10,000/day), stimulus control, family involvement.

eProgression and precautions

Progress load and duration ~5–10% every 2 weeks; watch for knee/back pain (modify mode), exercise-induced asthma, hypoglycaemia in diabetics on medication, and heat intolerance. Maintenance: 200–300 min/week activity plus monthly weigh-ins — relapse prevention is the real challenge.

Fig 7 — The energy-balance seesaw: intake on one plank, expenditure on the other, the deficit arrow doing the explaining. Draw it, then write the FITT table beside it.
"Prescribe" is the operative word — write an actual FITT table, not an essay on obesity. An answer without frequency/intensity/time/type numbers is a 5/10 however beautifully written.

  3. McArdle, Katch & Katch. Exercise Physiology. 8th ed. (Paper-I reference 13).
  4. Misra A et al. JAPI 2009 consensus (Indian cutoffs).
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Analyze the Instrumentation for neuromuscular electrical stimulation?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 5c — Instrumentation for NMES

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Block diagram & function of each component3
Waveform & key parameters3
Electrodes & application technique2
Precautions & clinical uses2
★ Memory hook — Russian current: 2.5 kHz carrier, 50 bursts/s, 10:50 on:off. Motor NMES: 35–50 Hz, 200–400 µs, duty cycle 1:3–1:5.

aBlock diagram of an NMES stimulator

NMES instrumentation: mains/power supply (battery → stabilised DC) → oscillator/pulse generator (sets frequency, pulse duration via timing circuits) → control/timer unit (on-off cycle, ramp) → amplifier (raises the signal to the required voltage/current) → output/transformer + coupling (safety isolation, charge-balanced output) → electrodes → tissue. Modern units are digital: microprocessor-generated pulsed currents with user-set parameters.

bWaveform and parameters

  • Waveform: symmetrical/asymmetrical biphasic pulsed current is preferred (charge-balanced → no skin irritation under electrodes; monophasic pulsed (faradic-type) causes chemical polarisation).
  • Frequency (pulses/s): 30–50 pps for functional tetanic contraction (typical NMES 35–50 Hz; Russian current 2.5 kHz carrier modulated at 50 bursts/s for torque); low rates (2–10 Hz) for sensory/analgesic or muscle-pumping effects.
  • Pulse duration: 200–400 μs suits motor stimulation of large muscles (shorter for small muscles).
  • Amplitude (intensity): to strong but comfortable tetany, typically 20–100 mA depending on impedance.
  • Duty cycle / on:off: duty cycle 1:3 to 1:5 (e.g., 10 s on, 30–50 s off) to postpone fatigue — stimulated muscle fatigues faster than voluntary contraction.
  • Ramp-up: 1–2 s for comfort.

cElectrodes and technique

Large motor electrode over the muscle's motor point, smaller/dispersive electrode at the distal tendon or the opposite side of the belly; size governs current density; low-impedance hydrogel pads; skin preparation and exact motor-point mapping determine efficiency.

dPrecautions, contraindications, uses

Avoid pacemakers/implanted devices, pregnancy over uterus, active malignancy in the region, thrombosis, and broken skin. Uses: muscle strengthening/re-education after injury or surgery (e.g., post-TKR quadriceps), disuse atrophy, NMES-assisted gait, oedema pumping, and preserving muscle plasticity (unit 5d).

Fig 8 — The NMES block diagram: five boxes, each labelled with the parameter that box controls. Examiners give the diagram mark for exactly this label-per-block discipline.
The examiner wants the analogy with physiology: every parameter you name, tie it to a nerve-physiology fact (frequency→tetany; duration→motor fibre recruitment threshold). And "charge-balanced biphasic prevents skin irritation" is a distinction line.

Sources

  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. — membrane/action potential chapters.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — electrical muscle stimulation sections.
  4. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (MSK syllabus reference 10).
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Psychometric Properties of SPADI

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 1 — Use of standardized scales; psychometric properties and interpretation

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Structure & scoring of SPADI3
Reliability (test–retest, internal consistency)2.5
Validity2
Responsiveness & MCID1.5
Clinical interpretation & versions1
★ Memory hook — SPADI = 5 + 8 = 13 items, 0–100, higher = worse; MCID ≈ 8–10, MDC95 ≈ 18. QuickDASH cuts it to 11 items.

aThe instrument

The SPADI (Shoulder Pain and Disability Index, Roach et al. 1991) is a 13-item self-report, region-specific measure for shoulder pathology: 5 pain items (pain at its worst, lying on the involved side, reaching up high, touching the back of the neck, pushing with the involved arm) + 8 disability items (daily self-care and lifting tasks — washing hair, washing the back, dressing, fastening behind the back, carrying heavy objects and similar). Each item on a 0–10 NRS/VAS; scores are averaged and expressed as a percentage (0–100) — higher = worse.

bReliability

Test–retest reliability: ICC 0.84–0.94 across studies over 1–2 weeks in stable patients. Internal consistency: Cronbach's α 0.86–0.98 for subscales and total. Cronbach's alpha >0.9 here shows items measure one construct — with a caution against item redundancy.

cValidity

Content/face: developed from patients' own reports (37 patients in the original development study; later validation studies enlarged the base). Construct: convergent correlations with the DASH (r ≈ 0.6–0.8), goniometric ROM and pain ratings. Cross-cultural: validated translations (Hindi, Kannada, Marathi, Tamil, Chinese, Portuguese, etc.) with equivalent factor structure.

dResponsiveness

Effect sizes 0.8–1.4 across interventions (frozen shoulder, RC pathology); MCID ≈ 8–10 points (7–13% in various studies) — below that, change is measurement noise. No floor/ceiling problems in typical MSK shoulder populations, unlike generic measures.

eInterpretation

Use for tracking individual progress and as a research endpoint; pair with objective measures (ROM, strength) for a complete ICF picture: SPADI maps largely to activity/participation, not body structure.

Fig 9 — SPADI's structure as a splitting box: 13 items → 5 pain + 8 disability → 0–100%. Sketch it and the scoring rule writes itself.
Psychometric properties = reliability + validity + responsiveness. Anything else (e.g., only structure) caps at 5/10. Quote ICC, alpha and MCID values with their meaning in one bracket each — exact decimals to one place are enough, and never invent a value you don't remember.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 1 (standardized scales & psychometric properties).
  2. Roach KE, Budiman-Mak E, Songsiridej N, Lertratanakul Y. Development of a shoulder pain and disability index. Arthritis Care Res. 1991;4:143–9. (primary)
  3. Williams JW et al. Responsive and important: SPADI vs SF-36. J Clin Epidemiol. (responsiveness evidence)
  4. Hicks CM. Research Methods for Clinical Therapists. (psychometric interpretation — Indian MPT standard)
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. What is formulated intended learning outcomes? Explain in detail the six objectives of Bloom's Taxonomy?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 6c — Formulating ILOs; Tyler's principles, Bloom's Taxonomy, Miller's Pyramid

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition & qualities (SMART) of an ILO1.5
Structure of an ILO statement1.5
Six levels of Bloom's (revised) taxonomy with examples5
Application in physiotherapy teaching + conclusion2
★ Memory hook — Bloom’s verbs climb R-U-A-A-E-C: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create. Miller’s pyramid peaks at Does.

aIntended learning outcomes

An ILO is a statement, written before teaching begins, of what the learner is expected to know, do or value at the end of a defined learning episode — the destination the teacher designs towards (Tyler's rationale: objectives → experiences → organisation → evaluation). Good ILOs are SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound, and use observable action verbs ("demonstrate", "differentiate") rather than vague ones ("understand", "know"). Structure: "By the end of this session, the student will be able to <action verb> <content> <context/standard>."

bBloom's taxonomy — the six cognitive levels

Bloom's original 1956 taxonomy (knowledge → evaluation) was revised by Anderson & Krathwohl (2001) to verb-form levels, each with a physiotherapy example:

  1. Remember — recall facts: list the six determinants of gait.
  2. Understand — explain concepts: explain the gate-control theory in your own words.
  3. Apply — use in new situations: apply the Fick equation to an exercise prescription.
  4. Analyse — decompose relationships: differentiate neuropathic from nociceptive pain patterns in a case.
  5. Evaluate — judge with criteria: appraise an RCT's methodological quality and decide whether to apply its result.
  6. Create — produce new work: design a 6-week rehabilitation protocol for a post-TKR patient.
Fig 10 — Bloom's pyramid (revised). Write a physiotherapy example next to each level — evaluators check for the examples, not just the ladder.

cWhy it matters in physiotherapy education

ILOs align teaching, assessment and content (constructive alignment — Biggs): a viva that only asks "define…" while the ILO promised "design a protocol" is a misalignment. Alongside Miller's pyramid (knows → knows how → shows → does), they shape competency-based education: the levels of Bloom map onto "knows/knows how", while clinical demonstration maps to "shows/does".

Two credit-earning moves: write one complete model ILO ("By the end of this session, the student will be able to demonstrate the modified Ober's test on a peer without prompting") and say "constructive alignment" with Bloom + Miller in the conclusion.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus, Paper I Unit 6 (a–c).
  2. Anderson LW, Krathwohl DR (eds). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing. 2001 (revision of Bloom 1956).
  3. Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Acad Med. 1990 (Miller's pyramid).
  4. Biggs J. Teaching for Quality Learning at University. (constructive alignment)
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper I — Practice, Pedagogy & Research

QP 8129 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Physiotherapy & EBP

  • Definition (World Physiotherapy): develop, maintain, restore maximum movement & function — primary-contact, autonomous, ICF-based.
  • EBP triad: best evidence + clinical expertise + patient values (Sackett); 5 steps: Ask (PICOT) → Acquire (PubMed, PEDro) → Appraise → Apply → Assess.
  • Hierarchy: SR/meta-analysis → RCT → cohort → case-control → cross-sectional → case series → opinion.

2Ethics

  • 4 principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice + World Physiotherapy standards + ICMR 2017.
  • Issues: informed consent, confidentiality, scope of practice, overtreatment, boundaries, documentation, equity, advertising.

3Pilot study

  • Tests the PROCESS (recruitment, protocol, instruments, drop-out, cost) — never the hypothesis; provides SD for sample size; don't pool its data.

4Sampling

  • SRS = equal independent chance (lottery/RNG). Stratified = SRS within strata (guarantees subgroups).
  • Cluster = random groups, all members. Systematic = every k-th after random start. Multi-stage = successive random stages.

5Qualitative research

  • Designs: phenomenology (lived experience), grounded theory (builds theory), ethnography (culture).
  • Purposive sampling → saturation (no new themes). Thematic analysis 6 phases (Braun & Clarke).
  • Trustworthiness: credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability (= internal/external validity, reliability, objectivity).

6Energy transfer

  • First law: energy only converted (food → work + heat); ATP ~7.3 kcal/mol; CP shuttle fastest.
  • Systems: ATP-PC 10 s → glycolysis ~2 min → oxidative (unlimited). Efficiency only 20–25%; 1 MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min.

7Weight control

  • Deficit 500–750 kcal/day → 0.5–1 kg/wk; goal 5–10% in 3–6 months.
  • FITT: 150 → 250–300 min/wk moderate aerobic + resistance 2–3 d/wk; Indian waist ≥90/80 cm = abdominal obesity.

8NMES instrumentation

  • Chain: power → oscillator (Hz, µs) → timer (on:off, ramp) → amplifier (mA) → charge-balanced biphasic output → electrodes.
  • Motor: 35–50 Hz, 200–400 µs, duty cycle 1:3–1:5; Russian = 2.5 kHz carrier, 50 bps; large electrode on motor point.

9SPADI psychometrics

  • 13 items (5 pain + 8 disability), each 0–10 → 0–100% (higher = worse).
  • Reliability ICC 0.84–0.94; α 0.86–0.98; MCID ≈ 8–10 points; Hindi/Kannada versions validated.

10ILOs & Bloom

  • ILO = pre-written, SMART, observable action verb ("demonstrate", not "understand").
  • Bloom (revised): remember → understand → apply → analyse → evaluate → create; Miller: knows → knows how → shows → does; constructive alignment (Biggs).
Keep-if-nothing-else: the EBP 5 steps, the 4 ethics principles, T-score-like trio of numbers (7.3 kcal/mol ATP; 500–750 kcal deficit; 1:3–1:5 duty cycle), and Bloom's six verbs in order. These four alone anchor 6 of 10 questions.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. What are the articulating structures in the musculoskeletal system? Explain in detail about them.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 1 — Basic Concepts of Musculoskeletal System (skeletal, articular, neuro-muscular systems)

How the evaluator distributes the 10 marks

Expected content in your scriptMarks
Introduction — the MSK system and its articulating components1
Bone: types, structure, functions, blood supply & healing note2
Cartilage — hyaline, fibro, elastic; properties1.5
Joint classification — fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial (with types & examples)3
Structure of a typical synovial joint (all components)2
Ligament–tendon–muscle unit + neat labelled diagram0.5
★ Memory hook — Joint classification anchor: what tissue unites the bones? Fibrous (suture, syndesmosis) — cartilaginous (synchondrosis = hyaline, symphysis = disc) — synovial (cavity + cartilage + capsule). The intervertebral disc is a symphysis.

aIntroduction

The musculoskeletal system is composed of articulations formed between bones, stabilised by connective tissue elements, and moved by the neuro-muscular unit. An articulation (joint) is defined as the site where two or more bones meet, whether movement occurs between them or not. Four families of structures participate in a joint: bone, cartilage, the fibrous capsule–ligament complex, and the muscular–tendinous unit, all supervised by the nervous system.

bBone — the primary articulating tissue

The adult skeleton has 206 bones, divided into the axial skeleton (80) and appendicular skeleton (126). Structurally: long, short, flat, irregular and sesamoid bones. A long bone bears an epiphysis covered by hyaline articular cartilage at each end, a metaphysis, and a diaphysis built of dense cortical bone enclosing medullary cavity.

  • Functions: protection, mineral (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻) reservoir, haemopoiesis, muscle attachment, and transmission of compressive forces — Wolff's law: bone remodels along lines of mechanical stress.
  • Composition: ~35% organic matrix (mainly type I collagen, osteoid) giving tensile strength, ~65% inorganic hydroxyapatite giving compressive rigidity.
  • Bone is vascular and innervated by periosteal nerves, so fracture pain is sharp and localised — unlike cartilage, which is aneural and avascular.

cCartilage — the bearing surface

  • Hyaline (articular) cartilage — covers the weight-bearing ends of bones in synovial joints; type II collagen; avascular, aneural, alymphatic; nourished by synovial fluid diffusion and cyclic loading ("use it or lose it" of chondrocytes). Low friction (~0.01 coefficient) and load distribution.
  • Fibrocartilage — dense type I collagen; forms labra (glenoid, acetabular), menisci of the knee, intervertebral discs and articular discs (TMJ); resists compression and shear.
  • Elastic cartilage — with elastin; ear, epiglottis (relevant to general articulating structure knowledge).

dJoint classification — the heart of the answer

1. Fibrous joints — bones united by fibrous tissue, minimal movement: sutures of the skull (synarthrosis), syndesmosis (inferior tibiofibular joint, interosseous membranes), and gomphosis (tooth in socket).

2. Cartilaginous joints — united by cartilage: synchondrosis (epiphyseal/growth plate, first costochondral — temporary, hyaline) and symphysis (pubic symphysis, intervertebral disc — permanent, fibrocartilage, slight movement).

3. Synovial (diarthrodial) joints — freely movable, the most important group clinically. By shape and axes:

TypeExampleAxes
Plane (gliding)Acromioclavicular, intercarpalNon-axial
HingeElbow (ulnohumeral), ankle, IP jointsUniaxial
PivotAtlanto-axial, superior radio-ulnarUniaxial (rotation)
Condyloid (ellipsoid)MCP, wristBiaxial
SaddleFirst CMC (thumb), sternoclavicularBiaxial
Ball-and-socketShoulder (glenohumeral), hipMultiaxial

eStructure of a typical synovial joint

  • Articular (hyaline) cartilage — 2–4 mm thick bearing surface.
  • Joint capsule — outer fibrous capsule (dense irregular CT) + inner synovial membrane which secretes synovial fluid (~1–3 mL in a knee), a dialysate of plasma plus hyaluronic acid; lubricates (boundary lubrication) and nourishes cartilage.
  • Ligaments — intrinsic thickenings of the capsule (e.g. glenohumeral ligaments) and extrinsic check-reins (e.g. coracohumeral); mainly type I collagen, mostly mechanoreceptors at insertions — the basis of reflex joint stabilisation.
  • Accessory structures — intra-articular fibrocartilaginous discs/menisci, labra that deepen sockets, bursae, and fat pads (Hoffa's) filling dead space.
Fig 1.1 — Typical synovial joint (sketch for your answer script). Draw this one; it earns the diagram credit.
Marks are lost when students write "206 bones and types of joints" as one blob. Keep the classification pyramid visible: fibrous → cartilaginous → synovial, then the six synovial subtypes WITH examples. Saying "hip is a hinge joint" in the table is an instant credibility loss — ball-and-socket.

★ Memory hook — Asian-Indian cut-offs: BMI 23 overweight, 25 obese; waist ≥90 cm (men) / ≥80 cm (women) = abdominal obesity.

aDefinition and calculation

BMI (Body Mass Index, formerly Quetelet's index) is an anthropometric index of weight-for-height used to classify individuals into body-size categories. It is the ratio of body mass to the square of height:

BMI = weight (kg) / height² (m²)

Worked example (an Indian clinic patient): a 58-year-old woman weighing 68 kg with height 1.55 m → BMI = 68 / (1.55 × 1.55) = 68 / 2.40 = 28.3 kg/m² → Class I obesity by Indian criteria. Measurement technique: wall-mounted stadiometer, shoes off, weight on a calibrated balance in minimal clothing.

bClassification

BMI (kg/m²)WHO categoryAsian-Indian consensus*
< 18.5Underweight< 18.0 underweight
18.5–24.9Normal18.0–22.9 normal
25–29.9Overweight23–24.9 overweight
30–34.9Obese class I≥ 25 obese
35–39.9Obese class II—
≥ 40Obese class III—

*Indians develop metabolic risk at lower BMI ("thin-fat Indian phenotype"); Indian consensus thresholds are stricter than WHO global cutoffs.

Fig 2.1 — The formula, boxed the way I sketch it in correction margin notes. The cm-vs-m slip is the commonest arithmetic error I see.

cApplications in degenerative conditions

  • Load on weight-bearing joints: each step transmits about 3–4 times body weight through the knee; every extra kilogram of fat multiplies tibiofemoral and patellofemoral load over thousands of steps per day → accelerated cartilage wear in knee osteoarthritis. Obesity is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for knee OA, particularly in women.
  • Obesity–inflammation link: adipose tissue is metabolically active — adipokines (leptin, adiponectin imbalance) act as a systemic inflammatory drive that worsens synovitis and pain in OA and chronic low-back degeneration.
  • Prognosis and management triage: BMI decides whether arthroplasty risk counselling (wound healing, infection, anaesthetic risk) is needed, and gates conservative versus surgical planning.
  • Physiotherapy prescription: high BMI modifies exercise selection — non/low-weight-bearing aerobic work (cycling, aqua therapy) early, treadmill jogging later; it also re-baselines the MET targets for endurance dosing.
  • Outcome prediction: weight reduction of ~10% with exercise gives clinically meaningful functional improvement and pain relief in overweight/obese knee-OA patients (IDEA trial evidence classically quoted in Indian theses on tibiofemoral OA).
  • Low BMI in the elderly: flags sarcopenia and fall/fracture risk, poor bone stock (osteoporosis screening) and poor postural endurance — degeneration is not only an overweight story.

dLimitations and conclusion

BMI cannot distinguish fat mass from lean mass (a stocky athlete is "obese" by BMI), says nothing about fat distribution (waist circumference / waist-hip ratio should be added for metabolic risk), and is unreliable in pregnancy, oedema and amputees. Used together with waist circumference and body-composition methods, it remains the fastest screening anthropometric tool in an Indian outpatient department.

Always write the Indian cutoffs — RGUHS evaluators love the Asian-Indian consensus values (23/25) alongside WHO's 25/30. And do the arithmetic: I award the "worked example" mark only when a real patient's numbers appear.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Role of power and endurance in training.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 5 — Physiological Basis of Human Movement (exercise metabolism, exercise capacity); Paper IV Unit 1 — impaired muscle performance

How the evaluator distributes the 10 marks

Expected content in your scriptMarks
Definitions: strength, power, endurance — with units and formula2.5
Physiological basis — fibre types, energy systems2
Role of power in training (principles + clinical application)2
Role of endurance in training (principles + clinical application)2
Interplay + training principles table/diagram + conclusion1.5

aDefinitions — get these exact

  • Strength — the ability of a muscle or muscle group to generate force against a resistance.
  • Power — the rate of doing work: Power = Work / Time = Force × Velocity (measured in watts). It has a force component AND a speed component — that is the whole secret of power training.
  • Endurance — the ability to sustain a physical activity (whole-body) or to perform repeated muscle contractions (muscle endurance) against a submaximal resistance for an extended time.
Fig 3.1 — Hill's force–velocity curve (blue) with the power curve (orange). Power peaks at roughly one-third of maximum shortening velocity — the reason a very heavy, very slow lift is NOT powerful.

bPhysiological basis

Muscle fibres: type I (slow oxidative — fatigue-resistant, mitochondria-rich → endurance machinery), type IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic — the hybrid, both force and endurance), type IIx (fast glycolytic — force and power, fatigable). Energy supply follows the task: ATP-PC (phosphagen) for seconds of explosive power, anaerobic glycolysis for ~2 minutes of high effort, and the oxidative (aerobic) system — the only sustainable one — for endurance. Motor-unit recruitment follows the size principle: small units first, large high-force units only when demand is high.

cRole of power in training

  • Functional demand is a power demand in real life — rising from a chair, stair ascent, a cricketer's bowling action, a sprinter's push-off. Loss of power (sarcopenia hits fast fibres hardest) explains why elderly patients fall during quick corrections of balance.
  • Training method: moderate loads moved as fast as possible (30–60% 1RM for upper, 0–60% for lower-body ballistic work (ACSM)), plyometrics — stretch-shortening cycle drills (box jumps, medicine-ball throws).
  • Adaptations: improved rate of force development, motor-unit firing frequency and synchronisation, elastic-tendon stiffness, and inter-muscular coordination — largely neural.
  • Clinical application in MSK rehab: late-stage ACL/arthroplasty return-to-sport criteria include hop tests — pure strength clearance is not enough; power plus landing mechanics decide safe return.

dRole of endurance in training

  • Endurance is the platform for recovery and repeated function — the postural muscles (trunk stabilisers, soleus) are endurance organs by design.
  • Training method: low load, high repetitions (muscle endurance: > 12–15 reps at < 60% 1RM) and continuous aerobic exercise (whole-body endurance: walking/cycling ≥ 20–30 min, target ~60–80% HR reserve for 150 min/week, ACSM).
  • Adaptations: increased mitochondrial density, capillary density, myoglobin, oxidative enzyme activity, improved lactate clearance; central adaptations — increased stroke volume and VO₂max, decreased resting HR, better autonomic balance.
  • Clinical application: endurance work counters fatigue-related compensations — e.g., the tired knee-OA patient who develops a vaulting gait at 200 m; endurance of the scapular stabilisers prevents late rotator-cuff overload.

eTheir interplay — what the examiner wants to see

Strength, power and endurance lie on one continuum of muscle performance, and both derive from a strength base: power = strength expressed fast, endurance = strength sustained. Prescription follows the SAID principle (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand) and overload; sequencing is strength → power → endurance integration within a periodised plan.

Two things separate a 6/10 from a 9/10 here: (1) writing the power formula with BOTH force and velocity — "power = strength × speed" in one line; (2) giving at least one Indian-context clinical example (chair-rise in the elderly, return-to-field after ACL reconstruction). Fibre types must be mentioned by name.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe about the oxygen supply during training in post-traumatic knee stiffness.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 5 — Physiological Basis of Human Movement (oxygen supply during exercise; physiology of movement in MSK injury and dysfunction)

How the evaluator distributes the 10 marks

Expected content in your scriptMarks
Oxygen transport chain — ventilation → diffusion → circulation → extraction3
Fick principle and exercise response (HR, SV, CO, a-vO₂ diff)2
Local muscle adaptations — capillary bed, arterioles, muscle pump2
Effect of trauma + immobilisation on oxidative capacity in the stiff knee2
Training implications + conclusion1
★ Memory hook — Write Fick and annotate: VO₂ = (HR × SV) × (a−v)O₂ — each term is one adaptation site of aerobic training.

aThe oxygen transport chain (must be drawn as a chain)

Oxygen travels from atmosphere to mitochondrion through four linked steps:

  1. Pulmonary ventilation — alveolar ventilation rises from ~6 L/min at rest to ~100+ L/min in maximal exercise (respiratory rate and tidal volume both climb).
  2. Diffusion across the alveolo-capillary membrane (driven by a PO₂ gradient of about 60 mmHg — alveolar PO₂ ~104 mmHg versus venous PO₂ ~40 mmHg at rest, widening during exercise as venous PO₂ falls).
  3. Circulatory transport — cardiac output rises from ~5 L/min to ~20–25 L/min in young adults; the Frank–Starling mechanism (increased venous return stretches the ventricle) plus sympathetic drive raise both stroke volume and heart rate.
  4. Peripheral extraction — the arterio-venous O₂ difference widens (from ~4–5 to ~15+ mL O₂/dL) as working muscle pulls oxygen out of blood.

Summed in the Fick equation: VO₂ = Cardiac Output × a-vO₂ difference — every training adaptation fits into one of its two terms.

Fig 4.1 — The oxygen transport chain with the Fick equation underneath. In viva, draw the four boxes and this equation first.

bLocal (muscle-level) oxygen supply during exercise

  • Arteriolar dilatation — local metabolites (CO₂, H⁺/lactate, adenosine, K⁺) relax arteriolar smooth muscle; muscle blood flow rises up to 15–20-fold, far beyond the ~4–5-fold rise in cardiac output, because flow is also redistributed from splanchnic and non-working beds.
  • Capillary recruitment and better perfusion — at rest some capillaries are closed; exercise opens the reserve, shortening diffusion distance.
  • The muscle pump — rhythmic contraction milks venous blood proximally, and the venous valves keep it one-way; this is why pain-free, active cyclical exercise beats passive work for stiff knees.
  • Oxygen extraction — myoglobin releases O₂ as PO₂ falls; the Bohr effect (acidosis shifts the Hb-dissociation curve right) unloads more O₂ exactly where it is needed.

cWhat happens in post-traumatic knee stiffness — the clinical core

Post-traumatic knee stiffness (after intra-/peri-articular fracture, multi-ligament injury, prolonged immobilisation) is associated with:

  • Disuse atrophy of quadriceps, preferentially type I (slow oxidative) fibres of vastus medialis obliquus and the anti-gravity extensors; decreased mitochondrial density and oxidative enzyme activity → early fatigability.
  • Reduced capillarisation and prolonged re-perfusion after ischaemic effort; intra-compartmental pressure from effusion and capsular tightening can further impede perfusion at low angles of knee flexion.
  • Pain inhibition (arthrogenous muscle inhibition) delays activation — recruitment of large motor units suffers, and the patient fatigues long before the target repetition range.

dTraining implications

  • Start early with pain-free cyclical, rhythmic activity (stationary cycling with seat raised, foot pumps, heel slides) to use the muscle pump without provoking reactive synovitis.
  • Isometrics in a pain-free arc sustain trophic tone — but sustained maximal isometrics occlude local blood flow; use rhythmic/brief-hold isometrics ("hold 6 s, breathe, repeat ×10) so oxygen delivery continues between holds.
  • Avoid the Valsalva manoeuvre — breath-holding against a closed glottis spikes blood pressure and reduces venous return; teach exhale-on-effort.
  • Progress toward aerobic conditioning (walk/cycle programmes at ~60% HR reserve) to rebuild the central oxygen-transport capacity that bed rest deconditioning erodes; add interval work only after reactive inflammation settles.
  • Warm-up literally raises tissue temperature and shifts the Hb curve rightward — a physiologic justification every answer should include.
This question is where pure physiology answers die: if you never write the words "post-traumatic knee stiffness" after page one, you lose the 4 application marks. Chain the physiology to the pathology in every paragraph. Fick equation = guaranteed half-mark.

Q5. Applied mechanics and pathomechanics following rotator cuff injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 6 — Mechanics and Pathomechanics of Joints (upper extremity joints, soft tissues)

How the evaluator distributes the 10 marks

Expected content in your scriptMarks
Applied anatomy of the cuff (SITS) + GH stability problem2
Normal applied mechanics — force couple, concavity compression, scapulohumeral rhythm3
Pathomechanics following cuff tear — head migration, impingement, rhythm breakdown3.5
Functional consequences + clinical note + diagram1.5
★ Memory hook — SITS = Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis. The cuff is the deltoid’s brake — depressor force couple keeping the head centred in the glenoid.

aApplied anatomy — why the shoulder needs the cuff at all

The glenohumeral (GH) joint sacrifices bony congruence for range of motion: the large humeral head sits on a small, shallow glenoid cavity (only about a third of the head is in contact at any position) deepened a little by the glenoid labrum. Static restraints (capsule, glenohumeral ligaments) are lax by design, so dynamic stability depends on the rotator cuff — supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis (SITS).

bNormal applied mechanics

  • Concavity compression: supraspinatus, and the cuff as a whole, compresses the humeral head into the concave glenoid — the primary mechanism keeping the head centred through mid-range, where ligaments are slack.
  • Transverse (force) couple: during abduction, the line of deltoid pull passes above the centre of the head and would translate the head upward; the inferiorly-directed pull of subscapularis (anterior) and infraspinatus + teres minor (posterior) depresses and centres the head. Cuff–deltoid balance converts deltoid's shear into pure rotation.
  • Scapulohumeral rhythm: ~2:1 ratio — for 180° of elevation, ~120° occurs at GH and ~60° at scapulothoracic (upward rotation by trapezius/serratus anterior), keeping the glenoid track facing the moving head and preserving the subacromial space.
  • Supraspinatus also contributes an initial abduction torque and, with the others, provides proprioceptive guarding — the reflex stiffening of the joint under load.
Fig 5.1 — The force couple in health and after a cuff tear. This two-panel sketch is exactly what a 10/10 script draws in the margin.

cPathomechanics following rotator cuff injury

  • Loss of concavity compression & depressor action → superior translation of the humeral head during elevation — the deltoid now pulls the head upward unopposed against the coraco-acromial arch.
  • Secondary subacromial impingement — the head, greater tuberosity and bursal tissue crowd the subacromial space, already narrowed in abduction–external rotation positions; repetitive micro-trauma → bursitis, tendinopathy, partial- then full-thickness tear (a self-perpetuating cycle).
  • Scapulohumeral rhythm breakdown — pain inhibits serratus anterior/lower trapezius, producing scapular dyskinesis (excessive scapular elevation, reduced upward rotation, dysrhythmia); the glenoid no longer follows the head, so GH elevation reduces and scapular substitution (shoulder shrug) appears.
  • Strength and function: painful arc and weak abduction/external rotation; night pain lying on the side is classical. In massive chronic tears the head may erode the acromion — cuff-tear arthropathy.
  • Glenohumeral arthrokinematics change: the normal spin of the head is replaced by an abnormal roll-and-slide, further jamming the head under the arch.

dClinical consequence in one line

The patient loses smooth overhead function and, untreated, enters the impingement–tear–weakness cycle; rehabilitation therefore restores the depressor/cuff–deltoid force couple and scapular control before loading power.

Name the muscles (SITS) and the two force-couple concepts (concavity compression + transverse force couple) by name. "Rotator cuff injury" scripts that only describe impingement pain never cross 6/10 — half the question is normal MECHANICS, don't skimp on it.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Define Posture. Explain the methods to control posture following IVDP.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 7 — Posture (normal/abnormal posture, control of posture, postural deformities); Paper IV Unit 3 — postural stability and core stability

How the evaluator distributes the 10 marks

Expected content in your scriptMarks
Definition of posture (classic + physiological)1.5
Normal postural control mechanism — sensory inputs, integration, outputs2.5
What IVDP changes — direction-specific disc mechanics2
Methods to control posture following IVDP (the core of the answer)3.5
Conclusion0.5
★ Memory hook — Posture control pair: TrA = corset, multifidus = segmental strings; feed-forward fires BEFORE the limb moves — delayed after LBP.

aDefinition

Posture is the relative alignment of body segments to one another and to gravity at any given moment — classically, "the position from which movement begins and ends." Ideal upright posture places the plumb line through the ear, shoulder, hip, knee and lateral malleolus, with the cervical and lumbar lordoses balanced by the thoracic and sacral kyphoses.

bNormal postural control (the machinery)

  • Sensory input: visual (eyes), vestibular (otoliths for static, semi-circular canals for dynamic), and somatosensory/proprioceptive input from joints, muscles and skin — the dominant input in healthy adults.
  • Central integration: spinal reflex arcs (stretch reflex for tone), brainstem (vestibulo- and rectospinal tracts), cerebellum (timing/smoothing), and cortical representation for anticipatory and voluntary corrections.
  • Motor output: tonic postural muscles and phasic mobilisers, plus anticipatory feed-forward postural adjustments — e.g., transversus abdominis fires before limb movement — and reactive strategies: ankle, hip and stepping strategies.

cWhat changes in IVDP

In intervertebral disc prolapse, a posterior/postero-lateral prolapse (the common direction) is aggravated by flexion + loading, which raises intradiscal pressure and pushes nuclear material backward toward the posterior annulus and nerve root — the basis of a peripheralising pain pattern. Patients adopt a shift/list, lose the lumbar lordosis and inhibit their deep stabilisers (transversus abdominis, multifidus) reflexively through pain. The goal of postural control is therefore to maintain the neutral spine — the position of least disc stress — and to abolish peripheralisation (McKenzie's centralisation principle).

dMethods to control posture following IVDP — the answer's centre of gravity

  1. Education and conscious correction: teaching neutral spine in sitting, standing and lifting; avoiding prolonged flexion, and combining flexion with rotation (the classic provocative couple) — use of a lumbar roll/cushion for chair sitting, knees and hips at 90°, feet supported; sitting-reclined alternative in the acute phase because a reclined posture lowers the load on the disc: Nachemson's classic intradiscal-pressure studies showed sitting slumped loads the L3–4 disc more than standing.
  2. Positioning and bed rest discipline: short-term rest in the most reducing posture (commonly prone extension or side-lying with pillow between knees); log-rolling technique to get in and out of bed; avoid early-morning unsupported sitting (disc is hydrated and turgid after overnight water imbition).
  3. Core stabilisation programme: re-training transversus abdominis drawing-in, multifidus activation, diaphragmatic breathing and pelvic floor co-activation — progressing from isolated activation to integrated functional positions (Hook-lying → quadruped → standing).
  4. Direction-specific exercise (McKenzie method): prone/supported extension to centralise symptoms when the derangement responds to extension; the sagittal-plane rule — movements that centralise pain are prescribed, those that peripheralise are avoided.
  5. Proprioceptive/balance retraining: wobble-board and unstable-surface work to restore somatosensory postural reflexes once pain settles.
  6. Ergonomics and ADL modification: workstation redesign, hip-hinge lifting with load close to body, micro-breaks every 30–40 min, and avoidance of prolonged postures of flexion.
  7. External support: a temporary lumbosacral corset as a proprioceptive reminder — never a substitute for the muscle corset.
  8. General conditioning: weight reduction, walking programme and thoracic mobility work to distribute stress across the whole spine.
Fig 6.1 — Neutral spine with the four balanced curves vs the flexed IVDP spine with posterior bulge and root irritation.
Two marking magnets: Nachemson's intradiscal pressure data (slumped sitting > upright sitting > standing) and centralisation vs peripheralisation. Also, "IVDP" must be expanded — "intervertebral disc prolapse" written once in full. Centralisation is McKenzie's single most examinable concept in this paper.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Define Gait. Describe the determinants of gait with examples.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 8 — Gait and function (gait cycle, biomechanical analysis of gait, energy expenditure and gait)

How the evaluator distributes the 10 marks

Expected content in your scriptMarks
Definition of gait + gait cycle in brief (stance/swing, 60:40)1.5
The problem: COM trajectory without determinants (why they exist)1.5
Six determinants — each with mechanism + value + example6
Energy-conservation conclusion + diagram1
★ Memory hook — Gait: stance 60 : swing 40; phases IC → LR → MSt → TSt → PSw | ISw → MSw → TSw; the six determinants exist to flatten the COM curve.

aDefinition

Gait is the manner or style of walking — the pattern of locomotion produced by the cyclic, coordinated movement of body segments. One gait cycle = heel strike of one foot to the next heel strike of the same foot: a stance phase (60%) and a swing phase (40%) — the two together spanning the eight phases of the cycle from initial contact through terminal swing (IC → LR → MSt → TSt → PSw | ISw → MSw → TSw).

bWhy determinants exist

If the legs were rigid struts and the pelvis fixed, the body's centre of mass would travel in a series of arcs as high as each leg length step-over, wasting enormous energy lifting and dropping the body ~7–8 cm twice each step. The six determinants of gait (Saunders, Inman & Eberhart) are the pelvic and lower-limb movements that flatten these arcs, cutting vertical COM displacement to about 5 cm (2 inch) and horizontal sway to ~2.5 cm — conserving energy.

cThe six determinants — with values and examples

  1. Pelvic rotation — the pelvis rotates ~4° forward on the swing side (total ~8°) in the transverse plane at initial contact. This lengthens the step and flattens the arc's base. Example: loss of rotation after hip fusion forces the patient to "square-off" and circumduct — gait looks stiff and costlier.
  2. Pelvic tilt (obliquity) — the pelvis drops ~4–5° on the swing side (controlled eccentrically by the stance-side hip abductors — gluteus medius), lowering the apex of the COM arc. Example: weakness of abductors (safe-side Trendelenburg pattern) produces an exaggerated drop and lateral lurch.
  3. Knee flexion in stance — after loading response the knee stays flexed ~15–18° until mid-stance; it shortens the stance limb exactly when the COM would otherwise be highest. Example: after knee fusion/arthrodesis the leg becomes a long lever and the patient vaults on the sound side to clear it.
  4. Foot and ankle mechanisms — from heel strike (ankle plantarflexed with the heel as rocker) to foot-flat, then the ankle rocker, then heel-off with the forefoot rocker: a smooth rolling radius instead of a point pivot. Example: ankle equinus/calcaneus deformity after trauma destroys the rockers and substitutes hip circumduction.
  5. Knee mechanisms — the knee's linked flexion with the ankle rockers at the start and end of stance: since the ankle plantarflexes while the knee flexes (and vice versa), the combined limb length stays nearly constant, again smoothing the COM path. Example: a stiff-knee gait (rectus femoris spasticity/post-op arthrofibrosis) produces compensatory hip-hiking in swing.
  6. Lateral pelvic displacement — the pelvis (and COM) shifts ~2.5 cm over the weight-bearing limb in the frontal plane, with a functional genu valgum at the knee keeping the COM near the supporting foot. Example: coxa vara or wide-based gait increases sway and the energy cost of walking.
Fig 7.1 — The red dashed line is the COM path without determinants (rigid struts); the green line is the real, flattened trajectory (~5 cm) that the six determinants buy us.

dConclusion

The six determinants therefore act as an energy-saving system: each one flattens part of the COM trajectory, and the reciprocal (pathological) gait deviations we treat in clinic — Trendelenburg lurch, circumduction, vaulting, hip hiking — are simply the loss of one or more determinants. Quantify them clinically with observant video/10-metre walk analysis; the underlying principle is minimisation of energy expenditure (a 10-mark answer must close on this sentence).

The word "Saunders/Inman" attached to the determinants earns credit; so does stating the purpose (flattening the COM arc → energy conservation). Most students list the six correctly and forget the VALUES (4°, 4–5°, 15–18°, ~2.5 cm) — those numbers are what distinguish a first-class script. Also write 60:40 stance-to-swing — even though it's "defining gait" territory.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Explain the various theories of pain in detail.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 9 — Pain (definition, pathways, physiology and pathophysiology; theories and models of pain)

How the evaluator distributes the 10 marks

Expected content in your scriptMarks
IASP definition + brief pain pathway (nociceptor → dorsal horn → spinothalamic)2
Specificity theory and intensity theory1.5
Pattern theory1.5
Gate control theory — full detail (Melzack & Wall)3
Neuromatrix theory + biopsychosocial conclusion + diagram2
★ Memory hook — Pain fibres: Aδ = fast & sharp (first pain), C = slow & dull (second pain). Gate theory: large-fibre input closes the gate on small-fibre traffic.

aDefinition and the pathway first

Pain, per the International Association for the Study of Pain, is "an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage." The pathway in one line: nociceptors → Aδ and C fibres → dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa) → decussation → lateral spinothalamic tract → thalamus → somatosensory cortex & limbic centres. Theories of pain explain how this raw signal becomes the experience we treat.

bSpecificity theory (von Frey, 1895)

Dedicated, hard-wired pain pathways exist: specialised nociceptors connect via dedicated fibres to a pain centre in the brain, exactly as vision has its own line. Strengths: correct about specialised receptors and labelled lines (Aδ sharp/first pain, C dull/second pain). Fails to explain: phantom limb pain, chronic pain without ongoing tissue damage, and pain modulation by emotion/attention.

cIntensity theory

An old proposal that pain is merely excessive stimulation of any sensory receptor — strong touch = pain. Largely of historical value; disproved because intense stimuli of non-nociceptive kind do not reliably produce pain.

dPattern theory (Goldscheider, 1890s; revived by Weddell and Sinclair in the 1950s)

Pain is not a special sense but a pattern of neural firing — intense, frequent, temporally-patterned discharge from any receptor is decoded centrally as pain. It introduced the crucial idea of central processing and temporal summation (the ancestor of wind-up and central sensitisation), but it underplayed the specificity of nociceptors.

eGate control theory (Melzack & Wall, 1965) — the exam's centre of gravity

A "gate" in the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa, lamina II) regulates transmission from peripheral afferents to transmission (T) cells that project up the spinothalamic tract:

  • Large-diameter Aβ (touch/mechanoreceptor) fibres excite the T cells but ALSO excite the substantia gelatinosa (SG) interneurons, which inhibit transmission → gate closes.
  • Small-diameter Aδ/C (nociceptive) fibres excite T cells and inhibit the SG interneurons → gate opens → pain ascends.
  • Central control: descending fibres from the brain (periaqueductal grey, raphe magnus — serotonergic/noradrenergic) can bias the gate — the physiology behind attention, anxiety, expectation and placebo changing pain.

Clinical applications physiotherapists use daily: TENS (large-fibre stimulation closing the gate), rubbing a knock, cognitive reassurance reducing descending facilitation. Limitation: pain is more than a spinal gate — no account of chronic plasticity or emotional colour, which the next theory supplies.

Fig 8.1 — Gate control theory (Melzack & Wall, 1965). Draw the gate as a shaded box in substantia gelatinosa with Aβ closing and Aδ/C opening it.

fNeuromatrix theory (Melzack, 1999) and the biopsychosocial close

Phantom limb pain in people without peripheral input forced the next leap: the brain contains a body-self neuromatrix — a widespread network (somatosensory, limbic, thalamic, parietal) that continuously generates the experience of the body. Pain is the output of this matrix shaped by sensory, cognitive-evaluative and emotional-motivational dimensions — the neuroscientific scaffold of the biopsychosocial model we now use for chronic MSK pain, and the justification for pain neuroscience education, graded activity and cognitive-behavioural methods (which sit in RGUHS Paper IV, Unit 2c).

Conclusion: each theory is partly right — specificity gave us nociceptors, pattern gave us central processing, gate control gave us modulation (and TENS), and the neuromatrix gives us the modern biopsychosocial treatment of persistent pain.

Dates earn easy marks: von Frey 1895, Melzack & Wall 1965, Melzack's neuromatrix 1999. Then link each theory to one physiotherapy intervention — TENS for gate control, graded exposure/pain education for neuromatrix. A theory answer with no clinical link stays an essay, not a physiotherapy answer.
