Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Write the biophysical effects of heat on various systems in the body.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 10 — Electro Physics (biophysical effects of heat and cold; clinical decision making in electro-modalities)

How the evaluator distributes the 10 marks

Expected content in your scriptMarks
Physics of heat transfer (conduction, convection, radiation, conversion) + superficial vs deep2
Local thermal response — metabolism, blood flow, capillary permeability2.5
Systemic effects — cardiovascular, neuromuscular, skin3
Therapeutic applications, precautions/contraindications + diagram2.5
★ Memory hook — Heat rule: stretch while hot, hold while cooling — that is what makes the collagen gain permanent.

aPhysics first

Therapeutic heat reaches tissue by four modes: conduction (hot packs, paraffin wax — direct contact), convection (hydrotherapy, fluidotherapy — moving medium), radiation (infrared lamp), and conversion (ultrasound, shortwave diathermy, microwave — energy converted to heat within tissue). Superficial agents heat skin and subcutaneous tissue to ~1 cm; deep heating (ultrasound, SWD) reaches muscle-joint depths. Local tissue temperature is the product of energy delivered, tissue depth and perfusion — the physiotherapist's dose, not the machine's dial, decides it.

bBiophysical effects — tissue by tissue

Metabolic: tissue metabolism rises roughly 10–13% per 1 °C increase (van 't Hoff/Arrhenius-type Q₁₀ effect) — the basic biophysical justification of every heating agent. Heat applied in the inflammatory proliferative phase (after ~48 h) supports repair by raising metabolic and enzymatic activity.

1. Skin and subcutaneous tissue: cutaneous vasodilatation (heat-sensitive cutaneous receptors → sympathetic vasoconstrictor withdrawal), erythema, sweating, increased capillary permeability (mild oedema risk if overdone), and softening of scar/collagen.

2. Cardiovascular system: local vasodilatation increases blood flow (up to several-fold) with its fresh oxygen, leukocytes and nutrients — accelerating removal of pain-metabolites (bradykinin, substance P). With generalised heating, heart rate and cardiac output rise, peripheral resistance falls, and blood pressure may drop — hence cardiac patients need caution with large-area heating.

3. Neuromuscular system: peripheral nerve conduction velocity changes — heat increases it in sensory nerves; combined with reduced muscle-spindle and Golgi tendon organ discharge, muscle spindle excitability falls → decreased muscle spasm/guarding and reduced tone in spastic or painful muscle guarding; sedative comfort effect on sensory endings. Pain relief operates via the gate-control mechanism (heat input through Aβ afferents closing the dorsal-horn gate) and by direct counter-irritant effects.

4. Connective tissue: increased collagen extensibility — the crucial effect in MSK physiotherapy: collagenous structures (capsule, tendon, ligament, scar) are best mobilised/stretched while heated, and the gain is maintained only if stretch is held during cooling.

5. Joint and synovium: decreased joint stiffness (reduced viscosity of synovial fluid gels — the waxy stiffness of a cooled joint melts with heat), improved articular cartilage nutrition via cyclic perfusion, and pain relief in chronic degenerative arthritis.

6. Haematological/immune: increased capillary exchange supports the delivery of antibodies and phagocytes to the heated region — supportive to tissue healing.

Fig 9.1 — The four-quadrant effect map of heat I sketch on the whiteboard before viva: perfusion, metabolism, spasm/pain, extensibility.

cApplications and precautions (the exam-safe finish)

  • Applications in MSK: pain and spasm relief before stretching a contracted joint (post-traumatic stiffness, frozen shoulder), subacute/chronic low-back pain, tendinopathy (deep heat), delayed-onset muscle soreness, and before manual therapy/mobilisation.
  • Precautions: over acute inflammation/bleeding, malignancy, ischaemic tissue, insensitive skin, acute injury < 48 h, and large-area heating in cardiac patients; never over the gravid abdomen or testes; caution with metal implants (SWD conversion).
Answers that describe each modality's technique get no marks here — the question asks BIOPHYSICAL EFFECTS on SYSTEMS. Write under the headings skin / cardiovascular / neuromuscular / connective tissue / joint, and anchor with the Q₁₀ metabolic rule. Mentioning that heat must be combined with stretch to make extensibility permanent is the final distinction between 8 and 10.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Explain the pathomechanics following TA rupture.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II, Unit 6 — Mechanics and Pathomechanics of Joints (lower extremity joints, soft tissues); Unit 8 — pathological gait

How the evaluator distributes the 10 marks

Expected content in your scriptMarks
Applied anatomy & normal mechanics — Achilles tendon, triceps surae, push-off3
Mechanism of rupture + phase affected1.5
Pathomechanics at the ankle — torque, ROM, eccentrics2.5
Pathomechanics of gait — push-off loss + compensations2.5
Rehabilitation significance + diagram0.5

aNormal mechanics — what the TA (tendo-Achilles) does

The triceps surae (gastrocnemius + soleus) converges into the tendo-Achilles, the thickest, strongest tendon in the body (withstands ~4000 N in walking), inserting on the calcaneal tuberosity. As the prime plantarflexor, it:

  • generates the propulsive push-off (terminal stance–pre-swing) — the A2 plantarflexor-knee power burst that vaults the body over the stance foot;
  • works eccentrically after heel strike to control tibial advancement (ankle dorsiflexion) — the soleus is postural, active through most of stance;
  • contributes to the windlass mechanism and shock absorption through mid-stance, and to venous return via the calf pump.
Fig 10.1 — The calcaneal lever with the Achilles pull intact vs retracted after rupture. Redraw with the arrow of the calf's force literally "cut".

bMechanism of rupture

Typical injury is in the 30–50-year-old "weekend athlete": a sudden, violent eccentric contraction on a dorsiflexing ankle — landing from a jump or push-off burst — often in a degenerated, hypovascular mid-tendon (watershed 2–6 cm above insertion). Patients report being "hit in the calf by a stone". Thompson's test (Simmonds') is positive: absent ankle plantarflexion on calf squeeze.

cPathomechanics at the ankle

  • Loss of plantarflexion torque: the calf's force is not transmitted to the calcaneus → plantarflexion strength is profoundly reduced and isolated plantarflexion is performed only by the long toe flexors, peroneals, tibialis posterior and plantaris (if present).
  • Loss of eccentric control: after initial contact the unrestrained tibia advances on the talus, so dorsiflexion is excessive and uncontrolled — the foot slaps into a flatter loading pattern.
  • Heel-cord insufficiency: the calcaneus loses its posterior tether and rides slightly anteriorly/proximally; if treated non-operatively with a gap, the tendon heals elongated → permanent weakness; with malalignment the calcaneus assumes a more vertical position because the plantarflexor pull line is lost (the "calcaneus-type" deformity in chronic neglected rupture).
  • Arch and shock absorption: diminished triceps surae contribution to the longitudinal arch mechanism alters mid-foot load sharing, increasing forefoot and medial-arch stress.

dPathomechanics of gait — the examiner's favourite part

  • Absent push-off / flat-foot gait: no heel rise, no terminal-stance plantarflexion power (loss of the A2 burst) — the affected step is shorter, with reduced or absent ankle plantarflexion at pre-swing.
  • Compensatory pattern: hip flexion and hip-hiking with a shorter contralateral step; the patient "walks through" the limb rather than over it; often an ipsilateral trunk lean and early hip-extensor substitution — the classic shift of propulsion from ankle to hip strategy.
  • Stance-phase effects: decreased terminal stance ankle plantarflexion moment, excessive dorsiflexion, reduced knee-extension moment → genu recurvatum avoidance patterns and increased demand on knee extensors; walking speed and cadence drop, and energy cost per metre rises (losing a gait determinant-like mechanism).
  • Functional losses: inability to do a single-limb heel raise, difficulty with stairs, running and jumping; altered venous return (calf-pump loss) → distal oedema risk.

eRehabilitation significance

Pathomechanics dictates protocol: protect (equinus cast/orthosis in plantarflexion, functional bracing allows early controlled tensioning), then progressively restore soleus–gastrocnemius eccentric strength, calf-pump conditioning, and finally push-off power and plyometrics before return to sport.

Structure this answer exactly as mechanics → rupture mechanics → ankle-level pathomechanics → gait-level pathomechanics. Two high-yield phrases that always draw the evaluator's pen: "loss of push-off with hip-flexor compensation" and "positive Thompson's test". Say which gait phase is destroyed: terminal stance–pre-swing.

Last-Hour Revision

The 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Articulating structures

  • Joint = site where two or more bones meet; components: bone, cartilage, capsule–ligament, musculotendinous, nerve.
  • Fibrous joints = suture / syndesmosis / gomphosis; cartilaginous = synchondrosis / symphysis; synovial = plane, hinge, pivot, condyloid, saddle, ball-and-socket.
  • Articular cartilage: hyaline, avascular, aneural, type II collagen, nourished by synovial fluid + cyclic loading.
  • Bone: 206 = 80 axial + 126 appendicular; 35% collagen (tension) / 65% hydroxyapatite (compression); Wolff's law.

2BMI

  • BMI = kg/m²; WHO: 18.5–24.9 normal, 25–29.9 overweight, ≥30 obese; Indian: 23 overweight, ≥25 obese.
  • Knee load ≈ 3–4× body weight per step; each kg matters; 10% weight loss → meaningful OA improvement.
  • Limitations: no fat-mass vs lean-mass, no fat distribution → add waist circumference.

3Power & endurance

  • Power = force × velocity = work/time (watts); peaks at ~⅓ max velocity; endurance = force sustained.
  • Type I = oxidative endurance; IIa = hybrid; IIx = power. ATP-PC (sec) → glycolysis (~2 min) → oxidative (hours).
  • Power training: 30–60% 1RM fast + plyometrics (SSC). Endurance: >12 reps < 60% 1RM + 150 min/wk aerobic.

4Oxygen supply in stiff-knee training

  • Chain: ventilation → diffusion → CO (5→20–25 L/min) → extraction (a-vO₂ 4→15 mL/dL).
  • VO₂ = CO × a-vO₂ diff (Fick). Muscle pump + arteriolar dilatation + capillary recruitment.
  • Immobilisation: type-I fibre atrophy, ↓mitochondria, ↓capillaries → fatigue early. Rhythmic isometrics, no Valsalva, exhale on effort.

5Rotator cuff

  • Glenoid covers only ~⅓ of head → dynamic stability: cuff compresses head into glenoid (concavity compression).
  • Transverse couple: subscapularis + ISP/TM depress head vs deltoid's upward shear; rhythm 2:1 (120° GH : 60° scapular).
  • Tear → superior migration → subacromial impingement → scapular dyskinesis → shrug substitution; chronic = cuff-tear arthropathy.

6Posture & IVDP

  • Posture = alignment of body segments relative to each other & gravity; "position from which movement begins and ends."
  • Inputs: visual + vestibular + somatosensory; outputs: ankle/hip/stepping strategies + feed-forward TrA.
  • IVDP: flexion+load worsens posterior prolapse → neutral spine, log-roll, McKenzie extension (centralise!), core stabilisation, lumbar roll, hip-hinge, temporary corset.

7Gait determinants

  • Stance 60% : swing 40%; 8 phases; determinants (Saunders/Inman): pelvic rotation 4°, pelvic tilt 4–5°, stance knee flexion 15–18°, foot–ankle rockers, knee mechanisms, lateral displacement 2.5 cm.
  • All flatten COM path to ~5 cm → energy conservation. Pathological gait = lost determinant.

8Pain theories

  • Specificity (von Frey 1895) — dedicated lines; Intensity — pain = excess stimulus; Pattern (Goldscheider) — firing pattern decoded centrally.
  • Gate control (Melzack & Wall 1965): SG gate in dorsal horn; Aβ closes, Aδ/C opens; descending control → TENS logic.
  • Neuromatrix (Melzack 1999): pain = output of body-self network → biopsychosocial model, pain neuroscience education.

9Heat effects

  • Modes: conduction / convection / radiation / conversion; superficial ~1 cm vs deep (US, SWD).
  • Q₁₀: ~10–13% ↑metabolism per °C; skin vasodilatation; CV: ↑flow, ↑HR if generalised; nerve: ↓spasm, ↓spindle excitability, gate-based analgesia; collagen: ↑extensibility (stretch while hot!); joint: ↓stiffness.
  • Never: acute inflammation, bleeding, ischaemia, malignancy, insensate skin, <48 h injury.

10TA rupture

  • Triceps surae → strongest tendon (~4000 N); push-off in terminal stance + eccentric control after heel strike.
  • Rupture: eccentric load on degenerated mid-tendon; Thompson's test positive.
  • Pathomechanics: no plantarflexion torque → flat-foot gait, absent heel rise, no A2 push-off burst, hip-flexor/hip-hike compensation, short step, calf-pump loss, chronic = calcaneus-type foot.
If you retain nothing else: Fick equation, gate control with dates, six determinants with values, force couple, Indian BMI cutoffs, Thompson's test. These six alone appear across three questions every year.
Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the role of assessment in diagnosis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 1 — Introduction to assessment; basic assessment methods; physical assessment as a screening tool; Unit 6a — functional assessment

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Concept: assessment vs diagnosis; PT diagnosis2
Components of assessment (subjective → objective)2.5
Hypothesis-oriented diagnostic process2.5
ICF framework + outcome measures & decision-making3

aConcept

Assessment is the systematic collection of data about a patient's status; diagnosis is the label drawn from interpreting that data. In physiotherapy, assessment culminates in a physiotherapy (movement-system) diagnosis — a cluster of signs and symptoms identifying the dysfunction the therapist is qualified to treat (e.g., "subacromial impingement with scapular dyskinesis"), distinct from, but always linked to, the medical diagnosis.

bComponents

  • Subjective (history): demographic data, chief complaint (ONSET-location-duration-aggravating/easing factors), pain behaviour (24-hour pattern), functional limitations, past history, medications, red/yellow-flag screening — this alone steers 80% of the hypothesis list.
  • Objective examination: observation (posture, deformity, gait), palpation, active/passive/physiological and accessory ROM (PPIVMs, PAIVMs), strength (MMT), joint mobility and special tests, neuro screening (dermatomes, myotomes, DTRs), and functional measures.

cHypothesis-oriented process

Good assessment is not a checklist but a hypothetico-deductive cycle: generate competing hypotheses from the history, design examination tests to confirm or refute each, and commit to the working diagnosis — reassess after each treatment to confirm the reasoning (Jones & Rivett's clinical-reasoning model).

dICF and decision-making

Findings are mapped to the ICF: body structure/function (restricted flexion, weak abductors), activity (can't squat) and participation (can't work as a farmer) — this defines both treatment targets and outcome measures for reassessment. Assessment thus (i) establishes a baseline, (ii) enables differential diagnosis and red-flag screening for referral, (iii) guides treatment selection, (iv) measures change, and (v) provides the legal/professional documentation of autonomous practice.

Fig 1 — The hypothesis-oriented clinical cycle with the treat-and-reassess loop. The single sketch that shows an examiner you assess like a postgraduate, not a checklist operator.
Aim to present the answer as a PROCESS (history → hypotheses → tests → diagnosis → reassessment), not a list of tests. Examiners award the reasoning marks when the words "hypothesis" and "differential" appear and are actually used.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe the screening of neck following C3-C4 disc prolapse.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2a — Screening the Head, Neck and Back

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
History & observation2
Palpation, ROM & segmental mobility2.5
Neurological screening (C4 root)2.5
Special tests2
Red flags & conclusion1
★ Memory hook — Myotome ladder: C5 abduct, C6 wrist extend, C7 elbow extend, C8 finger flex, T1 finger abduct; Spurling (compression) pairs with distraction (relief).

aHistory & observation

C3–C4 prolapse typically compresses the C4 nerve root: pain in the suboccipital/neck region radiating to the shoulder cap and clavicular area (C4 dermatome — a "high-collar" distribution, with C3 giving occipital/sub-occipital referral). Ask onset, trauma, posture/occupation (prolonged laptop flexion), night pain, and screen red flags: myelopathy signs (gait change, hand clumsiness, bowel/bladder), fever, weight loss, trauma.

bPalpation, ROM & mobility

  • Observation: forward head posture, loss of cervical lordosis, antalgic tilt.
  • Palpation: paraspinal muscle spasm/guarding, segmental tenderness at C3–C4 level, upper trapezius trigger points.
  • ROM: flexion/extension, side-flexion, rotation — painful arcs, capsular vs non-capsular pattern; extension combined with ipsilateral rotation reproduces radicular symptoms in the affected dermatome.
  • Segmental mobility: central and unilateral posterior-anterior glides (PAIVMs) at C3–C4 for stiffness vs pain response; intersegmental movement testing (PPIVMs).

cNeurological screen — the C4 root

Myotome C4: scapular elevation (shoulder shrug) and diaphragm (C3–C5 — "C3,4,5 keep the diaphragm alive"); test resisted shrug. Reflex: no pure C4 DTR — biceps jerk (C5) and brachioradialis (C6) are tested to exclude adjacent-root involvement. Sensation: pinprick/light touch over the neck, clavicle and upper shoulder cap. Complete the screen of the upper limb for a broader deficit pattern.

dSpecial tests

Spurling's test (extension + ipsilateral rotation + axial compression — radicular reproduction), cervical distraction test (relief is confirmatory), shoulder-abduction (bakery) relief sign, ULNT/neurodynamic testing for mechanosensitivity, Hoffman's test for myelopathy, and quadriceps/Babinski if cord signs are suspected.

eClose

Integrate findings into a working PT diagnosis and baseline (NDI — Neck Disability Index), referring urgently for MRI if myelopathy or red flags appear.

Fig 2 — The C3–C4 'high-collar' dermatome map with myotome, reflex and special-test annotations parked beside it. The whole answer's neurological screen in one drawing.
The examiner's trap: writing a generic neck exam. Anchor EVERY neurological line to C3/C4 — dermatome map, shrug myotome, "no C4 reflex — test C5/C6 adjacent." That specificity is what separates 8+/10 from 5/10.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 2a.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier (reference 4) — cervical spine chapter.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1)

On the evaluation form — Q2: Cervical disc prolapse C3-C4 with C4 radiculopathy

I. Subjective examination

Female, 34 years, desk worker. Chief complaint: neck pain radiating to the outer shoulder and upper scapular region for 6 weeks, with associated tingling over the shoulder cap. Symptom analysis — site: lower cervical/parascapular region, referring to the lateral neck and mid-deltoid (C4 dermatome); onset: gradual, after long hours at a computer; duration: 6 weeks; type: deep ache with sharp shooting pain into the shoulder; severity: NPRS 6/10. Aggravating factors: neck extension, side-flexion toward the painful side, prolonged static postures, coughing and sneezing. Relieving factors: rest, a supported shoulder, hand-behind-head posture. Red-flag screen negative (no trauma, fever, weight loss, gait change or bladder involvement). Vitals recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Forward head posture, protracted rounded shoulders and protective elevation of the shoulder girdle; no wasting or scars.

On palpation. Tenderness over the C3-C4 facet region and the paraspinals; increased deep-tissue tension (hypertonicity) of the upper trapezius and levator scapulae; no crepitus or swelling.

1. Motor assessment. AROM: cervical extension and rotation to the affected side reduced to about half range; PROM shows the same limitation with a muscle-spasm end-feel. Resisted isometrics of neck side-flexion reproduce the scapular pain. MMT (MRC 0-5): shoulder shrug (upper trapezius, C4) 4/5 on the affected side; shoulder abduction (C5), wrist extension (C6), triceps (C7) and finger flexion (C8) 5/5. Reflexes: biceps, brachioradialis, triceps and lower-limb reflexes normal. Arm girth symmetrical.

2. Sensory assessment. Dermatomes: diminished light touch and pinprick over the C4 dermatome (lateral neck, clavicular area, mid-deltoid); C2-T1 screen otherwise intact. Myotomes: C4 weakness as above; no upper motor neurone signs.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Sitting tolerance limited to 20-30 minutes; overhead reach and driving affected. Outcome measures: Neck Disability Index (NDI, 0-50) baseline items scored; NPRS 0-10; PSFS 0-10 for reading, desk work and sleeping; cervical ROM by goniometry.

4. Gait analysis. Gait normal.

5. Balance. No balance deficit.

6. Hand function. Overhead reaching and driving affected; hand-behind-head posture used for symptom relief.

7. Coordination. No upper motor neurone signs on the neurological screen.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Spurling's testExtend and side-flex the neck to the symptomatic side, then apply axial compressionReproduction of radicular shoulder painForaminal compression of the C4 nerve root — positive in this patient
Cervical distractionSupine; cradle the occiput and distract the headReduction of radicular painConfirms a compressive origin of symptoms — positive in this patient (relief with distraction)
Shoulder abduction (Bakody) testPatient rests the hand on top of the headRelief of radicular painReduces tension on the compressed nerve root — positive in this patient (relief in the hand-behind-head posture)
Upper limb neurodynamic test 1Shoulder abduction, elbow extension, forearm supination, wrist/finger extension, neck side-flexion awaySymptom reproduction with an inter-side difference of about 10°Mechanosensitivity of the brachial plexus/nerve root — positive in this patient
Hoffmann's signFlick the tip of the relaxed middle fingerReflex thumb and finger flexionMyelopathy screen, refer if positive — negative in this patient (no upper motor neurone signs)
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Neck and radicular pain
  • Reduced cervical ROM
  • C4 dermatomal sensory change
  • Paraspinal (upper trapezius and levator scapulae) spasm

Functional limitations

  • Reduced sitting tolerance
  • Limited overhead activity

Disabilities

  • Unable to sustain full-time desk work
11. Functional diagnosis

Cervical disc prolapse at C3-C4 with C4 nerve-root compression, causing radicular pain, reduced cervical ROM, C4 dermatomal sensory change and paraspinal muscle spasm, limiting sitting tolerance and overhead activity and preventing full-time desk work.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): reduce pain from 6/10 to 3/10 on NPRS; gain 25% more painless cervical rotation; sleep through the night.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): full-time desk tolerance with hourly posture breaks; full painless AROM; NDI reduced by at least 10 points.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1-2): intermittent cervical traction, cryotherapy/TENS, pain-free gentle ROM. Stage 2: manual therapy and mobilisation as tolerated, scapular stabilisation, craniocervical (deep neck flexor) training, posture and workstation ergonomics.

14. Home programme

Chin tucks, shoulder-blade setting, posture diary, activity pacing.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe the screening of upper back for fibromyalgia.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2 (b, e) — Screening the shoulder/upper extremity and chest; musculoskeletal screening

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition & diagnostic criteria (ACR 1990/2010/2016)2.5
History & observation1.5
Tender-point palpation (9 paired sites — 4 upper-trunk)3
Extramuscular screen & differentials2
Documentation & conclusion1
★ Memory hook — Fibromyalgia numbers: ACR 1990 — 18 sites, 4 kg pressure, ≥11 needed; ACR 2016 — WPI + SSS, no palpation. Trigger point = taut band (local); tender point = systemic (central sensitisation).

aWhat you are diagnosing

Fibromyalgia: chronic widespread pain (axial + bilateral, above and below waist) for >3 months, with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms. ACR 1990: ≥11 of 18 tender points on ~4 kg thumb pressure. ACR 2010/2016 revision: Widespread Pain Index (0–19) + Symptom Severity Scale — criteria now usable without a tender-point count; both are worth quoting.

bScreening the upper back

  • History: female predominance (7:1), ages 30–50; pain "all over" and migrating; sleep disturbance, morning stiffness >30 min, irritable bowel/bladder, mood symptoms; absence of mechanical relieving postures.
  • Observation: often normal posture but "hurting everywhere" on light touch; guarded, protective posturing.
  • Palpation of the 9 paired sites (4 in/around the upper trunk): suboccipital muscle insertions; low-cervical (C5–C7) interspinous ligaments; mid-upper trapezius; supraspinatus at the medial scapular border. Complete the set with 2nd rib costochondral junctions, lateral epicondyles, gluteal and greater-trochanteric sites — thumb pressure ≈4 kg, positive when the patient winces ("jump sign").
  • ROM & chest: thoracic mobility, chest expansion (normal ≥5 cm; markedly restricted suggests ankylosing spondylitis, not fibromyalgia), scapulothoracic rhythm.

cDifferentials & associated screen

Distinguish myofascial trigger points (local, taut band, reproducible referral — fibromyalgia points are systemic tender points with no taut band), hypothyroidism, polymyalgia rheumatica (age >50, raised ESR), inflammatory arthritis and cervical/thoracic spondylosis. Screen for central sensitisation features (allodynia to light touch), and quantify with the FIQR (Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire) and pain diagram.

dConclusion

Document a body map of positive sites, score FIQR for baseline, and coordinate a multidisciplinary plan — education, graded aerobic exercise, sleep and stress management — since physiotherapy is a cornerstone of fibromyalgia management.

Fig 3 — Tender-point map: upper-body sites in red; complete the 9 pairs with 2nd rib, lateral epicondyle, gluteal and trochanteric sites (blue) to reach the ACR 1990 count of 18.
State BOTH criteria sets (1990 tender-point count AND 2010 WPI + SSS) — this shows current knowledge, and quoting 4 kg thumb pressure is the practical detail examiners remember.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 2.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4).
  3. Wolfe F et al. The American College of Rheumatology 1990 / 2010/2016 criteria for fibromyalgia. Arthritis Rheum / Semin Arthritis Rheum. (primary)
  4. McCarty DJ, Koopman WJ. Arthritis and Allied Conditions. (syllabus reference 11).

On the evaluation form — Q3: Fibromyalgia (upper back screening)

I. Subjective examination

Female, 42 years. Chief complaint: widespread aching pain, worst in the neck and upper back, for over 3 years — above and below the waist, bilateral and axial (Widespread Pain definition met). Past medical history: prior investigations normal; no inflammatory joint disease. Symptom analysis — site: widespread, worst in the neck and upper back; duration: over 3 years; type: aching with morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes; severity: average NPRS 7/10. Aggravating factors: poor sleep, physical or emotional stress, cold weather. Relieving factors: warmth, rest. Associated features: fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, poor concentration ("fibro fog"), tension headaches and irritable bowel symptoms. Vitals and BMI recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Guarded round-shouldered posture; no swelling, deformity or wasting; gait mildly slowed by pain.

On palpation. The 1990 ACR tender-point sites examined with about 4 kg of thumb-pad pressure — bilateral suboccipital insertions, low cervical (C5-C7 anterior), mid-upper trapezius, supraspinatus above the scapular spine, second costochondral junctions, lateral epicondyles, greater trochanters and medial knee fat pads; control sites (mid-forehead, mid-deltoid, thumbnail) non-tender, indicating widespread allodynia rather than local pathology.

1. Motor assessment. AROM/PROM of the cervical spine, thoracic spine and shoulders full but slow and painful; no capsular end-feel. MMT: give-way (breakaway) weakness on sustained effort rather than a true deficit. Resisted isometrics of the upper trapezius reproduce the upper-back pain. Reflexes and girth symmetrical.

2. Sensory assessment. No dermatomal loss; hyperaesthesia and allodynia to light touch and clothing over the upper back; peripheral nerve screen normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Reduced activity tolerance with pacing difficulty; a two-week activity pacing diary issued to identify boom-bust cycles. Outcome measures: Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ-R) for the overall impact of fibromyalgia on function and symptoms; WPI and SSS as below; NPRS 0-10; PSFS 0-10 for sleep, walking and household work; six-minute walk test for aerobic capacity; timed 30-second sit-to-stand.

4. Gait analysis. Gait mildly slowed by pain; gait speed recorded.

5. Balance. Not formally documented at this assessment.

6. Hand function. Not formally documented at this assessment.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Prior investigations as per the medical records were normal, with no evidence of inflammatory joint disease; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
ACR 1990 tender point countDigitally palpate the 18 defined sites with about 4 kg pressurePain reported at 11 or more of 18 sitesClassifies widespread hyperalgesia — the defined sites were tender on palpation in this patient (exact count not documented)
Widespread Pain Index (WPI)Patient marks painful areas on a body chart (19 zones)WPI ≥7 with SSS ≥5 (or WPI 4-6 with SSS ≥9), symptoms ≥3 monthsSupports fibromyalgia (2010/2016 criteria) — the Widespread Pain definition is met in this patient
Symptom Severity Scale (SSS)Rate fatigue, waking unrefreshed, cognitive and somatic symptomsScore 5 or moreCombined with WPI confirms fibromyalgia — corresponding symptoms present in this patient (score not documented)
Control-site palpationPalpate non-tender control sitesTenderness at control sites tooGeneralised allodynia, not local pathology — control sites were non-tender in this patient
Beighton scoreScore 9 joint hypermobility manoeuvres4 or more in adultsScreens associated joint hypermobility — result not documented in this patient
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Widespread pain
  • Allodynia
  • Fatigue
  • Unrefreshing sleep

Functional limitations

  • Reduced activity tolerance
  • Pacing difficulty

Disabilities

  • Household and occupational roles disrupted
11. Functional diagnosis

Fibromyalgia syndrome with widespread pain, allodynia, fatigue and unrefreshing sleep, reducing activity tolerance and disrupting household and occupational roles.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): reduce average pain by 1 point on NPRS; establish a paced 10-minute walk twice daily.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): graded aerobic progression to 30 minutes of brisk walking most days; better sleep quality; return to family and occupational routines using pacing.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: education on central sensitisation, sleep hygiene, pacing diary. Stage 2: graded aerobic training (walking, cycling, warm-water pool exercise) and gentle stretching of the upper back and neck. Stage 3: light progressive resistance training, relaxation and breathing retraining; physician co-management and cognitive-behavioural therapy referral.

14. Home programme

10-minute walking bouts, stretch breaks at work, fixed sleep-wake timings.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe the importance of direct access in Physiotherapy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 3 — Direct access and self-referral; primary care; autonomous practice; decision making

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition & concept1.5
Importance — patient, profession, system (5 points)4.5
Global & Indian scenario2
Responsibilities & safeguards2

aDefinition

Direct access means patients may seek physiotherapy assessment and treatment without a physician's referral — the physiotherapist acts as a first-contact, autonomous practitioner within a primary-care musculoskeletal service (patient self-referral being the operational form).

bWhy it matters

  • Earlier treatment: no waiting for referral — early intervention in acute LBP/ankle sprain improves outcomes and prevents chronicity.
  • Cost-effectiveness: studies (US military, UK NHS self-referral pilots) show fewer physician visits, imaging and medication without worse outcomes.
  • Professional autonomy: recognises the physiotherapist's competence to diagnose within scope, screen for red flags and refer appropriately — the foundation of the "doctor of physiotherapy" and primary-spine-care models.
  • Patient choice & satisfaction: shorter care pathways, fewer consultations, better access in underserved areas.
  • System decongestion: frees physician time for complex disease; in India, addresses the specialist-burden crisis.

cScenario

Direct access is legal in 50+ US states, the UK, Australia, Netherlands and much of the EU. In India it remains partial: some states' practice and the IAP support autonomous practice, but referral culture, insurance rules and the Clinical Establishments Act implementation vary — an evolving frontier for the profession.

dThe responsibilities it imposes

First-contact practitioners must be competent in differential diagnosis and red-flag screening (cancer, fracture, infection, visceral referral), maintain strict referral criteria, indemnity insurance, meticulous documentation and continuing competency — autonomy is earned by clinical rigour, not demanded.

Fig 4 — The two-lane access comparison. Drawing the slow lane and the fast lane makes the importance argument visually before you write a word of it.
Balance is the scoring key: importance for patient + profession + health system (three angles), then the safeguard paragraph. An answer that only celebrates autonomy and never mentions red-flag screening reads as naive to an examiner.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 3 (a–d).
  2. World Physiotherapy (2011/2019) policy statement — Description of physiotherapy / direct access and patient self-referral.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. A 30-year-old female comes with a history of ankle injury. Describe the various special tests for the ankle.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4b — Special tests used in musculoskeletal examination

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
History, grading & why each test is chosen1.5
Lateral ligament tests (anterior drawer, talar tilt)3.5
Syndesmosis tests2
Other tests (deltoid, Ottawa rules)2
Conclusion & outcome measures1
★ Memory hook — Ankle ligament tests: plantarflexion → ATFL (drawer), 90° → CFL (talar tilt); syndesmosis trio = Squeeze, Kleiger, Cotton.

aSetting the scene

A 30-year-old woman with an inversion injury most likely sprains the lateral ligament complex — anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) first, then calcaneofibular (CFL), rarely posterior talofibular (PTFL). Grade I (stretch), II (partial), III (complete). Acutely effusion and pain limit testing — examinations are more reliable at day 4–5.

bLateral ligament tests

  • Anterior drawer — for ATFL integrity: patient prone/supine, foot relaxed in ~10–15° plantarflexion, one hand stabilises the tibia while the other draws the talus forward on the fibula; >4–5 mm anterior translation (or a clunk/soft end-feel) suggests ATFL rupture.
  • Talar-tilt (inversion stress) — for CFL: foot at 90°, invert the talus in the mortise; compare sides — >5–10° asymmetry or soft end-feel indicates CFL injury.
  • Squeeze test at the mid-calf and cross-over pain help localise ligament territory.

cSyndesmosis tests

  • Calf/squeeze test — compress the fibula against the tibia at mid-calf; distal syndesmotic pain is positive.
  • External rotation (Kleiger) test — stabilise the leg, dorsiflex + externally rotate the foot — syndesmotic and deltoid pain.
  • Cotton (fibular translation) test — anteroposterior fibular glide; and the point-toe (plantarflex–external rotation) test.

dOthers that complete the screen

  • Deltoid ligament (eversion stress) — medial pain/valgus laxity; implies possible syndesmosis/fracture.
  • Ottawa ankle rules (not laxity but fracture triage): X-ray if pain over malleolar zone plus bone tenderness over posterior edge/tip, or inability to bear weight 4 steps.
  • Thompson/Simmonds test for an intact Achilles, anterior impingement test, and peroneal-tendon subluxation screen complete the ankle work-up.
Fig 5 — Lateral ligament complex and the anterior drawer. Draw the ATFL/CFL pair and mark the drawer arrow — the two sketches the evaluator expects side by side.

eConclusion

Cluster the tests by structure (lateral ligaments → syndesmosis → medial → tendon/fracture screen), grade the sprain, and baseline the patient with the FAAM/Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool.

Position details separate grades: drawer in 10–15° plantarflexion for ATFL, 90° for CFL in talar tilt. Mentioning that acute-day testing is unreliable (test day 4–5) is a hallmark of clinical sense.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 4b.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — ankle & foot chapter.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1) — ankle biomechanics.
  4. Stiell IG et al. Ottawa ankle rules. JAMA. 1993 (primary, for triage).

On the evaluation form — Q5: Acute lateral ankle sprain (30-year-old female)

I. Subjective examination

Female, 30 years, badminton player. Chief complaint: left ankle pain and swelling. Symptom analysis — site: left lateral ankle; onset: 2 days ago, sudden inversion injury on landing, felt a "pop" over the outer ankle; duration: 2 days; type: sharp lateral ankle pain; severity: NPRS 7/10 at rest, 9/10 on stairs. Aggravating factors: weight bearing, stairs, uneven ground. Relieving factors: ice, elevation, rest. History: able to bear weight to the chair immediately after the injury (recorded for the Ottawa ankle rules); no previous sprain. Vitals recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Anterolateral swelling with ecchymosis spreading to the lateral foot; antalgic gait; unable to hop on the left; limb held in slight plantarflexion-eversion for comfort; no deformity.

On palpation. Marked tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament and mild tenderness over the calcaneofibular ligament; no tenderness over the malleoli, navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal (Ottawa ankle rules negative for radiography); mild warmth; no crepitus.

1. Motor assessment. AROM: plantarflexion and inversion limited and painful; dorsiflexion and eversion near full. PROM shows the same pattern with a pain-limited end-feel. MMT: eversion (peronei) 3/5 due to pain; other motions 4/5. Resisted isometric inversion painful. Figure-of-eight girth 2 cm more on the left. Reflexes and myotomes (L4-S1) normal.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact over the sural and superficial peroneal territories; distal pulses and capillary refill normal; no paraesthesia.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Stair descent needs support; currently off play and unable to commute normally. Outcome measures: Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) for foot and ankle function in daily living and sport; LEFS (0-80); NPRS 0-10; girth by figure-of-eight tape.

4. Gait analysis. Antalgic gait with reduced stance time on the left.

5. Balance. Single-leg stance held for 5 seconds only; unable to hop on the left (dynamic balance impaired).

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this lower-limb case.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Radiography not indicated — the Ottawa ankle rules were negative (no bony tenderness at the malleoli, navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal, and the patient could bear weight immediately after injury); no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Anterior drawer testStabilise the tibia, grasp the heel with the ankle in 20° plantarflexion, glide the talus anteriorlyExcessive anterior translation of the talusAnterior talofibular ligament laxity — result not documented at this acute (2-day) presentation
Talar tilt testAnkle in neutral; invert the talus on the tibiaExcessive lateral tilt or a soft end-feelCalcaneofibular ligament laxity — result not documented at this acute presentation
Squeeze testCompress the fibula against the tibia at mid-calfPain over the anterior tibiofibular areaSyndesmotic (high ankle) injury — result not documented in this patient
External rotation (Kleiger) testStabilise the tibia, externally rotate the foot with the knee at 90°Pain over the syndesmosisSyndesmosis disruption — result not documented in this patient
Thompson testProne; squeeze the calf muscleAbsent ankle plantarflexionAchilles tendon rupture — performed as a rule-out; no rupture signs recorded in this patient
Tinel's test at fibular neckPercuss over the fibular neckTingling along the lateral leg/dorsumCommon peroneal nerve involvement — negative in this patient (sensation intact, no paraesthesia)
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Pain
  • Swelling
  • Restricted AROM
  • Weak peronei
  • Impaired single-leg balance

Functional limitations

  • Altered gait
  • Stair difficulty

Disabilities

  • Off play
  • Unable to manage daily commuting
11. Functional diagnosis

Acute left lateral ankle sprain (inversion injury) with anterolateral pain, swelling, restricted and painful ankle ROM, peroneal weakness and impaired single-leg balance, producing an antalgic gait and stair difficulty and currently preventing sport and daily commuting.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): pain from 7/10 to 3/10; swelling reduced by 1 cm on figure-of-eight measurement; full pain-free AROM; normal-speed independent gait.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): single-leg stance for 30 seconds; peroneal strength 5/5; return to badminton drills with LEFS within 10 points of the pre-injury score.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (days 1-7): protection, relative rest, ice, compression, elevation, isometric peroneal sets. Stage 2 (weeks 1-3): graded AROM in all planes, stationary cycling, eversion strengthening with a band, wobble-board and single-leg balance. Stage 3 (weeks 4+): proprioceptive and agility drills, lateral movements, sport-specific rehabilitation, taping/bracing for return to play.

14. Home programme

RICE schedule, alphabet tracing with the foot, band exercises, balance progressions.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Write in detail about the various investigations used for osteoporosis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4d — Investigation methods / diagnostic imaging in musculoskeletal disease

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
DEXA — technique, T-score & Z-score3.5
FRAX & risk assessment1.5
Other imaging (X-ray, QCT, QUS)2
Laboratory work-up & markers2
Conclusion / role of PT1
★ Memory hook — T-score ladder: above −1 normal · −1 to −2.4 osteopenia · ≤−2.5 osteoporosis; a fragility fracture upgrades to severe. DEXA sites: L1–L4 + hip.

aDEXA — the gold standard

Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry measures areal bone mineral density (g/cm²) at the lumbar spine (L1–L4) and proximal femur with minimal radiation (~1/10 of a chest X-ray). Results as T-score (comparison with young-adult mean, WHO cutoffs in postmenopausal women & men ≥50: ≥ −1 normal; −1 to −2.4 osteopenia; ≤ −2.5 osteoporosis; with fragility fracture = severe osteoporosis) and Z-score (age-matched; ≤ −2 = "below expected for age" in premenopausal women/younger men).

bFracture-risk algorithms

FRAX computes 10-year probability of major osteoporotic and hip fracture from BMD plus clinical risk factors (age, sex, BMI, prior fracture, parent hip fracture, smoking, glucocorticoids, rheumatoid arthritis, alcohol, secondary causes) — treatment thresholds (e.g., hip-probability ≥3% in Indian guidelines adapt WHO/NOF cut-points) are FRAX-based, not BMD alone.

cOther imaging

  • Plain radiographs — show complications (vertebral compression, cortical thinning, trabecular rarefaction) only after 30–40% bone loss; vertebral fracture assessment morphometry.
  • Quantitative CT — true volumetric BMD, sensitive but higher dose; pQCT for peripheral sites.
  • Quantitative ultrasound (heel) — radiation-free screening (SOS/BUA), not for diagnosis.
  • MRI/bone scan — for occult fracture, malignancy differentiation.

dLaboratory work-up

To exclude secondary causes and mark turnover: serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D, PTH, TSH, renal/liver profile; in men testosterone; markers of resorption (serum/urine CTx) and formation (P1NP) for monitoring therapy.

Fig 6 — The T-score ruler. One glance, three zones — draw it exactly like this in the exam.
Three numbers decide the grade band: the cutoffs −1 / −2.5, the ~30–40% X-ray invisibility threshold, and "BMD is a risk factor, FRAX converts it into fracture probability." No answer gets full marks without DEXA sites (L1–L4 + hip).

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 4d.
  2. McKinnis LN. Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging. FA Davis (reference 8).
  3. Greenspan A, Beltran J. Orthopaedic Imaging: A Practical Approach. (reference 9).
  4. WHO Technical Report / Kanis JA. FRAX — Assessment of osteoporotic fracture risk (primary).

On the evaluation form — Q6: Postmenopausal osteoporosis work-up

I. Subjective examination

Female, 58 years, 8 years post-menopause. Chief complaint: intermittent mid-thoracic back pain for 1 year, with two severe episodes after lifting, and a documented height loss of about 4 cm. Risk-factor review: early menopause, thin build, low dietary calcium, sedentary lifestyle, no steroid use, mother had a hip fracture. No previous fracture. Red-flag screen negative (no fever, weight loss or features of malignancy). Severity: NPRS 4/10 at baseline. Vitals recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Increased thoracic kyphosis with a developing Dowager's hump; reduced rib-pelvis distance; standing height reduced versus young-adult height; mild increase in occiput-to-wall distance; slow gait with short steps.

On palpation. Mid-thoracic paraspinal tenderness and spasm; no step-off or radicular signs.

1. Motor assessment. Thoracolumbar AROM limited by pain in extension and rotation; PROM with a pain-limited end-feel. MMT: back extensors 4/5; hip abductors and knee extensors 4/5. Timed Loaded Standing and sit-to-stand performance reduced for age. Reflexes normal.

2. Sensory assessment. Dermatomes intact; peripheral neuropathy screen negative; no saddle anaesthesia.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Independence in household mobility and transfers documented; reduced lifting, bending and walking tolerance. Outcome measures: TUG and gait speed for fall risk; Berg Balance Scale (0-56) if balance is impaired; functional reach; 30-second sit-to-stand; QUALEFFO-41 questionnaire for quality of life in vertebral osteoporosis; serial height measurement; NPRS 0-10 and PSFS 0-10.

4. Gait analysis. Slow gait with short steps; gait speed recorded for fall risk.

5. Balance. Reduced balance; fall risk screened with TUG, functional reach and the Berg Balance Scale (0-56) as above.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this case.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations
  • Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA): low-radiation scan of the lumbar spine and proximal femur; a T-score of ≤ -2.5 confirms osteoporosis, and -1 to -2.5 indicates low bone mass.
  • Vertebral fracture assessment / lateral spine radiograph: lateral image of the thoracolumbar spine; a wedge or compression deformity indicates a prevalent vertebral fracture — the strongest predictor of future fracture.
  • FRAX tool: country, age, BMI and clinical risk factors entered, with or without femoral-neck BMD; a high 10-year major osteoporotic/hip fracture probability guides pharmacological treatment decisions.
  • Serum 25-hydroxy vitamin D (fasting blood sample): deficiency per the laboratory reference is a correctable secondary cause of bone loss and myopathy.
  • Bone turnover markers: serum CTX (resorption) and P1NP (formation); values above the premenopausal reference indicate high turnover and are mainly used to monitor therapy.
  • Secondary-cause panel: serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, TSH, CBC, ESR/CRP and renal function, screening for hyperparathyroidism, thyroid disease, malignancy and other secondary causes.
9. Special tests

No musculoskeletal special tests are documented for this case; the diagnostic work-up for this patient (DXA, vertebral fracture assessment, FRAX and the laboratory panel) is detailed under Investigations above.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Low bone density with kyphosis
  • Thoracic pain
  • Weak back extensors
  • Reduced balance

Functional limitations

  • Reduced lifting, bending and walking tolerance

Disabilities

  • Fear of falls with activity restriction and social withdrawal
11. Functional diagnosis

Postmenopausal osteoporosis with thoracic kyphosis, back-extensor weakness and reduced balance, limiting lifting, bending and walking tolerance and leading to fear of falls, activity restriction and social withdrawal.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): pain 2/10 or less; independent, safe home programme; family-involved fall-risk reduction plan.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): back and leg strength to 5/5; balance retrained to age norms; 30 minutes of daily walking; adherence to calcium, vitamin D and prescribed anti-resorptive therapy with follow-up DXA.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: pain relief with electrotherapy/heat, posture care, avoidance of loaded spinal flexion and high-impact activity. Stage 2: site-specific loading — prone back extension, progressive resisted hip and knee work with cuffs/bands, weight-bearing walking. Stage 3: balance and fall-prevention training, home-hazard modification, nutrition counselling, medication education, and annual height and DXA follow-up with the physician.

14. Home programme

Prone back extensions, resisted hip and knee exercises with cuffs/bands, weight-bearing walking, balance and fall-prevention exercises, and home-hazard modification as trained.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Write in detail about the postoperative assessment following supracondylar fracture of elbow.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5a — Assessment of fractures (pre- & post-operative)

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
General post-op framework & fracture overview1.5
Neurovascular & compartment assessment2.5
ROM, angles & radiological union2.5
Strength, function & complications3
Conclusion0.5
★ Memory hook — Supracondylar alarm: the 5 Ps + pain on passive finger extension = compartment syndrome — the earliest sign. NEVER force extension (myositis ossificans); Baumann angle ≈ 75–80°.

aContext

Supracondylar humerus fracture (Gartland I–III) is the commonest elbow fracture of children (fall on outstretched hand); displaced types are treated by closed/open reduction and K-wire fixation, cast 3–4 weeks. Post-op assessment begins the day after surgery.

bNeurovascular — the first priority

  • Vascular: radial pulse, capillary refill, colour/temperature of the hand — brachial-artery injury/kinking threatens the limb; watch for Volkmann's ischaemic contracture — the 5 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis), especially pain on passive finger extension.
  • Neural: test anterior interosseous (median — OK sign), main median, radial (wrist/thumb extension) and ulnar nerves — all are at risk from both injury and K-wires.
  • Compartment syndrome screen: tense forearm, pain out of proportion.

cLocal, ROM & radiology

  • Wound/pin sites — discharge, infection; cast/splint condition.
  • ROM elbow flexion–extension, pronation–supination once the cast is off (expect stiffness; grade objectively by goniometer).
  • Carrying angle — normal valgus ~11° in men, ~13° in women (Dutton: 11–14° / 13–16°); loss = cubitus varus ("gunstock", the classic malunion). Baumann's angle on radiograph (humeral capitellar angle, ~75–80°; a falling value warns of varus) plus callus formation define union progression.

dStrength, function, complications

MMT of elbow/forearm/wrist musculature once pain allows; circumference for atrophy; functional tasks (writing, feeding); outcome instruments (QuickDASH, pediatric PROMIS). Hunt for complications: pin-tract infection, myositis ossificans (calcification anteriorly — avoid forceful passive stretching!), stiffness, malunion (varus), nerve palsy, growth disturbance.

eConclusion

Assessment findings set the rehabilitation stage — early gentle active motion, no forced passive stretching, progressive strengthening — re-assessed every visit against a documented baseline.

Fig 7 — The post-op elbow sketch: K-wires in place, the carrying angle marked, and the 5-P compartment-syndrome box beside it — the safety half of the answer in one glance.
The sentence that earns the safety mark: "NEVER force passive extension in a post-supracondylar elbow — myositis ossificans." Examiners invariably probe it in viva.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 5a.
  2. Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL. Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures. (reference 16).
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — elbow chapter.
  4. Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13).

On the evaluation form — Q7: Post-operative supracondylar humerus fracture (child, K-wires)

I. Subjective examination

Boy, 7 years, right-hand dominant. Chief complaint: stiff left elbow. History: fall on an outstretched hand 5 weeks ago; displaced (Gartland III) supracondylar fracture treated with closed reduction and percutaneous K-wiring; above-elbow cast and K-wires removed 1 week ago. The mother reports that the child holds the arm close and prefers the right hand for writing and eating. Pain evaluation: faces scale 3/10 on movement, none at rest. Red-flag screen: no night pain, fever or fresh trauma.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Healed pin-site scars on the lateral elbow; mild loss of left upper-arm bulk; limb carried in a guarded, slightly flexed attitude; carrying angle compared with the right.

On palpation. Mild scar tenderness with mobile scar tissue; no warmth, swelling or palpable bony mass over the distal triceps (myositis ossificans screen).

1. Motor assessment. AROM: elbow flexion 40-100° with a 40° extension lag; pronation-supination about half range. PROM: flexion to 110° with a firm end-feel; extension limited by a capsular feel. MMT (MRC 0-5): elbow flexors and extensors 4/5; wrist and hand muscles 5/5. Girth: left arm 1.5 cm less than the right at mid-arm. Reflexes (biceps, brachioradialis, triceps) present and symmetrical; no limb-length discrepancy.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact in the median, radial and ulnar territories; anterior interosseous nerve screen (tip-to-tip pinch, OK circle) normal; no Tinel's over the scar; hand vascular status normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Left-arm use in age-appropriate tasks — writing, eating, dressing and play — recorded, with school participation restrictions documented on the ICF-CY framework. Outcome measures: goniometric ROM (flexion-extension, pronation-supination); MRC grades 0-5; girth; Pediatric Outcomes Data Collection Instrument (PODCI) for paediatric function and participation.

4. Gait analysis. Gait unaffected.

5. Balance. Not affected in this upper-limb case.

6. Hand function. The child holds the left arm close and prefers the right hand for writing and eating; reaching, grasping and releasing with the left during age-appropriate tasks is reduced.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Follow-up radiographs per the orthopaedic records, including Baumann's angle (the angle between the capitellar physis and the long axis of the humerus on X-ray; deviation from the normal side by more than about 5° predicts the final carrying angle); no current films reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Carrying angle measurementGoniometry with the elbow extended and forearm supinated, compared side-to-sideLoss of valgus or a varus angle versus the normal sideCubitus varus malunion, the commonest late deformity — compared with the right side; deviation not documented in this patient
Anterior interosseous nerve screenAsk the child to make an OK circle or pick up a small coin with tip-to-tip pinchUnable to flex the thumb IP and index DIP jointsAIN palsy associated with supracondylar fracture — negative in this patient (screen normal)
Tinel's over pin sitesPercuss along the scar and pin-site tracksReproducible tingling in a nerve territoryNeuroma or nerve irritation — negative in this patient (no Tinel's over the scar)
Palpation for myositis ossificansPalpate the distal triceps and anterior elbow for a firm massFirm, tender bony lumpMyositis ossificans limiting extension, avoid forceful stretching — negative in this patient (no palpable bony mass)
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Elbow ROM restriction
  • Mild weakness
  • Disuse atrophy

Functional limitations

  • Difficulty writing, dressing and playing

Disabilities

  • Reduced school participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Post-operative left supracondylar humerus fracture (Gartland III, treated by closed reduction and percutaneous K-wiring, wires removed 1 week ago) with elbow ROM restriction, mild weakness and disuse atrophy, limiting writing, dressing, play and school participation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): flexion to 120° with an extension lag of 20°; painless self-care with the left arm.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): elbow arc of 0-130°; pronation-supination within 10° of the right side; symmetrical carrying angle; full school and play participation.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1-2 after wire removal): active and active-assisted exercises, gravity-eliminated flexion-extension in side-lying, pronation-supination with a bat or rolling pin; no passive stretching. Stage 2 (weeks 3-6): strengthening with putty, light weight-bearing through the arm, play-based reach activities. Stage 3: graded return to sports.

14. Home programme

10 repetitions of each movement 3-4 times daily as a game; hot packs before exercise; weekly girth and ROM checks; parents counselled to avoid forceful stretching (myositis ossificans risk); orthopaedic follow-up for the carrying angle.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe in detail the assessment following below-knee amputation.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5d — Assessment of amputations; Unit 6 — functional assessment

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Residual-limb assessment3
Musculoskeletal status (ROM/strength)1.5
Prosthetic & gait assessment2
Functional scales & mobility2
Psychosocial & pain assessment1.5
★ Memory hook — Ideal stump: gently cylindrical, firm, healed, volume-stable by 3–6 months, scar mobile, soft-tissue pad over bone. Assess with AMP / LCI-5 for mobility prediction.

aResidual limb

Residual-limb shape (ideal: firm — cylindrical for total-surface-bearing sockets, conical for traditional patellar-tendon-bearing — matured by 3–6 months post-op), skin (scars, grafts, moisture, breakdown over bony points), wound healing, adherent vs mobile scar, sensation (hyper-sensitivity, neuroma — Tinel's), oedema/volume fluctuation (circumferential measurements; test socks), limb length and soft-tissue padding over the bone end.

bMusculoskeletal

Hip and knee ROM — flexion contracture of the knee is the enemy of prosthetic gait (even 10° matters); strength of hip flexors/extensors, abductors, quadriceps and hamstrings (MMT); knee stability; upper-limb strength (crutch/transfer readiness) and trunk control/balance.

cPain & prosthetic/gait

  • Pain: differentiate phantom-limb pain (painful sensations in the absent foot) from residual-limb pain (neuroma, bone spur, socket pressure) and back pain.
  • Prosthesis: socket fit (pistoning, pressure marks, redness that doesn't fade in 10–15 min), suspension, alignment in standing and walking; component condition (foot category, SACH etc.).
  • Gait: observe for vaulting, circumduction, lateral trunk bending, knee instability and unequal step length — each names a fitting or weakness problem.

dFunctional assessment

Standardised instruments: Amputee Mobility Predictor (AMP) (with/without prosthesis), Locomotor Capabilities Index-5, Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire, 2-minute/6-minute walk test, TUG, and the SIGAM mobility grades; K-levels (0–4) classify mobility potential. Also energy expenditure (O₂ cost of amputee gait is higher — relevant to rehab planning).

ePsychosocial

Body image, depression screening, motivation, family support, occupation and financial access to prosthetic services — decisive in the Indian setting for prosthetic success.

Fig 8 — The below-knee stump sketch with the full assessment checklist beside it. Draw the limb, label six points, then list what each label tells you.
Structure wins: residual limb → proximal joints → prosthesis → gait → scales → psychosocial. Name-dropping AMP or LCI-5 with one-line purpose lifts a generic answer into the top band; "differentiate phantom pain from residual-limb pain" is the viva's pet question.

Sources

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Units 5d & 6.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10) — amputation chapters.
  3. Chui KC et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation. (reference 18).
  4. Gailey RS et al. Amputee Mobility Predictor. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. (primary)

On the evaluation form — Q8: Below-knee (transtibial) amputation assessment

I. Subjective examination

Man, 55 years. Chief complaint: right residual-limb pain with phantom sensations. History: right transtibial amputation 6 weeks ago after a road-traffic crush injury; stump healed and sutures removed. Pain evaluation distinguishes residual-limb pain (stump) from phantom limb pain (shooting foot pain, 4/10, worse at night) and from non-painful phantom sensation. Risk factors: smoker, borderline diabetic. Personal and social history: mobility by hop transfers and walker use at home. Goal: shop-floor work with a prosthesis. Vitals recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Residual-limb shape (conical versus cylindrical — of prosthetic relevance), well-healed scar, skin colour, oedema and redundant distal tissue; sound limb inspected for vascular and trophic changes; hop-to gait with a walker.

On palpation. Distal tenderness, scar mobility, tissue tone at the stump end (firm distal padding is needed for weight bearing), tibial and fibular ends not prominent, neuroma tenderness; pulses in the sound limb.

1. Motor assessment. AROM/PROM: knee flexion-extension full with a normal end-feel (no flexion contracture); hip motions full. MMT (MRC 0-5): right hip flexors, abductors and extensors 4/5; stump knee extensors/flexors 4/5; sound limb 5/5. Stump girth measured circumferentially at fixed intervals from the tibial tuberosity for shrinkage charting, with stump length recorded.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation over the residual limb with hypersensitivity at the scar; Semmes-Weinstein 10-g monofilament testing of protective sensation on the sound foot; sound-limb dermatomes and myotomes intact.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Medicare Functional Classification Levels (K0-K4) assigned; transfers and bed mobility; hop and walker distance; stairs. Outcome measures: Amputee Mobility Predictor (AMP) for prosthetic mobility potential; Locomotor Capabilities Index for walking capabilities with the prosthesis; Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire for satisfaction and quality of life; 6-minute walk test and TUG; stump-pain and phantom-pain NPRS 0-10.

4. Gait analysis. Hop-to gait with a walker at home; once prosthesis is fitted, stump weight bearing and gait parameters (velocity, cadence, step length) to be assessed.

5. Balance. Standing balance on the sound limb; further balance testing not documented at this pre-prosthetic stage.

6. Hand function. Upper-limb use required for walker handling (assistive device); no hand dysfunction recorded.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

No imaging or laboratory investigations reviewed at this assessment; stump-healing status as per the surgical records.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Distal Tinel's testPercuss along the scar and distal tibial/fibular nerve tractsReproducible electric tingling into the phantom footNeuroma at the nerve ending, refer if painful — neuroma tenderness present on palpation in this patient
Knee flexion contracture assessmentSupine; heel on the plinth, attempt full knee extensionExtension lag with a firm end-feelContracture will impair prosthetic alignment and gait — negative in this patient (full extension with a normal end-feel)
Thomas testSupine; one hip flexed to flatten the lumbar spine, test the other hipLack of full hip extensionHip flexion contracture affecting prosthetic stance — negative in this patient (hip motions full)
Prone hip extension (gluteal) testProne; lift the limb into extension against gravity/resistanceWeak extension with trunk substitutionWeak hip extensors/abductors, predicting a Trendelenburg prosthetic gait — positive for weakness in this patient (hip extensors 4/5)
Stump maturity assessmentSerial circumferential girth, volume and skin checksContinued shrinkage over weeksDetermines readiness for the definitive socket — serial charting initiated; stump not yet mature at 6 weeks post-amputation
10-g monofilament (sound foot)Apply the filament to plantar sitesFailure to feel at any siteLoss of protective sensation in the remaining limb — testing performed; result not documented
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Phantom and residual-limb pain
  • Hip-muscle weakness
  • Stump oedema/immaturity
  • Sound-limb overload risk

Functional limitations

  • Mobility dependent without a prosthesis

Disabilities

  • Unable to resume work and community ambulation
11. Functional diagnosis

Right transtibial amputation 6 weeks post-operative, with residual-limb and phantom pain, hip-muscle weakness and an immature, oedematous stump, causing mobility dependence without a prosthesis and preventing return to work and community ambulation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): independent hop transfers; phantom pain 2/10 or less; elastic stump-wrapping regime established; hip and knee strength 5/5.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): mature stump for a definitive prosthesis; independent prosthetic gait without aids on level ground; 6-minute walk distance consistent with community ambulation; return to work.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (pre-prosthetic): elastic stump wrapping or shrinker sock, desensitisation (towel rubbing, textured materials), mirror therapy and TENS for phantom pain, graded hip/knee strengthening, sound-limb conditioning and stump skin-care education. Stage 2 (prosthetic training): stump weight tolerance, donning/doffing, standing balance, then gait training from parallel bars to level ground, ramps and stairs, with falls training.

14. Home programme

Bandaging, daily stump and sound-foot inspection, strengthening sets, graded walking.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe various outcome measures used for shoulder pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 6 (b, c) — Functional assessment scales; selection of outcome measures

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Selection principles (ICF levels, psychometrics)1.5
Body-function measures (ROM, strength)2.5
Region- & condition-specific self-reports (SPADI, DASH, ASES, Constant, UCLA…)3.5
Interpretation (MCID, tracking)1.5
Conclusion1

aChoosing measures

Select by ICF level (impairment / activity / participation), region vs condition specificity, psychometric quality in the target population, and responsiveness with a known MCID.

bBody structure & function

  • ROM — goniometry of flexion, abduction, rotations (pain arc 60–120°); inclinometer/ smartphone apps.
  • Strength — handheld dynamometry / MMT of rotator cuff and scapular muscles.
  • Pain — VAS/NRS at rest and with provocation; pain diary.

cSelf-report scales — the core of the answer

ScaleItems / rangeBest for
SPADI13 items (5 pain, 8 disability), 0–100General shoulder pathology; sensitive in frozen shoulder
DASH / QuickDASH30 / 11 items, 0–100Upper-limb-wide disability; good for multiple joints
ASES13 items, 0–100RC pathology; physician- + self-rated
Constant-Murley100 pts (35 subjective + 65 objective)European standard incl. ROM & strength
UCLA / SST / Penn / WORC / WOSIvariedArthritis & arthroplasty / 12 yes–no single-answer / general shoulder pathology / rotator-cuff disease / instability
PSFS3 patient-chosen activities (0–10)Individualised, very responsive

dInterpretation

Report baseline → discharge change against the MCID of the chosen scale (SPADI ≈ 8–10 points; DASH ≈ 10–15 points); use two complementary levels (an impairment measure + a self-report scale) for a defensible ICF-rounded evaluation.

Fig 9 — The ICF pyramid with shoulder measures slotted by level. Arguing 'one measure per level' is what turns a list of scales into a selection rationale.
One sentence with each scale's item-count and best-use is worth more than a paragraph on any one scale. And never write "VAS is the gold standard for shoulder function" — VAS measures pain intensity, not function.

Sources
