Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the documentation procedure adopted in terms of assessment, management in rehabilitation based on International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF).

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 1a — history taking, documentation and the ICF framework

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition and purpose of ICF (WHO 2001)1.5
Components of the ICF model2
Assessment documentation through ICF codes and qualifiers2.5
Management / rehabilitation planning and documentation2.5
Advantages, limitations and Indian clinical application1.5

aWhat the ICF is — the mechanism first

The ICF is the World Health Organization's operational form of the biopsychosocial model: instead of documenting only the disease (ICD), we document what the disease does to the person. Functioning and disability are described as the interaction of a health condition with body functions, body structures, activities, participation, and the environmental and personal factors that surround the patient. This is the core shift examiners look for — from "what is wrong with the knee" to "what the stiff knee does to the farmer who has to squat to work."

bThe architecture you must be able to draw

Two parts. Part 1 covers functioning and disability with three components: body functions (coded b), body structures (coded s), and activities and participation (coded d). Part 2 covers contextual factors: environmental factors (coded e) and personal factors, which are described but not classified. Every code carries a qualifier from 0 to 4 — no impairment to complete impairment — so d450.2 means moderate difficulty walking.

Fig 1 — the ICF map: health condition on top, the three functioning boxes in the middle, contextual factors at the bottom. Drawing exactly this earns the component mark in under sixty seconds.

cAssessment documentation — the procedure

Take a post-stroke patient in a district hospital OPD. History and examination findings are first organised by level: body function and structure — b730 muscle power impairment 2, spasticity b735.1, shoulder subluxation s73016; activity — d450 walking with quadripod, moderate limitation; participation — d920 recreation and d850 remunerative employment severely restricted. Contextual factors: e310 immediate family is supportive (facilitator, +3), e140 work products absent, e115 assistive products unavailable in the village (barrier). Each finding gets a code plus a qualifier — that pairing is what turns a case sheet into ICF documentation.

dManagement documentation — assessment into plan

Write SMART goals at each level: body level — improve shoulder abduction power by one MRC grade in six weeks; activity — independent walking for 200 metres with a stick by week eight; participation — return to light farm work by twelve weeks. Every intervention column must cite the level it targets, and every re-assessment must use the same qualifiers so the change is measurable. Link standardized scales to codes: the SPADI documents shoulder pain and disability, a 10-metre walk test documents d450.

eWhy examiners award this — closing the loop

The ICF prevents impairment-only physiotherapy, gives a common language to the whole rehabilitation team, and justifies goal setting that the family understands. In the Indian context it forces us to document environmental barriers — a house with a squat toilet, a workplace with no seating, a bus with a high step — which is exactly what decides whether our exercise programme translates to real life.

Examiner's tip: never describe ICF as a "classification of disability" — the C is functioning AND disability, and the omission of environmental factors is the commonest reason candidates lose the full two marks of the components row.

Sources

  1. World Physiotherapy. Standards of Practice.
  2. WHO. International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), 2001.
  3. Roach KE et al. The Shoulder Pain and Disability Index. Arthritis Care & Research, 1991.
  4. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Define Competency. Add a note on Competency-Based Physiotherapy Education.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 1b — competencies and the physiotherapy education framework

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition and domains of competency2
Principles of competency-based physiotherapy education3
Curriculum, outcomes and assessment tools (Miller, Bloom)3
Advantages, challenges and Indian implementation2

aDefinition — say it in one breath, then unpack it

Competency is the habitual and judicious integration of knowledge, skills and attitudes displayed in real clinical practice. Three domains, never two — a therapist who can pass a written test on gait training but cannot communicate the plan to an anxious grandfather is knowledgeable, not competent. Add the word "habitual": one lucky performance on exam day is not competency; it must be reproducible over time and across situations.

bThe mechanism of CBPE — outcomes drive everything

Competency-Based Physiotherapy Education (CBPE) turns the curriculum inside-out: instead of "we taught ten lectures on electrotherapy, therefore the student is ready," it declares the desired graduate outcome first — the competent entry-level clinician — and designs teaching, learning and assessment backwards from it. This is constructive alignment. Content is organised into competencies with milestones that state observable behaviours, mapped to Bloom's revised taxonomy verbs: a student must be able to assess, plan, apply and evaluate — not merely describe. Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) convert competencies into real clinical units of work such as "assess and manage a patient with mechanical low back pain under supervision."

cAssessment — climb the pyramid

George Miller's pyramid is the framework examiners expect here. At the base, "knows" is tested by MCQs; "knows how" by case discussions and vivas; "shows how" by OSCE stations on simulated patients; and only the apex, Miller's pyramid summit — "does" — is assessed at the patient's side through workplace-based assessment and direct observation. In CBPE the dominant assessment becomes the apex, feedback becomes continuous and formative rather than a single summative verdict, and progression is by demonstrated achievement, not time served.

Fig 2 — Miller's pyramid with the matching assessment tool beside each tier. Note the arrow: CBPE is judged at the apex, "does," on real patients.

dAdvantages and the Indian reality

Advantages: transparency of outcomes, learner-centred flexibility (a student may take twelve weeks or sixteen to master a skill), early clinical exposure, and assessment that mirrors actual practice. Challenges in India: batch sizes of sixty-plus make individualised feedback expensive; faculty need training in direct observation; workplace assessment demands clinical infrastructure that colleges attached to small hospitals struggle to provide; and a national competency framework for physiotherapy is still maturing, though the CBME model adopted for MBBS gives us a ready template.

Examiner's tip: the definition must contain all three domains AND the word habitual — and link CBPE to assessment at the apex of Miller's pyramid; candidates who quote Bloom's taxonomy verbs (assess, evaluate, create) instead of "understand" pick up easy extra marks.

Sources

  1. Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Academic Medicine, 1990.
  2. Anderson LW, Krathwohl DR (eds). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing (Bloom revised).
  3. World Physiotherapy. Physiotherapist education framework and Standards of Practice.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe various methods of sampling and sample size determination.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3a — sampling methods and sample size in research methodology

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Population, sample, sampling frame — definitions1.5
Probability sampling methods with examples2.5
Non-probability sampling methods with examples2
Sample size determination (formulas, inputs)3
Errors, power and practical pearls1

aWhy we sample, and the three terms that frame the answer

We study a sample because studying the entire population of Indian knee-osteoarthritis patients is impossible — but the sample must behave like the population it came from. Define the target population, the accessible population, and the sampling frame — the complete, reachable list of population members from which you actually draw. In India the frame is the honest weak link: electoral rolls miss migrants, hospital registers miss those who never reach hospital, and every such gap is selection bias before your study begins.

bProbability sampling — every subject has a known, non-zero chance

Simple random sampling: every member has an equal chance; use random number tables or software; unbiased but needs a complete frame and spreads travel over wide geography. Systematic sampling: pick every k-th person from a list after a random start — convenient for OPD registration queues. Stratified sampling: split the frame into layers — sex, age band, urban or rural — and sample within each, guaranteeing that a minority group is not wiped out by chance. Cluster sampling: randomly select whole clusters — villages, schools, anganwadi centres — then study everyone inside; cheapest for community surveys in dispersed rural populations, at the price of design effect and lower precision. Multistage sampling stacks these: random districts, then random PHCs, then households.

cNon-probability sampling — practical, but generalisation dies

Convenience sampling: whoever walks into your OPD that month — the default of most Indian student dissertations, acceptable for pilot studies only. Purposive sampling: you deliberately select information-rich cases, the backbone of qualitative work. Snowball sampling: each enrolled subject recruits peers from the same hidden network — essential when studying stigmatised groups such as drug users. Quota sampling: fill fixed numbers in each category for speed. Consecutive sampling: every eligible patient during a defined window — the least-biased clinical option and always worth naming.

Fig 3 — the sampling tree. Draw the frame in the middle: examiners specifically check whether you know that probability methods die without a complete frame.

dSample size determination — the four inputs

Sample size is not a tradition of thirty per group; it is calculated from four inputs: the expected effect size or prevalence, the acceptable margin of error d, the confidence level (usually 95%, Z = 1.96), and the power (usually 80%, Z = 0.84) against the assumed type II error. For a proportion or prevalence: n = Z squared times p times q, divided by d squared — with no prior estimate, take p = 0.5, d = 0.05, giving 384, the number behind most Indian prevalence surveys. For comparing two means: n = 2 times Z-squared times s-squared divided by effect-size squared, where the standardised difference is Cohen's d. Add 10 to 20 percent for attrition, and for cluster designs multiply by the design effect. Too small a study misses a true effect; too large wastes scarce resources and exposes more subjects than needed to risk — both are ethical failures, which links this question to Unit 2.

eErrors, power, and the practical pearl

Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis (false alarm), guarded by the significance level alpha; type II error is missing a real effect, guarded by power — one minus beta. Report that you calculated sample size before, not after, data collection: a post-hoc power justification reads as an excuse. In ICMR-funded multicentric trials the statistician finalises this calculation in the protocol stage — say so, and you sound like a researcher rather than a student.

Examiner's tip: the formula for a proportion, with the worked figure of 384, is the single highest-yield fact in this unit — and always write "sample size was calculated for the primary outcome," because a study powered for one outcome is not powered for all of them.

Sources

  1. Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  2. Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics.
  3. ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Explain the ethical principles in practice of physiotherapy in a hospital and community.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 2a — World Physiotherapy standards, ICMR guidelines and ethical issues

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Ethical framework and professional codes2
Four cardinal principles with physiotherapy examples3
Hospital practice — consent, confidentiality, boundaries2.5
Community practice — camps, equity, culture1.5
ICMR 2017, research and documentation duties1

aThe frame — principles plus codes

Ethics in physiotherapy rests on two legs: the four prima facie principles of Beauchamp and Childress, and the professional codes that convert them into rules of conduct — the World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice and, for research and community programmes in India, the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines 2017. In your answer, principles give the philosophy and codes give the enforceable behaviour; quoting both is what lifts the answer from a philosophy essay to a professional one.

bThe four principles — mechanism with an Indian example each

Autonomy: the patient's right to decide — exercised through informed consent, truth-telling about the diagnosis, and respect for refusal; an OPD patient may decline a passive-mobilisation technique and we document and respect it. Beneficence: act for the patient's benefit — choose the exercise programme with the best evidence for that person, not the most profitable for the clinic. Non-maleficence: do no harm — screen for red flags, avoid over-pressure on osteoporotic spines, apply a risk-benefit justification for every modality. Justice: fairness in distribution — equal quality of care for a ward patient and a private cubicle patient, transparent fees, no discrimination by caste, religion, gender, HIV status or ability to pay.

Fig 4 — the four-quadrant ethics map with the physiotherapy hook under each principle; the examiner asks for examples, and this figure is your memory palace.

cHospital practice — where the principles bite

In hospital: obtain consent before the first assessment and again for any change of plan, in the patient's language, and remember a signature without understanding is not consent. Guard confidentiality — no case discussions in hospital corridors, no patient photos on personal phones, and digital records protected as the ICMR data-protection expectations require. Maintain professional boundaries — no personal relationships with patients under care. Document every session honestly; the case sheet is the ethical record that protects the patient and you. Practise within your scope: refer onwards to an orthopaedician or a physician when red flags exceed physiotherapy. Follow infection control, be truthful about fees and likely outcomes, and do not promise cures — "guaranteed pain relief in three sittings" is an ethical breach, not marketing.

dCommunity practice — the same principles, rougher terrain

In the community — health camps, school screening, industrial ergonomic visits — the same principles apply but the machinery is weaker. Voluntariness must be real: a free camp attended by the whole village because the employer sanctioned leave is not entirely voluntary. Cultural and religious sensitivity decides whether an exercise programme is followed: prescribing knee flexion postures where squatting is required for daily life is poor rehabilitation. Justice dominates community work: reaching patients who cannot reach us, and using ICMR 2017 standards when the programme involves data collection — ethical committee approval, anonymised records, and benefit flowing back to the community studied, not only to the researchers.

Examiner's tip: candidates write the four principles and stop; the distinction marks come from the hospital versus community contrast — consent machinery, confidentiality machinery and justice issues all change when the patient is in a village square rather than on a plinth. One line each, and you cross the first-class boundary.

Sources

  1. ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
  2. World Physiotherapy. Standards of Practice.
  3. Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Explain the instrumentation for neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES).

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 5b — NMES instrumentation and electrotherapeutic currents

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Principle and how NMES activates muscle1.5
Block diagram and circuit components3
Waveform and parameter control3
Electrodes, safety and contraindications1.5
Stimulator types (Russian, FES, denervated)1

aPrinciple — the mechanism before the machine

NMES does not excite the muscle fibre directly; it depolarises the motor axon under the cathode, and the action potential travelling to the neuromuscular junction produces contraction exactly as voluntary effort does. Because it bypasses the voluntary motor drive, even a patient with upper motor neuron weakness contracts — but note the reversal of recruitment order: electrical stimulation recruits large, fast type II axons before small type I axons, which is the opposite of the Henneman size principle and the reason NMES fatigues muscle faster than voluntary work.

bBlock diagram — follow the signal from the wall socket to the patient

The mains at 230 volts AC enters a step-down transformer, is rectified to DC and smoothed by a filter to give a safe, stable low-voltage supply. This powers the oscillator — the timing circuit, classically a 555-type timer — which generates the pulse train: it sets frequency, phase duration and on-off timing. The oscillator output drives the output stage, a transistorised amplifier that raises current to the therapeutic level, usually through a coupling transformer that isolates the patient from the mains — the safety heart of the instrument. Finally the current reaches the skin through electrodes placed over the motor point of the target muscle.

Fig 5 — the four-block signal chain with the five parameters listed beside it. Draw this chain and the examiner can see the current physically travelling; that is the whole instrumentation mark.

cWaveform and parameters — the clinician's five dials

The waveform of choice is a symmetrical or asymmetric biphasic pulsed current, because balanced charge leaves no net DC component and prevents iontophoresis-like skin irritation and burns under the electrode. Frequency: low rates 2 to 10 Hz twitch the muscle for drainage and the muscle pump; 20 to 50 Hz produce tetanic contraction for strengthening; up to 80 to 100 Hz are used for spasm inhibition, at the cost of fast fatigue. Phase duration: 200 to 400 microseconds sits over the strength-duration curve's comfortable motor threshold for innervated muscle. Duty cycle — the on:off ratio — is 1:5 in early reconditioning and about 1:1 for strengthening; more off-time means less fatigue. Ramp-up and ramp-down of 100 to 300 milliseconds let the patient tolerate higher amplitude, and amplitude itself is turned to the maximum tolerated, aiming for a strong, comfortable tetanic contraction.

dElectrodes, safety and contraindications

Electrode size is matched to muscle bulk — larger electrodes lower current density and improve comfort; placement over the motor point lowers the threshold. Skin must be prepped and impedance checked; broken current paths cause burns. Contraindications and precautions: cardiac pacemakers and implanted devices, the carotid sinus, the pregnant uterus, active deep vein thrombosis, areas of active malignancy, and sensory loss where the patient cannot report excessive current.

eInstrument types — one line each

Besides conventional NMES stimulators, know Russian current (medium frequency 2500 Hz, burst-modulated at 50 bursts per second, for strengthening), functional electrical stimulation (stimulation synchronised to a task such as foot-drop walking), TENS (sensory-level sibling for pain), and stimulators for denervated muscle, which must deliver long pulse durations of tens of milliseconds — often triangular or exponential — because denervated fibre has no axon to depolarise.

Examiner's tip: "instrumentation" answers must contain physics, not just parameter lists — say the words transformer, rectifier, oscillator, coupling transformer and patient isolation, and mention that phase duration, not the machine's frequency label, decides which tissue depolarises. That single sentence separates the 7-mark script from the 10-mark one.

Sources

  1. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain the various study designs in research.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3b — research designs, experimental and observational

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Classification framework (observational vs experimental)2
Observational designs with measures of association3
Experimental designs — RCT and its controls3
Qualitative designs and the evidence hierarchy2

aThe classification tree — sort before you describe

Start with the axis that earns the structure marks: does the investigator allocate the exposure? If not, the design is observational — descriptive (case report, case series, cross-sectional survey) or analytical (case-control, cohort). If yes, the design is experimental — randomised controlled trial, quasi-experiment, pre-experimental pre-post designs, and the single-case (n-of-1) experiment. A second axis is timing: retrospective looks backwards from outcome, prospective looks forward from exposure. Every design below is one cell of this grid; say the grid first.

bObservational designs — nature allocates, we observe

Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at one time point; they give prevalence, not incidence, and cannot prove sequence — useful for a survey of low back pain prevalence among Bengaluru autorickshaw drivers. Case-control studies start from the outcome: past exposure is compared between cases and controls, yielding an odds ratio; efficient for rare outcomes like transient brachial plexopathy, but memory bias is the toll. Cohort studies start from exposure and follow forward for the outcome — relative risk, temporal sequence established, the ethical design when withholding treatment is impossible; the price is time, expense and loss to follow-up. Case reports and series generate hypotheses, one patient at a time.

cExperimental designs — we allocate, so we can prove

The randomised controlled trial is the reference standard: randomisation distributes known and unknown confounders equally between groups, concealed allocation prevents selection bias, blinding of patient, therapist and assessor prevents expectation bias, and an intention-to-treat analysis preserves the randomisation. State the PICO question explicitly — population, intervention, comparison, outcome — and the design becomes obvious rather than memorised. Below the RCT sit quasi-experimental designs (allocation by ward or by week, when randomising individuals is impossible), pre-post single-group designs (no control, only a hypothesis), the single-case experimental design with repeated baseline phases — a clinician's research method for one patient — and crossover trials, where each patient is their own control and a washout period separates phases.

Fig 6 — the evidence pyramid: the level of evidence ladder you climb when grading any published answer. Higher means better protection against bias, not automatic truth.

dQualitative designs and choosing wisely

Not every clinical question is answered by numbers. Why patients abandon home programmes, or how families experience stroke caregiving, needs qualitative designs — phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography — analysed by the Braun and Clarke six-phase thematic analysis. Matching the design to the question is itself a research skill: a therapy question wants an RCT or systematic review, a prognosis question wants a cohort, a diagnostic accuracy question wants a cross-sectional comparison against a gold standard, and a meaning question wants qualitative work.

Examiner's tip: for every design, give one physiotherapy example and one statistic it produces — odds ratio for case-control, relative risk for cohort, and the phrase "randomisation plus concealment plus blinding plus intention-to-treat" for the RCT. Designs described without their bias controls read like a menu, not an answer.

Sources

  1. Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  2. Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine.
  3. Herbert R et al. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy.
  4. Braun V, Clarke V. Using thematic analysis in psychology, 2006.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Discuss in brief parametric and non-parametric tests.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3c — biostatistics: parametric and non-parametric tests

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definitions and assumptions of parametric tests2.5
Common parametric tests and their settings2.5
Common non-parametric tests and their settings2.5
How to choose; conversion, efficiency, pitfalls2.5

aWhat "parametric" means — assumptions first, tests second

Parametric tests assume that the data follow a specific distribution — the normal, Gaussian curve — and estimate its parameters, mean and standard deviation. Their four assumptions: the normality assumption, data measured on interval or ratio scale, homogeneity of variance across compared groups, and independence of observations. Non-parametric tests make no such distributional assumption — hence "distribution-free" — and work on ranks, so they tolerate ordinal scales like pain scores and skewed data like hospital stay or income. Verify normality in your answer with the Shapiro-Wilk test, or by eyeballing the histogram and Q-Q plot; naming an actual check is worth more than reciting the assumption.

bParametric tests — one per design

One group versus a known value: one-sample t-test. Two paired measurements — pain before and after ten sittings of interferential therapy: paired t-test. Two independent groups — conventional exercise versus physiotherapist-supervised exercise in two OPD cohorts: unpaired (independent) t-test. Three or more independent groups: one-way ANOVA, with a post-hoc test such as Tukey to find which pair differs. Repeated measurements across time: repeated-measures ANOVA. Relationship between two continuous variables: Pearson's correlation coefficient r. Each test outputs a p-value and, in modern reporting, a confidence interval — say "p less than 0.05 means evidence against the null, not proof of a large effect."

cNon-parametric tests — the rank twins

Every parametric test has a rank-based twin. Paired setting: the sign test (direction only) and the more powerful Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Two independent groups: Mann-Whitney U test. Three or more groups: Kruskal-Wallis H test. Repeated measures: Friedman test. Correlation: Spearman's rho. For categorical data the chi-square test — goodness of fit, and independence in a contingency table — belongs here too, with Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts fall below five.

Fig 7 — the choosing tree: the question box in the middle is where marks live; the test names are just leaves.

dChoosing well — conversion, efficiency, honesty

Decision path: normality and interval data with comparable variances choose parametric; ordinal, ranked, skewed or outlier-heavy data choose non-parametric. Both paths must still respect independence and the pairing structure of the design — a paired test on unpaired data is a more serious error than choosing the wrong family. If the data look nearly normal, prefer the parametric test: on normal data it is the more powerful, and on mildly non-normal data the rank tests retain roughly 95 percent of that efficiency, so little is lost either way. The commonest viva trap: applying a paired t-test to two independent groups, or an unpaired test to before-after data — always state the design first, then the test.

Examiner's tip: write the answer as a paired table — parametric test on the left, its non-parametric twin on the right — and add one line on why you chose each: "VAS pain is ordinal, so Wilcoxon signed-rank." Choosing tests from the data's own scale and shape, rather than from memory, is exactly what the examiner means by "discuss."

Sources

  1. Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics.
  2. Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Considerations for exercise prescription in obesity.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4c — exercise prescription across conditions and body compositions

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definitions and Indian (Asian) anthropometric cutoffs2
Pre-participation screening and comorbidity review2.5
FITT-VP prescription with numbers3.5
Progression, safety, behaviour and Indian context2

aDefine your patient first — the Indian cutoffs are different

Obesity is excess body fat with health risk, and for Asian Indians the thresholds arrive early: by the Misra et al. JAPI 2009 consensus, obesity is a body mass index of 25 or more (overweight 23 to 24.9) — not the Western cutoff of 30 — and central obesity is a waist circumference of 90 cm or more in men and 80 cm or more in women. Indians also develop the "thin-fat" phenotype: metabolic risk at lower BMI, which is why we screen and treat earlier and why quoting these Indian numbers earns the definition mark over reciting Western values.

bBefore the first session — screen, then prescribe

Review comorbidities: type 2 diabetes and its medication timing (exercise after insulin or a sulfonylurea dose risks hypoglycaemia — advise carrying glucose, adjusting the dose with the physician), hypertension (record resting blood pressure; defer if 180/110 or above until controlled), dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, and painful knees or low back from the mechanical load. Stratify cardiovascular risk — the apparently healthy obese adult can begin moderate activity without testing, while symptomatic patients or those planning vigorous exercise need medical clearance. Baseline measures to document: waist circumference, resting heart rate and blood pressure, a six-minute walk test, and functional joint status.

cThe prescription itself — FITT-VP with numbers attached

Dose it like a drug, using the FITT principle grid plus volume and progression. Frequency: aerobic exercise on five days a week (or every day if lighter), resistance on two to three non-consecutive days. Intensity: moderate, 40 to 60 percent of heart-rate reserve, or a talk-test pace where the patient can still converse, rating of perceived exertion 11 to 13 on the Borg 6-to-20 scale. Time: 30 to 60 minutes daily, accumulated in bouts of at least ten minutes, building to the guideline volume of 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity weekly. Type: load-friendly aerobic choices first — brisk walking, stationary cycling, swimming or aqua exercise (buoyancy unloads the knees), later progressing to jogging; plus large-muscle resistance training, because each kilogram of added muscle raises resting metabolic rate and preserves lean mass during weight loss. Quantify energy cost in METs — brisk walking is about 4, cycling about 8 — so the patient can see walking thirty minutes burns roughly the calories of one chapati, and that diet must change in parallel: exercise alone rarely outpaces a calorie surplus.

Fig 8 — the FITT pillars with a number against each; the bottom banner is the sentence examiners want to see quoted verbatim.

dProgression, safety and the Indian context

Progress volume first, intensity later — add roughly five to ten minutes per fortnight of tolerated walking before touching speed or incline. Protect joints: aquatic exercise, cycles and graded walking paths for the painful knee; cushioned footwear on hard Indian roads; avoid deep squats early. Time outdoor sessions for early morning or evening in Indian heat and humidity, and enforce hydration. Address behaviour, because adherence is the real prescription: written goals, step counters, exercise logs, walking groups for company, and family involvement — in Indian households the kitchen decides the calorie side of the equation, so involve whoever cooks. Reassess monthly with waist circumference and walk time, not the weighing scale alone, and coordinate with a dietitian and physician: exercise preserves lean mass during weight loss, which dieting alone squanders.

Examiner's tip: the answer must read as a prescription, not an essay on obesity — four FITT letters with numbers, the Asian Indian cutoffs (BMI 25, waist 90/80), and the hypoglycaemia-with-insulin warning. Candidates who write "advise exercise" without numbers cap at half marks; you are prescribing a drug called movement.

Sources

  1. Misra A et al. Consensus statement for diagnosis of obesity, abdominal obesity and the metabolic syndrome for Asian Indians. JAPI, 2009.
  2. McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Differentiate aerobic and anaerobic exercise in terms of energy expenditure.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4a — metabolism and energy systems in exercise

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Energy systems and their mechanisms3
Point-by-point comparison (table-worthy differences)3
Oxygen deficit, debt and EPOC2
Training adaptations and testing2
★ Memory hook — Aerobic vs anaerobic in three numbers: 10 seconds : 2 minutes : unlimited — then name the fuel each system burns.

aMechanism first — three systems, one timeline

All exercise is powered by ATP, regenerated by three systems on a time-and-intensity clock. The phosphagen system — stored ATP and creatine phosphate — fuels the first eight to ten seconds of all-out effort anaerobically, without oxygen, without lactate. Anaerobic glycolysis breaks glucose to pyruvate and, when oxygen supply lags demand, ferments it to lactate, regenerating ATP rapidly for roughly ten seconds to two minutes of heavy work — at the cost of hydrogen-ion accumulation and early fatigue. The oxidative (aerobic) system burns carbohydrate and fat in the mitochondria with oxygen, yielding far more ATP per glucose molecule but only at a slower rate; it dominates from about two minutes onward and supports hours of submaximal work. The systems never switch on and off; they share the load, and the intensity of the exercise decides the share.

bThe differentiation the question asks for

Intensity: aerobic work is moderate, sustainable and below the lactate threshold (roughly 55 to 70 percent of maximal oxygen uptake); anaerobic work is near-maximal, above the lactate threshold, where blood lactate climbs past about 4 mmol per litre. Oxygen demand: aerobic exercise is steady state — uptake meets demand; anaerobic exercise creates an oxygen deficit that must be repaid. Fuel: aerobic uses both carbohydrate and fat (fat burns only in a carbohydrate flame, and only aerobically); anaerobic burns carbohydrate alone. Duration and power: anaerobic delivers high power for seconds to about two minutes; aerobic delivers lower power for minutes to hours. By-products: anaerobic accumulates lactate and hydrogen ions; aerobic yields carbon dioxide and water. Examples a physiotherapist meets daily: a patient rising from a chair once (phosphagen), a stair-climbing test (glycolytic), a six-minute walk test (aerobic).

Fig 9 — the energy timeline every examiner wants: three boxes along the clock, and the crossing lines showing the anaerobic share falling as the aerobic share rises with duration.

cThe oxygen account — deficit and EPOC

At exercise onset, oxidative phosphorylation lags behind demand — the oxygen deficit, covered meanwhile by the phosphagen system and glycolysis. After stopping, oxygen uptake remains raised: EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, the modern name for oxygen debt) repays the phosphagen stores, clears lactate by gluconeogenesis in the liver (the Cori cycle), restores myoglobin, and funds the raised temperature and catecholamine-driven metabolism. Anaerobic exercise produces a large, fast-rising EPOC; aerobic exercise, when severe and prolonged, produces a slower but longer-lasting one — this elevated post-exercise metabolism is the physiological basis behind interval-training prescriptions for cardiometabolic patients.

dAdaptations and testing — close the loop

Aerobic training multiplies mitochondria and aerobic enzymes, raises capillary density and haemoglobin mass, lowers resting heart rate and raises maximal oxygen uptake — tested by graded exercise tests with gas analysis or field tests like the six-minute walk or 20-m shuttle. Anaerobic training enlarges phosphagen stores and glycolytic enzymes and improves hydrogen-ion buffering — tested by the 30-second Wingate anaerobic test or vertical jumps. For our patients, most rehabilitation is aerobic; anaerobic dosing belongs to return-to-sport phases, and the physiotherapist's skill is prescribing on the correct side of the lactate threshold.

Examiner's tip: the mark is for "in terms of energy expenditure" — so anchor every difference in ATP: which substrate, how much ATP per glucose molecule (2 versus about 32), how fast it arrives, and what it costs in oxygen and lactate. A pure list of "aerobic means jogging" scores half; the mechanism scores full.

Sources

  1. McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Describe electrical stimulation and its effect on various systems.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 5a — electrical properties of muscle and nerve, effects of stimulation

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition and classification of currents2
Effects on muscle2
Effects on the nervous system2
Effects on circulation and metabolism2
Other systems, precautions and conclusion2

aDefinition and classification — frame the family first

Therapeutic electrical stimulation is the application of controlled electrical current through surface electrodes to excite nerve or muscle and produce a physiological or therapeutic effect. Classify in one line each: by pulse shape (rectangular, triangular, exponential, sinusoidal), by continuity (direct versus pulsed), and by clinical intent — NMES for muscle activation, functional electrical stimulation synchronised to a task, TENS for sensory analgesia, and Russian current for strengthening. The unifying mechanism for almost all of them: depolarisation of excitable membrane under the cathode when the stimulus crosses the threshold defined by the strength-duration curve.

bEffects on muscle — the system we treat most

Stimulation produces contraction whose strength and character follow the frequency: twitches below about 10 to 15 Hz, tetanic contraction from 20 to 50 Hz, and rapid fatigue above that. Recruitment is reversed compared with voluntary effort — large type II motor axons fire first, which makes NMES a useful fast-twitch trainer but an early fatiguer. Used repeatedly, it maintains muscle mass in disuse and immobilisation, retards atrophy after injury or surgery, strengthens weak quadriceps and pelvic floor, re-educates a muscle the patient has "forgotten" to recruit, and pumps venous and lymphatic return through the muscle pump. Denervated muscle needs a different instrument entirely: long pulse durations of tens of milliseconds and triangular or exponential waveforms, because there is no axon to depolarise and the fibre itself must be excited.

cEffects on the nervous system — sensory and motor faces

On sensory nerves, low-intensity high-rate stimulation recruits large-diameter afferents and closes the pain gate in the dorsal horn — the mechanism of conventional TENS — while low-rate (2 to 4 Hz) stimulation recruits descending opioid pathways for diffuse analgesia. Stimulated sensory input also improves proprioceptive awareness of a joint. On motor nerves, stimulation preserves axonal excitability and conduction in disuse, and cyclic stimulation of the common peroneal nerve in foot drop is the classic functional application of motor-nerve stimulation.

Fig 10 — the systems web: a centre box with four targets is the fastest skeleton for "effect on various systems," and each box becomes one h4 of your answer.

dEffects on circulation and metabolism

Rhythmically stimulated skeletal muscle acts as a peripheral heart: the pumping action drives venous and lymphatic return, reduces oedema after injury and encourages arterial inflow. Large-muscle stimulation raises heart rate and blood pressure because the metabolic demand of contracting muscle triggers sympathetic cardiovascular responses — a consideration in cardiac patients. Local metabolism rises in the stimulated muscle with increased substrate use, and stimulation-induced movement aids nutrition of cartilage and soft tissue in immobilised joints.

eOther systems, precautions and conclusion

On bone, mechanical strain generates piezoelectric currents, and clinically applied electrical stimulation is used to support delayed-union fracture healing; on skin, long-standing sensory stimulation can produce trophic changes; smooth muscle and viscera respond poorly to brief pulses, though some bladder and pelvic-floor applications exist. Precautions and contraindications: cardiac pacemakers and implanted electronic devices, stimulation over the carotid sinus, the pregnant uterus, active deep vein thrombosis, malignant tissue and infected areas, and sensory loss where the patient cannot report excess current. In the Indian context, remember the practical system factors — cost, machine availability and adherence — that decide whether a stimulation programme survives beyond the OPD. Conclude with the physiotherapist's principle: electrical stimulation is an adjunct that activates the tissue; the retraining still comes from exercise and function.

Examiner's tip: the question says "various systems," so an answer that only discusses muscle caps itself at five marks — one heading each for muscle, nerve, circulation and at least two other systems, each with a mechanism, not just a claim. The type-II recruitment reversal and the pain-gate mechanism are the two most-tested mechanisms in this unit.

Sources

  1. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  3. ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper I

QP 8129 · 19-May-2025 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1ICF documentation

  • WHO 2001; functioning AND disability; codes b, s, d, e; personal factors never coded.
  • Qualifiers 0 to 4 = no to complete problem; assessment documents impairment + activity + participation + context.
  • Management = SMART goals written at each ICF level, same qualifiers repeated at re-assessment.

2Competency and CBPE

  • Definition: habitual + judicious + knowledge, skills, attitudes — all three, always.
  • Miller: knows → knows how → shows how → does; apex = workplace assessment on real patients.
  • CBPE = outcomes first, constructive alignment, EPAs, milestones, Bloom's verbs, progression by demonstration not time.

3Sampling and sample size

  • Frame = the actual list you draw from; no frame, no probability sampling.
  • Probability: simple random, systematic (every k-th), stratified (layers), cluster (villages), multistage; non-probability: convenience, purposive, quota, snowball, consecutive.
  • n = Z²pq/d²; p = 0.5, d = 0.05 gives 384; power 80%, add 10–20% attrition.

4Ethics

  • Four principles: autonomy (consent), beneficence, non-maleficence, justice (equity).
  • Hospital: consent, confidentiality, boundaries, documentation; community: voluntariness, culture, data ethics.
  • Codes: World Physiotherapy Standards + ICMR 2017 for research and community programmes.

5NMES instrumentation

  • Signal chain: transformer → rectifier/smoothing → oscillator (555) → output stage with coupling transformer → patient.
  • Parameters: 20–50 Hz, phase duration 200–400 µs, duty cycle 1:1 to 1:5, ramp 100–300 ms, amplitude max tolerated.
  • Biphasic balanced = no net charge = no burn; denervated muscle needs tens of ms triangular pulses.

6Study designs

  • Investigator allocates? No = observational (cross-sectional → prevalence; case-control → odds ratio; cohort → relative risk); yes = experimental (RCT, quasi, n-of-1, crossover).
  • RCT quality quartet: randomise, conceal, blind, intention-to-treat.
  • Pyramid: systematic reviews over RCTs over cohort over case-control over case reports.

7Parametric vs non-parametric

  • Parametric needs: normality, interval/ratio, homogeneity of variance, independence; check with Shapiro-Wilk.
  • Twins: paired t ↔ Wilcoxon; unpaired t ↔ Mann-Whitney U; ANOVA ↔ Kruskal-Wallis; repeated ANOVA ↔ Friedman; Pearson ↔ Spearman; categories → chi-square.
  • Match the test to the pairing structure first — wrong pairing is the bigger sin.

8Exercise in obesity

  • Asian Indian cutoffs (JAPI 2009): obesity BMI 25 and above; waist 90 cm men, 80 cm women.
  • FITT: 5 d/wk aerobic, 40–60% HRR (RPE 11–13), 30–60 min in 10-min bouts, 150–300 min/wk; resistance 2–3 d/wk.
  • Insulin + exercise = hypoglycaemia risk; protect knees; aqua and cycling; involve the family kitchen.

9Aerobic vs anaerobic

  • ATP-PC 0–10 s; glycolysis 10 s–2 min, lactate ↑; oxidative beyond 2 min, fat burns only aerobically.
  • 2 ATP per glucose anaerobic versus roughly 32 aerobic; lactate threshold about 4 mmol/L.
  • EPOC = old oxygen debt: restore phosphagens, clear lactate (Cori cycle), raised temperature and catecholamines.

10Electrical stimulation on systems

  • Muscle: type II recruited first (reversed order), tetany 20–50 Hz, atrophy arrest; denervated needs long pulses.
  • Nerve: pain gate via large afferents; peroneal stimulation in foot drop.
  • Circulation: muscle pump drives venous/lymphatic return; bone: piezoelectric, delayed-union healing; pacemaker and carotid sinus are hard contraindications.
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall — the four ethics principles, the 384 sample-size figure, Miller's pyramid order, FITT with numbers, and the 20–50 Hz / 200–400 µs NMES pair.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Explain the components of the skeletal system.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 1 — Basic concepts of the MSK system: skeletal system

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition and functions of the skeletal system1.5
Axial skeleton with bone counts1.5
Appendicular skeleton with bone counts1
Classification of bones (shape and structure)2
Associated structures: cartilage, ligaments, joints2
Clinical application and bone remodelling2

aDefinition first — a living scaffold, not a dead rack

The skeletal system is the body's living framework: 206 bones in the adult, plus the cartilage, ligaments and joints that bind them. Mechanism first — bone is metabolically active tissue that constantly remodels itself in response to the loads it feels. Five functions you must name: support (rigid levers for posture), protection (skull for brain, rib cage for heart and lungs), movement (levers for muscle pull), haemopoiesis (red marrow makes blood cells), and mineral storage (about 99% of body calcium and most phosphorus, with yellow marrow storing fat).

bAxial skeleton — the central column, 80 bones

The axial skeleton forms the upright axis of the body: the skull (22 bones plus 6 ear ossicles and the hyoid), the vertebral column (26 bones — 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum, 1 coccyx), and the thoracic cage (24 ribs and the sternum). Mechanism: this column transmits the entire superimposed body weight downwards and protects the spinal cord — which is why axial loading injuries (a fall from a scaffold, so common at Indian construction sites) damage it most at the thoracolumbar junction.

cAppendicular skeleton — the locomotor appendages, 126 bones

Pectoral girdles (clavicle and scapula, 4 bones) anchor the upper limbs (60 bones), and the pelvic girdles (2 hip bones) anchor the lower limbs (60 bones). Mechanism: the pectoral girdle sacrifices stability for mobility (shallow glenoid), while the pelvic girdle sacrifices mobility for stability (deep socket, strong ligaments) to bear weight in standing and gait — a comparison examiners reward.

dClassification of bones — two axes, learn both

By shape: long (femur), short (carpals), flat (ilium), irregular (vertebra), sesamoid (patella — the largest, embedded in quadriceps tendon to improve its leverage and shield the knee). By structure: compact bone (dense outer shell, resists bending) and cancellous bone (spongy inner mesh with trabeculae aligned along stress lines, resists compression). Developmentally, bones form by intramembranous or endochondral ossification.

eAssociated components — where physiotherapy lives

Articular hyaline cartilage covers joint surfaces (low friction, no blood supply — heals poorly), fibrocartilage forms menisci and discs (resists compression), ligaments passively limit joint range, and joints are classified as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial. The synovial joint — with its capsule, synovial membrane, cartilage and reinforcing ligaments — is the functional unit we treat every day.

Fig 1 — the two-division tree with bone counts, plus the five shapes. Reproduce both rows and the numbers: counts are where the easy marks hide.

fClinical application — make it a physiotherapy answer

Bone is dynamic: Wolff's law states that bone remodels along lines of mechanical stress — thickening where loaded, resorbing where unloaded. So prolonged immobilisation causes disuse osteoporosis, while graduated weight bearing rebuilds stock. Indian context: with widespread vitamin D deficiency and postmenopausal osteoporosis, axial bone loss presents as thoracic kyphosis and fragility fractures — early weight-bearing exercise and DEXA screening are our preventive tools.

Examiner's tip: most students stop at a bone list. The 2 clinical marks sit in Wolff's law plus one Indian-context line (vitamin D deficiency, osteoporotic kyphosis) — write those and you separate yourself from the pack.

Sources

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — skeletal tissue structure.
  2. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — axial and appendicular divisions.
  3. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — bone remodelling and calcium homeostasis.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Enumerate the tools for measurement of body fat analysis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 2 — Anthropometry: body composition measurement

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Why body fat is measured; fat mass vs fat-free mass1
Anthropometric field tools: tape, BMI, skinfold caliper2.5
Bioelectrical impedance analysis1
Densitometry: hydrostatic weighing, air displacement2
Imaging and criterion methods: DEXA, isotope dilution, others2
Comparison of tools and Indian cutoffs1.5

aWhy we measure — mechanism first

Body composition divides body mass into fat mass and fat-free mass (water, protein, bone mineral). Total body weight alone hides the difference between a muscular athlete and a sarcopenic obese patient — both can share a BMI of 28. Fat measurement quantifies obesity, tracks rehabilitation progress, and stratifies cardiometabolic risk. Arrange your answer as a ladder: from cheap field tools to criterion laboratory methods.

bField / anthropometric tools — the outpatient clinic set

Measuring tape: waist circumference and waist–hip ratio estimate central (visceral) fat — for Asian Indians the cutoffs are 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women, lower than the western 102/88, because Indians develop diabetes at lower BMI. BMI (weight in kg divided by height in metres squared) is an obesity screen; the Asian-Indian action point is 23 kg/m², not 25. The skinfold caliper pinches subcutaneous fat at standard sites — the Durnin–Womersley four sites (biceps, triceps, subscapular, suprailiac) or Jackson–Pollock three or seven sites — and estimates total body fat from regression equations.

cBioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA)

A painless, portable current (50 kHz) is passed through the body; fat-free mass, being water- and electrolyte-rich, conducts better, and fat resists the current — impedance predicts total body water and hence fat-free mass. Mechanism worth stating: it assumes constant tissue hydration, so dehydration or post-exercise readings distort it.

dDensitometry — from the classic tank to the egg-shaped pod

Hydrostatic (underwater) weighing: the patient is submerged and fully exhales; body density is computed from underwater weight by Archimedes' principle, then the two-compartment Siri equation converts density to fat percentage. Accurate but laborious and unpleasant. Air-displacement plethysmography (Bod Pod) replaces water with air displacement in a sealed chamber — same principle, far better tolerated.

eImaging and criterion methods

DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) is today's practical gold standard — it splits the body into fat, lean soft tissue and bone mineral with a low radiation dose and regional (trunk vs limb) output. Isotope dilution (deuterated water) measures total body water. Others to name for the enumeration mark: near-infrared interactance, ultrasound of subcutaneous fat, and, for research, CT and MRI volumetry. Add potassium-40 whole-body counting if you remember it.

Fig 2 — the accuracy ladder, left to right, with the Indian cutoffs boxed below. Draw the ladder and name the tool on every rung: that alone is half the enumeration marks.

fChoosing a tool — close like a clinician

Match the tool to the purpose: tape and BMI for every clinic screening; calipers where you need percentage fat on a budget; DEXA when you need regional fat and bone together (obesity plus osteoporosis in the postmenopausal patient); isotope and CT methods stay research tools. One comparison line earns the last 1.5: field tools are cheap and repeatable but population-specific; criterion methods are accurate but costly and immobile.

Examiner's tip: the question says "enumerate" — the marks are for the complete list, not deep detail on any one tool. Seven-plus tools, one mechanism line each (how it actually estimates fat), and the Indian cutoffs as your finishing flourish.

  2. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — anthropometry in clinical practice.
  3. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — body fluid compartments underlying BIA.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe the applications of Newton's second law in the human body.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 3 — Biomechanics: force, kinetics and kinematics

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
The law stated, with angular (torque) form2
Linear applications: gait, jumping, load carriage2
Angular applications: limb acceleration, throwing2
Injury mechanics: falls, whiplash, ACL2
Clinical and treatment applications2

aState the law — then translate it for the body

Newton's second law: the net force acting on a body equals its mass times its acceleration (net force = mass × acceleration), and acceleration is in the direction of the net force. Angular form: net torque = moment of inertia × angular acceleration. Mechanism first — the law is the bridge between muscle (which creates force) and motion (which is acceleration); almost every therapeutic exercise we prescribe is an application of it.

bLinear applications — where the body pushes the world

In walking, the ground reaction force is roughly 1.1 to 1.5 times body weight at loading response, rising to 2 to 3 times body weight in running — every step is your mass being decelerated and re-accelerated. In a vertical jump the athlete must generate force well above body weight to leave the ground. In sit-to-stand, quadriceps force must exceed body weight enough to produce upward acceleration of the trunk — which is exactly why elderly patients rock forward first, building acceleration over a longer path. Indian context: head-load carriers and porters walk with shorter, smoother steps — minimising the acceleration component lowers peak force on the spine.

cAngular applications — limbs as rotating segments

Muscles create torque about joints; the segment's angular acceleration depends on its moment of inertia, which depends on how mass is distributed about the axis. A figure skater pulling the arms in reduces moment of inertia and spins faster with unchanged angular momentum. A cricket bowler or a badminton-smash player sequences proximal-to-distal so each segment accelerates off the previous one — the kinetic chain. A long lever arm (outstretched arm holding a dumbbell) multiplies the torque demand on the shoulder compared with the elbow-bent position.

dInjury mechanics — the same law read backwards

Injury occurs when net force produces an acceleration the tissue cannot survive. A fall on the outstretched hand dissipates the body's momentum through the wrist in milliseconds — large deceleration, large force, hence Colles' fracture. Whiplash: the head accelerates forward on a fixed trunk, loading cervical soft tissue beyond its tolerance. Non-contact ACL rupture: a strong quadriceps contraction decelerates an extending tibia rapidly — the same force that protects also tears. Helmets and crash helmets work by extending the deceleration time, which by the impulse relationship lowers the peak force.

Fig 3 — left: mass and acceleration feeding net force; right: the joint as an axis with torque spinning a segment. One line of algebra plus one limb sketch carries both forms of the law.

eClinical and treatment applications

Progressive resistance training works because strength adapts to the force demand. In osteoarthritis we teach slow, controlled movement — small accelerations mean small peak joint forces. In plyometrics we deliberately train rate of force development. The same principle guides assistive devices: a walker with a heavy patient requires a controlled, gradual rise from a chair rather than a quick push, because force needed falls when acceleration falls. This closes the loop: understand force, and you can both break and rebuild the body.

Examiner's tip: write the linear equation AND the angular (torque) equation — students who give only force = mass times acceleration cap themselves at 4 of the 10. Then give one named example per domain: gait, throwing, fall injury, and one treatment application.

Sources

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — kinetics chapters.
  2. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — torque and levers.
  3. Saunders, Inman & Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — determinants of gait and force in locomotion.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Write basic concepts of exercise metabolism during core muscle strengthening.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 5 — Physiological basis of movement: exercise metabolism

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Core musculature: local stabilisers and global movers2
Energy systems and what core work actually uses2.5
Metabolic events inside a sustained hold2.5
Training adaptations of the stabilisers1.5
Clinical application and precautions1.5

aWhat "core" means — anatomy before metabolism

The core is a cylinder: local stabilisers — transversus abdominis, multifidus, diaphragm and the pelvic floor — working at low intensity, continuously, anticipating limb movement; and global movers — rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques, erector spinae — producing force and trunk motion. Mechanism first: the deep system provides segmental stiffness (spinal stability at low energetic cost), the superficial system produces torque. Their metabolic demands differ, and the examiner wants you to see why.

bEnergy systems — which one dominates a plank

Three systems supply ATP: the phosphagen system (immediate, about 10 seconds of all-out work), anaerobic glycolysis (up to roughly 2 minutes, lactate-forming), and aerobic metabolism (unlimited in duration at low intensity, yielding about 36 ATP per glucose molecule in the mitochondria). Core strengthening is classically low-load, high-duration — sustained submaximal isometric holds of 10 to 30 seconds, repeated many times — so it runs predominantly on the aerobic system, with anaerobic glycolysis contributing as hold time and fatigue build up.

cMetabolic events inside a sustained hold

Recruitment follows the size principle: small, fatigue-resistant type I motor units fire first; type II units join only as force demand rises. A sustained isometric hold above about 15 to 20% of maximal voluntary contraction compresses intramuscular vessels, occluding local blood flow — oxygen delivery falls while the muscle keeps consuming ATP, so stored phosphocreatine depletes, glycolysis accelerates, and hydrogen ions and inorganic phosphate accumulate. That accumulation — not lactate itself — is what the student feels as burning, trembling and the breath-holding urge. Release of the hold restores reperfusion and clears metabolites.

dTraining adaptations — what weeks of core work builds

Neural adaptations come first (better anticipatory activation timing of transversus abdominis and multifidus), then peripheral ones: increased mitochondrial density and capillarisation of the deep stabilisers, higher oxidative enzyme activity, and greater fatigue resistance. This is why stabiliser training emphasizes endurance — more repetitions, longer holds, brief rests — rather than heavy loading, which would merely recruit the global movers.

Fig 4 — the three-system continuum over hold time, with the aerobic block oversized because that is what core work mainly uses. Label the time boundaries: they carry the metabolic marks.

eClinical application — metabolic thinking at the plinth

Prescription follows the metabolism: begin with 5 to 10 second holds with rest, progress to 20 to 30 seconds, because brief rests allow reperfusion and metabolite clearance. Teach diaphragmatic breathing during holds — a core exercise is also a breathing exercise, and breath-holding (a Valsalva manoeuvre) spikes blood pressure, which matters in the many hypertensive Indian patients in our OPDs. In type 2 diabetes, regular aerobic-dominant core and endurance work improves glucose uptake. If a patient trembles or burns early, that is metabolic fatigue telling you the load — not the willpower — is wrong.

Examiner's tip: the question asks for metabolism, not a list of core exercises. Anchor every paragraph to ATP: which system, why, and how the isometric hold changes it. Then one line on Valsalva avoidance shows you can translate theory into safe practice.

Sources

  1. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — energy systems and muscle metabolism.
  2. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — metabolic responses to resistance training.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — core stabilisation progression.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Explain mechanics and pathomechanics of the knee joint.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6 — Mechanics and pathomechanics: knee joint

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Osteokinematics and the screw-home mechanism2
Menisci: structure, function, arthrokinematics2
Patellofemoral joint and the Q angle2
Pathomechanics: alignment, ligament, extensor mechanism2.5
Clinical application to assessment and treatment1.5

aOsteokinematics — a hinge pretending to be simple

The knee moves mainly in the sagittal plane: flexion about 0 to 135 or 150 degrees, extension to 0, with hyperextension up to about 5 to 10 degrees in some. Rotation is only possible when the knee is unlocked — about 45 degrees total when flexed, and it is coupled: as the knee approaches terminal extension the tibia rotates laterally about 10 to 15 degrees, the screw-home mechanism, which locks the knee into a close-packed, energy-efficient standing position (the femur rotates medially on the tibia if you describe it from the femur's side — state your reference). Popliteus unlocks it by laterally rotating the femur.

bMenisci and arthrokinematics — the load distributors

Arthrokinematically the femoral condyles both roll and glide posteriorly on the tibia during flexion, and the menisci travel with the femur — moving posteriorly in flexion, anteriorly in extension. The menisci are fibrocartilage (mostly circumferentially arranged type I collagen) carrying roughly half the joint load; their wedge shape converts vertical compression into hoop stress along their circumference, spreading load onto the tibial rim. After total meniscectomy, contact stress in that compartment rises several-fold — which is why degenerative changes follow, and why we now preserve, repair or transplant menisci.

cPatellofemoral joint — the biggest sesamoid doing the hardest job

The patella acts as a pulley, increasing the quadriceps extensor moment arm by roughly 30% in early flexion. The Q angle — anterior superior iliac spine to patella centre to tibial tuberosity, about 13 to 18 degrees — directs the quadriceps pull laterally on the patella, resisted by the vastus medialis obliquus and the medial retinaculum. Patellofemoral joint reaction force rises with knee flexion — near 3 times body weight climbing stairs, up to about 7 times body weight in a deep squat. That single number explains anterior knee pain in deep-squatting activities.

dPathomechanics — four named scenarios

Coronal malalignment: genu varum (bow legs — not uncommon in India from nutritional rickets) shifts load medially and accelerates medial compartment osteoarthritis; genu valgum shifts it laterally. Ligament failure: anterior cruciate ligament insufficiency removes the check to anterior tibial translation and rotational laxity — the pivot-shift give-way on pivoting; posterior cruciate injury reverses the translation, worse on downhill steps. Extensor mechanism: excessive Q angle, weak vastus medialis obliquus or tight lateral retinaculum cause lateral patellar tracking, retropatellar compression and eventual chondromalacia. Meniscal derangement: the locked bucket-handle tear blocks terminal extension — a knee that will not fully straighten is a mechanical sign, not pain behaviour.

Fig 5 — left: the Q angle from ASIS through patella to tibial tuberosity; right: the screw-home rotation of the tibia in terminal extension. Draw the two together and both the patellofemoral and tibiofemoral stories are told in one figure.

eClinical application — assessment and treatment in brief

Assessment: varus and valgus stress tests for the collateral ligaments, Lachman (most sensitive) and the anterior drawer for the ACL, posterior sag and drawer for the PCL, McMurray for meniscal tears, and patellar apprehension for instability. Treatment follows mechanism: strengthen quadriceps (especially vastus medialis) and hamstrings, correct dynamic valgus in landing and squatting, restore full extension after a locked knee, and respect the deep squat and cross-legged sitting so central to Indian daily life — after meniscal repair or arthroplasty, graded return to floor sitting is a realistic, culturally relevant goal.

Examiner's tip: "mechanics and pathomechanics" means normal first, abnormal second — keep the symmetry. Score the easy anchors: screw-home (with popliteus unlocking), meniscal hoop stress, Q angle with the 3×–7× body weight patellofemoral reaction, and one named malalignment with its compartment consequence.

Sources

  1. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — knee arthrokinematics.
  2. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — joint forces and meniscal load sharing.
  3. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — knee special tests.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain postural abnormalities seen in the thoracic region.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 7 — Posture: normal and abnormal, deformities

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Normal thoracic posture and its purpose1.5
Postural (flexible) kyphosis2
Scheuermann's disease2
Flat back and thoracic scoliosis2
Assessment of thoracic posture1.5
Treatment principles1

aNormal first — what the thoracic curve is for

The thoracic spine is a primary (kyphotic) curve, present from birth, measuring roughly 20 to 45 degrees of forward convexity. Mechanism first: the curve is a shock absorber — it increases column flexibility and raises load-bearing capacity, and the attached rib cage converts the thorax into a stiff protective cylinder for heart and lungs. Normal posture is assessed against a plumb line through the ear, shoulder and greater trochanter; the small, compensatory interplay of cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis keeps the head over the pelvis at minimal energy cost.

bPostural kyphosis — the flexible slouch

Increased round-back from sustained slouched sitting, weak thoracic extensors and tight anterior structures. The defining test: the deformity corrects on voluntary extension or on lying prone over a bolster. It causes fatigue-type ache across the mid-scapular region, and typically responds to postural re-education, thoracic extension strengthening and ergonomic correction — in young students, heavy backpacks carried on one shoulder make this a daily OPD presentation.

cScheuermann's disease — the structural round-back

Scheuermann's disease is a structural adolescent kyphosis: at least three adjacent vertebrae each wedged 5 degrees or more, with irregular vertebral end-plates and Schmorl's nodes, classically in the thoracic or thoracolumbar spine of teenage boys. It is rigid — it does not correct on extension or prone hyperextension over a bolster. Pain is variable; cardiopulmonary compromise appears only in severe curves. Differentiating rigid from flexible is the diagnostic hinge of the whole answer.

dFlat back and thoracic scoliosis — the two you must not omit

Thoracic flat back is loss of the normal kyphosis — a straight, stiff thoracic spine that transmits axial load more like a column, reducing shock absorption and often associated with a flat scapular posture and posterior ligamentous strain. Thoracic scoliosis is a lateral curvature with vertebral rotation — most often adolescent idiopathic, with asymmetric shoulder height, a prominent scapula, and a rib hump on forward bending. Osteoporotic compression fractures in the elderly form a third, increasingly common structural kyphosis — multiple wedge fractures in the postmenopausal Indian woman present as the dowager's hump, with loss of height and a compensatory cervical extension posture to keep the eyes level.

Fig 6 — left: the normal S with the plumb line; right: the exaggerated rigid kyphosis and the rib hump of scoliosis seen on forward bending. Mark the 20–45 degree normal range and the "three vertebrae, five degrees" rule.

eAssessment — how you demonstrate it in the exam hall

Inspect from the side and behind with the patient standing: plumb line alignment, shoulder and scapular symmetry, depth of the cervical and lumbar curves. The prone extension test distinguishes flexible from rigid kyphosis. The Adam's forward bend test with a scoliometer quantifies the rib hump; radiographic Cobb angle grades scoliosis (10 degrees defines it; bracing is usually considered above 25 to 40 degrees in a growing child). Always screen the whole spine — a primary lumbar curve produces a compensatory thoracic one.

fTreatment principles — brief, mechanism-linked

Flexible kyphosis: postural re-education, thoracic extensor and scapular retractor strengthening, anterior chest stretching, ergonomic advice. Structural kyphosis: extension exercises over a roll or bolster, and for progressive Scheuermann's in the growing child, a brace plus a structured exercise programme. Scoliosis: observation for small curves, bracing for moderate progressive curves in the immature, physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises as an adjunct, and surgery for severe ones. The osteoporotic spine additionally needs medical bone protection, safe weight-bearing and balance training to prevent the next fracture.

Examiner's tip: the structure of this answer is the marks. Normal parameters, then each abnormality with its one discriminating feature — flexible versus rigid, rib hump versus plumb line — and always end with assessment. Students who write four kyphosis paragraphs and forget flat back and scoliosis lose 2 easy marks.

  2. McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine — postural syndrome and sagittal alignment.
  3. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — scoliosis and kyphosis examination.

Q7. Write the biomechanical analysis of gait in ankle instability.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 8 — Gait and function: gait analysis, gait deviations

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Normal ankle and subtalar mechanics in gait2
Stance phase deviations in instability2.5
Swing phase deviations and compensations2
Kinetic and EMG changes1.5
Clinical implications and rehabilitation2

aNormal ankle mechanics in gait — the reference trace

At initial contact the ankle is neutral; through loading response it plantarflexes, then dorsiflexes progressively to about 10 degrees by terminal stance as the tibia advances over the foot, and finally plantarflexes sharply to about 20 degrees at push-off. The subtalar joint pronates at loading response (mobile adapter, shock absorption), then supinates into a rigid lever through push-off. The ankle plantarflexors deliver the burst for push-off, and the triceps surae works eccentrically through mid-stance to control tibial advancement. Keep this trace in mind: every deviation below is a corruption of it.

bStance phase — what the unstable ankle does

Chronic instability follows the typical inversion sprain; define both halves. Mechanical instability is ligament laxity (anterior talofibular ligament, calcaneofibular ligament) on stress testing. Functional ankle instability is recurrent giving way without measurable laxity — a sensorimotor failure. Mechanism: damaged mechanoreceptors in the torn ligaments and capsule feed inaccurate proprioception to the central nervous system, so reflex correction of sudden inversion arrives late. During stance the patient shows excessive or prolonged pronation or sudden inversion episodes at loading response, early heel rise from a shortened, guarded push-off, reduced single-limb support time on the affected limb, decreased stride and step length, slower comfortable speed, and a wider base of support. The ground reaction force vector passes lateral to the ankle precisely when the peroneals are least ready.

cSwing phase — clearance at any cost

The unstable foot is carried in slight plantarflexion and inversion to protect the lateral structures, so toe clearance suffers. Compensations appear from the next joint up: increased hip and knee flexion (an exaggerated steppage-like strategy), hip hiking of the swing-side pelvis, and sometimes circumduction. The result is an energy-costly swing with poor foot placement accuracy at the next initial contact — and the cycle of self-distrust continues.

dKinetic and EMG changes — the measurable story

Laboratory gait analysis shows reduced peak plantarflexion moment and power burst at push-off (a weak push), altered vertical ground reaction force shape with a flattened second peak, and increased ankle inversion moments in some patients. Electromyography reveals delayed peroneal reaction time, reduced peroneus longus strength, and co-contraction of the pretibial group with the triceps surae to splint the joint. Dynamic balance tests such as the Star Excursion Balance Anterior reach (anterior reach deficit greater than about 4 cm between limbs predicts future sprain) and single-leg hop tests objectify it in the clinic.

Fig 7 — one gait cycle bar with the four key deviations flagged along it. Anchoring each deviation to its phase converts a memorised list into a biomechanical analysis.

eClinical implications — what rehabilitation must fix

Because the mechanism is sensorimotor, rehabilitation is more than strengthening: proprioceptive and balance training (single-leg stance progressions, wobble board, eyes closed), peroneal strength and reaction training, perturbation and hopping/landing control, agility before return to sport, and taping or bracing during the vulnerable early weeks. Barefoot balance work on uneven surfaces is practical in the Indian setting where much daily life occurs unshod — a culturally native form of proprioceptive training.

Examiner's tip: "biomechanical analysis" demands phase-by-phase structure — normal first, then stance, then swing, then the measurable kinetics. Spend the first paragraph on the normal trace; deviations only earn marks when the reader can see what they deviate from.
