Adams forward-bend test with scoliometerChild bends forward; inclinometer placed over the rib prominenceAngle of trunk rotation at or above 5–7°Rotational scoliosis; refer for radiographs
Cobb angle measurementAP radiograph; angle between the most tilted end vertebrae10° or moreDefines and grades scoliosis; serial value tracks progression
Mehta rib-vertebral angle difference (RVAD)Measured on the AP radiograph of an infantile curveRVAD of 20° or moreHigh risk of progression in infantile scoliosis
Leg-length assessment with blocksMeasured blocks under the short limb until the pelvis levelsCurve disappears with levellingFunctional (leg-length) scoliosis, not structural
Dysraphism/developmental screenSkin inspection, abdominal reflexes, milestone review, spinal ultrasound in infancyCutaneous stigmata, reflex asymmetry, delayed milestonesNon-idiopathic cause — refer for MRI and paediatric opinion

In this child: Adams forward-bend test positive (rib hump present); limb lengths equal, so functional (leg-length) scoliosis is unlikely; Cobb angle and RVAD awaited (radiographs pending); dysraphism/developmental screen negative to date.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Lateral spinal curvature with rib rotation
  • Progression risk if the RVAD is raised

Functional limitations

  • None — milestones appropriate for age

Disabilities

  • Potential future cardiopulmonary restriction if a severe curve progresses
11. Functional diagnosis

Probable infantile idiopathic scoliosis in a 2-year-old (breech delivery, painless curve, normal neurological screen, age-appropriate milestones), with the risk of curve progression to be quantified by the Cobb angle and RVAD.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Complete the work-up (radiograph, RVAD, neurological screen); baseline Cobb angle documented; family educated.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks and beyond). Curve stable or resolving (no increase of 5° or more between radiographs); milestones maintained; skin intact under any cast or brace; surgery avoided if possible.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: observation — most infantile curves resolve spontaneously; radiographs every 4–6 months. Stage 2: for progressive curves, serial Mehta derotational casting under anaesthesia every 2–3 months, then a custom TLSO once the child stands reliably. Stage 3: surgery (growing rods or magnetically controlled growing rods) only for severe progressive deformity.

14. Home programme

Prone play, symmetric carrying, skin checks under any cast or brace; report new weakness, limp or bladder/bowel change.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Explain the pre- and post-operative assessment of fracture neck of femur.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5a — assessment of fractures: pre-operative and post-operative

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Classification (Garden) and medical pre-operative assessment2
Structured pre-operative physiotherapy assessment3
Post-operative assessment by fixation type, with precautions3
Complications screening and outcome measures1
Rehabilitation phases, discharge and home planning1

aClassification and the medical picture before you start

Fracture neck of femur is the classic fragility fracture of an elderly woman after a trivial fall; in Indian practice, expect osteoporotic bone, comorbid diabetes or hypertension, and often a delay before admission from a village home. Classify with the Garden system: types I and II are undisplaced (valgus impacted or incomplete) and are usually treated by fixation — cancellous screws or a dynamic hip screw; types III and IV are displaced and typically treated by arthroplasty — hemiarthroplasty in the frail or cognitively impaired, total hip replacement in the active elderly — with cemented stems allowing immediate weight-bearing. The physiotherapist's pre-operative assessment is embedded in this medical picture: note the comorbidities, American Society of Anesthesiologists grade, frailty and nutritional status, medications (anticoagulants, steroids), and remember that this same fall may reflect a FRAX-level osteoporotic risk that will need addressing after the hip heals.

bStructured pre-operative physiotherapy assessment

Four clusters. Function and cognition: pre-injury mobility level (walking to the field? using a stick?), independence in activities of daily living, cognitive state — delirium risk predicts rehabilitation success more than the fracture pattern does. Regional examination: the injured hip held in shortening and external rotation, pain, skin integrity over the heel and sacrum (pressure ulcers begin in the first hours on the ward), bilateral hip range of motion and strength to serve as the patient's own baseline, peripheral pulses. Cardiorespiratory: chest expansion, breath sounds, baseline effort tolerance — elderly supine patients decondition within days. Pre-operative teaching — which is assessment turned therapeutic: deep-breathing and incentive spirometry, ankle pumps and circulation exercises, log-rolling technique, and rehearsing the first transfers, so the post-operative day is not the first teaching day.

cPost-operative assessment: the surgical decision shapes yours

Assess systematically on day one and document daily. General: vital signs, pain score, wound and dressing, drain if present, hydration, and a delirium check. DVT screen: daily calf circumference and tenderness — calf pain on dorsiflexion alone is unreliable, so examine for swelling, warmth and circumference difference, and remember pharmacological prophylaxis is the main protection. Regional by fixation: after internal fixation, weight-bearing is often restricted (touch or partial) until union is shown radiographically at about six to twelve weeks, and assessment focuses on protecting the fixation while maintaining mobility; after cemented arthroplasty, weight-bearing as tolerated usually begins day one, and assessment focuses on the dislocation precautions of a posterior approach — no hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation — while an anterolateral approach relaxes these. Then measure: hip range of motion, abductor and quadriceps strength, sitting and standing balance, and gait with the correct aid — frame first, then stick. Above all, re-assess daily, because a post-operative hip deteriorates fast when it is not looked at.

Fig 9 — Draw the timeline with four nodes and the two weight-bearing tracks (fixation versus arthroplasty) beneath it. Showing that the surgical choice changes your assessment is the mark-scoring insight of the figure.

dComplications and outcome measures

Screen at every session for the five classical complications: deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism (sudden dyspnoea is an emergency), wound infection, dislocation of an arthroplasty (shortened, internally rotated limb after an awkward movement), avascular necrosis and non-union after fixation (persistent groin pain with late failure to progress), and pressure ulcers plus chest infection from immobility — the last two are the physiotherapist's own preventable complications. Outcome measurement should be named and specific: the Harris Hip Score (100 points — 44 for pain, 47 for function, 4 for absence of deformity, 5 for range of motion) is the classic post-operative hip instrument, complemented by the timed up-and-go test and an activities-of-daily-living scale for the geriatric picture.

eRehabilitation phases, discharge and home planning

Phase the programme: bed mobility and breathing on day zero; sitting and transfers day one; standing and walking with a frame days two to three; progression to a stick and stairs within the first fortnight; then strengthening of abductors and quadriceps, balance re-education, and endurance. Discharge planning is assessment applied to the house: most Indian homes have floor-level toilets, squatting baths and possibly stairs — teach the patient and family accordingly, supply a raised toilet seat if needed, train a caregiver in safe handling, and arrange follow-up for osteoporosis management, because the fracture that predicts the next fracture is this one.

Examiner's tip: the question asks for both pre- AND post-operative assessment — students who rush the pre-operative half cap themselves at half marks. Pre-operative teaching is physiotherapy assessment with a therapeutic intent; say exactly that, and split your answer visibly fifty-fifty.

Sources

  1. Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL — Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures (ref 16): neck of femur management and rehabilitation.
  2. Maxey L, Magnusson JA — Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient (ref 13): post-operative hip protocols.
  3. Garden RS — J Bone Joint Surg Br, 1961: the classification of femoral neck fractures.
  4. Harris WH — J Bone Joint Surg Am, 1969: the hip rating score.
  5. Kanis JA et al. — Osteoporos Int: FRAX and fracture-risk context.

On the evaluation form — Q9: Fracture neck of femur — pre- and post-operative

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 72-year-old woman; slipped in the bathroom; groin pain and unable to bear weight (pre-operative presentation). Risk screen: comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, ischaemic heart disease), anticoagulant use (inform the surgical team), last meal, bladder and bowel habits, pressure areas, cognition and delirium risk, previous falls, home layout and support. The Garden classification (I–IV) drives fixation versus arthroplasty; watch for dehydration and hypothermia.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Pre-op: limb shortening with external rotation and adduction; cannot lift the heel. Post-op: scar clean and dry; sacral and heel skin checked every session.

On palpation. Pre-op groin tenderness; post-op calf tenderness screened for DVT.

1. Motor assessment. Post-op ROM: after a posterior-approach arthroplasty avoid combined adduction–internal rotation and flexion beyond 90°; the fixation group follows the surgeon's protocol. MMT: hip abductors, extensors and quadriceps graded serially; limb length re-measured after arthroplasty. End-feel and reflexes not documented.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation over the foot and lateral leg (sciatic/peroneal territory) and ankle power; any new deficit is reported immediately. Dermatomes and myotomes screened accordingly.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Pre-op: bed mobility and spirometry teaching. Post-op: transfers, walker gait and stairs before discharge. Outcome measures: Oxford Hip Score (0–48), Harris Hip Score (0–100), TUG (seconds), Berg Balance Scale (0–56), NPRS (0–10).

4. Gait analysis. Post-op walker gait, weight-bearing per the plan — protected after screw/DHS fixation, as tolerated after cemented arthroplasty; stairs before discharge. Formal stance/swing, cadence and step/stride parameters not documented.

5. Balance. Berg Balance Scale recorded (0–56); balance retraining included in the plan.

6. Hand function. Grips the walking frame (assistive device); weaning off the frame is planned; reaching, grasping and releasing otherwise not documented.

7. Coordination. Not documented.

8. Investigations

Radiographs with the Garden classification (I–IV) of the femoral neck fracture guide fixation versus arthroplasty; no films reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Log roll testGentle passive internal rotation of the extended hipSharp groin pain, guardingIntracapsular hip pathology — NOF fracture
Axial heel percussionTap along the long axis of the leg through the heelGroin pain on the affected sideFemoral neck fracture
Patellar-pubic percussion (auscultatory) testStethoscope on the pubis, tap each patellaDuller note on the fractured sideOccult NOF fracture when radiographs are negative
True and apparent leg lengthASIS to medial malleolus (true); umbilicus to medial malleolus (apparent)Shortening on the affected sideDisplaced fracture pre-op; limb length after arthroplasty
Trendelenburg testSingle-leg stance on the operated sideContralateral pelvis dropsGluteus medius insufficiency post-operatively
Thomas testSupine; patient hugs the opposite knee while the tested leg is loweredTested hip lifts into flexionPost-operative hip flexion contracture

In this patient: limb-length assessment positive pre-op (shortening with external rotation and adduction on the affected side); the individual results of the log roll, axial heel percussion, patellar-pubic percussion, Trendelenburg and Thomas tests were not separately documented (Trendelenburg is reassessed serially after surgery).

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Post-surgical pain
  • Hip abductor and quadriceps weakness
  • Precaution-limited ROM

Functional limitations

  • Transfers and ambulation with an aid

Disabilities

  • Temporary loss of independent living
11. Functional diagnosis

Status post fracture neck of femur (fixation or arthroplasty) in an elderly woman, with post-surgical pain, hip abductor and quadriceps weakness and precaution-limited range, dependent for transfers and walker-assisted ambulation, and a temporary loss of independent living.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pain 3/10 or less on the NPRS; independent bed exercises, ankle pumps, breathing exercises and safe walker ambulation.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Ambulation with a stick or unaided; abductors 4–5/5 with a negative Trendelenburg; Berg and TUG at age-normal level; safe return home.

13. Treatment plan

Pre-op: chest care and incentive spirometry, ankle pumps, log rolling, pressure-area care, counselling. Post-op days 1–7: phased weight-bearing per fixation type; isometric quadriceps and hip abduction within precautions. Weeks 2–12: resisted strengthening, balance retraining, scar mobilisation, stairs, weaning off the frame. After a posterior-approach arthroplasty, dislocation precautions for 6–12 weeks: no low chairs or floor sitting, no crossing legs, no bending past 90°. Complications monitored: DVT, pressure ulcer, chest infection, dislocation, re-fall.

14. Home programme

Daily exercises, raised toilet seat, good lighting, loose rugs removed, osteoporosis follow-up and fall prevention.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Determine the use of ICF in musculoskeletal diagnosis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 6a — functional assessment and ICF

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Structure and components of the ICF2
Linking musculoskeletal findings across ICF levels with a worked example3
ICF core sets for musculoskeletal conditions2
Merits and limitations versus biomedical diagnosis2
Clinical application: goal setting and outcome measurement1

aWhat the ICF is

The ICF — the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, published in 2001 — is the framework that describes a health condition not only as pathology but as a lived experience. Its architecture is worth drawing: at the centre sits the health condition; around it, two components of functioning — body functions and structures (impairment at this level) and activity (limitation) — together with participation (restriction); and around everything, the contextual factors: environmental (products, people, attitudes, policies — barriers or facilitators) and personal (age, sex, coping style, occupation). Every arrow between these boxes is bidirectional, which is the whole point: disability is an interaction, not a property of the person, and the ICF replaced the older ICIDH's linear, consequence-based model with this dynamic one.

bLinking musculoskeletal findings to ICF levels

Apply it with one worked example and the abstract becomes marks. A 58-year-old farmer with knee osteoarthritis: at the level of body functions and structures — knee pain, crepitus, restricted flexion, quadriceps weakness (impairments). At the level of activity — limited walking distance, difficulty squatting, and — write the culturally specific ones, they earn marks — difficulty sitting cross-legged at meals, squatting over an Indian toilet, and climbing into a bus. At the level of participation — cannot plough his fields, cannot attend the temple festival or family functions, loses his role as breadwinner. Environmental factors: the house is on a hillock with steps (barrier), the village bus has high steps (barrier), a supportive joint family (facilitator), distance from a physiotherapy centre (barrier). Personal factors: 58 years, high pain tolerance, fear of surgery. Notice the diagnostic shift: the biomedical diagnosis says "knee osteoarthritis"; the ICF profile says what that disease does to this person's life — and physiotherapy is the profession whose whole value lies in that second statement.

Fig 10 — Draw the classic ICF box diagram with double-headed arrows in every direction and "knee osteoarthritis" in the centre. Writing the worked example into the boxes converts the diagram from decoration into the answer itself.

cICF core sets for musculoskeletal conditions

To make the classification practical at the bedside, the WHO's ICF research branch developed comprehensive and brief ICF core sets — agreed short lists of the categories most relevant to a condition, so that two clinicians assess the same things. Core sets exist for several musculoskeletal problems, notably chronic low back pain and osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. Using a core set turns the ICF from theory into a checklist: the clinician rates each category (for instance, pain, joint mobility, walking, remunerative employment) with a qualifier from 0 (no problem) to 4 (complete problem), producing a functioning profile at first assessment and a re-testable measure of change thereafter.

dMerits and limitations

Merits: it completes the diagnosis — the pathology plus what the pathology does; it creates a common professional language across orthopaedics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and social work; it justifies holistic intervention to funders and insurers; it is patient-centred because activity and participation are the patient's own goals; and it supports the legal and administrative documentation of disability, which in India matters for certification and benefits. Limitations: completeness costs time — a full ICF profile is heavy for a busy OPD; coding requires training; personal factors are deliberately not classified, so their use is inconsistent; and it does not name pathology — it grades the consequences of pathology, so the ICF supplements but never replaces the biomedical and movement-system diagnosis.

eDetermining its use in practice

Conclude the way the verb "determine" invites: use the ICF as the second half of every musculoskeletal diagnosis. Pair the impairment diagnosis (subacromial pain syndrome, L5 radiculopathy, knee osteoarthritis) with an ICF profile of activity limitation and participation restriction, and let environmental and personal factors be assessed explicitly. Set SMART goals at the activity and participation level — "walk to the temple without a stick" beats "improve hip abduction by 10 degrees" as a goal a patient understands — and choose outcome measures that map to those levels. Re-assess with the same qualifiers, and the ICF becomes the audit trail of the entire treatment.

Examiner's tip: the commonest failure is describing the ICF in the abstract. One named patient with culturally grounded examples — cross-legged sitting, squat toilet, farming, a festival — used consistently through every component, takes this answer from definition-recall to distinction.

Sources

  1. World Health Organization — International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), Geneva, 2001.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ — Physical Rehabilitation (ref 10): disablement frameworks and outcome measurement.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH — Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System (ref 1): linking impairment to mechanical limitation.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper III

QP 8131 · 14-Nov-2025 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1The assessment ladder

  • Subjective → look → feel → move → special tests → synthesis; history alone gives about 80 per cent of the diagnosis.
  • Cyriax order: AROM, then PROM with end-feel, then resisted — separates contractile from inert tissue.
  • Inspection: compare sides; wasting, swelling, gait, posture before ever touching.

2Shoulder impingement

  • Neer stages I–III: under 25 oedema, 25–40 fibrosis, over 40 spurs and tears.
  • Neer and Hawkins: sensitivity about 0.8, specificity about 0.5 — screen, never confirm alone.
  • Painful arc 60–120°; persistent weakness or lag sign = think cuff tear.

3Lumbar disc herniation

  • SLR: sensitivity 0.91, specificity 0.26; crossed SLR: 0.28 and 0.90 — rule out versus rule in.
  • L4–L5 hits L5 root; L5–S1 hits S1; L5 has no reflex — use great-toe extension.
  • Conclude on a cluster: dermatomal leg pain + objective deficit + positive neurodynamic + centralisation.

4Autonomous practice

  • First-contact physiotherapy under direct access: you decide treat-or-refer, and you own the decision.
  • Novice = hypothetico-deductive; expert = pattern recognition; wisdom = knowing when to switch.
  • Red-flag screen on day one AND whenever the patient fails to improve as expected.

5Knee instability

  • Lachman 0.85 / 0.94 at 20–30°; pivot shift 0.24 / 0.98 — confirm, never screen; anterior drawer weak acutely.
  • Valgus at 30° = MCL; at 0° = cruciate involved too; posterior sag = PCL.
  • Grades: I pain only, II laxity with endpoint, III laxity without endpoint; acute haemarthrosis after a pivot = ACL.

6Exercise testing

  • Purpose: quantify impairment, set baseline, prove progress; PAR-Q+ and vitals first.
  • Stop criteria: BP drop, angina, RPE above 17, dizziness — memorise all four.
  • 6-minute walk for endurance; 6–10 RM to estimate 1 RM; H:Q ratio about 0.6.

7Spinal orthoses

  • Three-point pressure and extension moment explain Taylor, Jewett and TLSO at one stroke.
  • Halo = unstable cervical; Jewett / TLSO = stable thoracolumbar; Milwaukee = apex above T8.
  • Every brace named must carry one indication and one limitation; wean to prevent disuse.

8The two-year-old with a thoracic curve

  • Under three = infantile idiopathic; left thoracic curve in a boy; most resolve spontaneously.
  • Cobb 10° threshold; Mehta RVAD above 20° or rib phase 2 = progression risk.
  • Always: skin (café-au-lait, hairy patch), neurological exam, hips and leg lengths; congenital needs cardiac and renal screening.

9Fracture neck of femur

  • Garden I–II undisplaced → fixation; III–IV → arthroplasty; cemented stem = weight-bearing day one.
  • Posterior precautions: no flexion beyond 90°, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation.
  • Harris Hip Score: 44 pain + 47 function + 4 deformity + 5 motion = 100; watch DVT, dislocation, AVN, non-union, pressure sores.

10ICF in musculoskeletal diagnosis

  • Five boxes around the health condition: body functions and structures, activity, participation, environmental, personal — all arrows bidirectional.
  • Impairment / limitation / restriction is the vocabulary triplet examiners look for.
  • Indian worked examples: squatting, cross-legged sitting, floor-level toilet, festival participation, farm work.
keep-if-nothing-else: the ladder (look-feel-move-test-synthesize), Neer-Hawkins-painful arc, SLR 0.91/0.26 with crossed SLR 0.28/0.90, Lachman 0.85/0.94, Cobb 10 degrees and RVAD 20 degrees, Garden I–IV with the fifty-fifty pre/post split, and the five ICF boxes with one knee-osteoarthritis worked example — that is the minimum cargo for the exam hall.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Discuss the interventions to improve the mobility of the shoulder joint following adhesive capsulitis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 1 — Interventions for physiologic impairments: mobility

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition, stages (freezing / frozen / thawing) and capsular pattern of restriction2
Graded joint mobilization (Maitland grades, sustained grade IV, Mulligan MWM)2.5
Prolonged end-range capsular stretching, pendular exercises, PNF hold-relax2
Self-mobilization, home program and progression logic1.5
Evidence, adjuncts and conclusion2

aMechanism first: what has actually stiffened?

Adhesive capsulitis is an idiopathic contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule with a chronic inflammatory-fibrotic cascade — the capsule thickens, folds in, and loses its normal extensibility. The restriction follows the capsular pattern: external rotation is lost most, then abduction, then internal rotation. Screen for the common Indian associations — diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and postmenopausal women in their fifth and sixth decades — because they change prognosis and the pace of recovery. Clinically stage it: freezing (pain more than stiffness, about 0–3 months), frozen (stiffness more than pain, 3–9 months), thawing (slow spontaneous recovery, 9–24 months). The stage decides how aggressive you dare to be.

bGraded joint mobilization — the spine of treatment

Use Maitland grades I–II oscillations purely for pain in the freezing stage, then move to grade III–IV stretching oscillations, and finally sustained grade IV glides in the directions of lost range — inferior glide for abduction, posterior glide for internal rotation and flexion, anterior glide for external rotation. Sustained glides of 20–30 seconds produce more creep in the contracted capsule than brief oscillations. Add Mulligan's mobilization-with-movement: a lateral glide of the humeral head combined with the patient's own elevation gives an immediate pain-free range gain that you then tape to hold.

cProlonged end-range stretching and PNF

Heat (hot pack or whirlpool) over the posterior capsule for 10 minutes before stretching makes the tissue more extensible. Follow with prolonged end-range stretches held 30–60 seconds: pendulum (Codman) exercises in the early painful stage, wall-climbing, overhead pulley, towel stretch for internal rotation behind the back, and finger-ladder for flexion. Add PNF hold-relax (contract-relax) of the internal rotators and adductors to exploit post-isometric relaxation before the final stretch. Each stretch should end-range the capsule, not just swing the arm.

dSelf-mobilization, home program and progression

Teach self-sustained inferior glide with a belt or towel while elevating, so the patient treats the capsule three times daily at home — the supervised session alone will never win this two-year disease. Progress by hold time, not by force: 30 seconds to 60 seconds, then add gentle weighted hangs in the thawing stage. Hydrotherapy in a warm pool is superb in India — the buoyancy and warmth allow pain-free end-range work.

Fig 1 — Capsular pattern on the left, three stages on the right; the stage tells you how aggressively to mobilize.
Examiner's tip: name the stage and justify the force from it — forceful stretching in the freezing stage worsens pain and loses marks; the same force in thawing earns them.

Sources

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 10th ed.
  3. Wilk KE, Brotzman SB. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation.

On the evaluation form — Q1: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)

I. Subjective examination

A 52-year-old female homemaker with an 8-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with four months of progressive right shoulder pain and stiffness. Chief complaints: she cannot hook her blouse, comb her hair or sleep on the affected side. Past medical history: type 2 diabetes of eight years' duration. Symptom analysis — site: right shoulder; onset: progressive, no trauma; duration: four months; type: dull ache, worst at night; severity: NPRS 6/10 at rest, 8/10 on movement; aggravating factors: shoulder movement and lying on the right side; relieving factors: not reported. Pain evaluation: night-dominant pain with a mechanical pattern on movement. Red-flag screen: no trauma and no radicular symptoms reported. Vital signs normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. The arm is held adducted and internally rotated; deltoid wasting with loss of the normal shoulder contour.

On palpation. Tenderness over the anterior capsule, the coracoid process and the deltoid insertion; no local warmth.

1. Motor assessment

Passive ROM follows the capsular pattern: external rotation most limited (20°), then abduction (80°), then internal rotation, all with a capsular end-feel. MMT 3+/5 through the available range. Biceps, triceps and brachioradialis reflexes normal. Deltoid girth 1.5 cm less than on the uninvolved side.

2. Sensory assessment

Sensation intact over the C4–T1 dermatomes; together with the normal reflex screen this excludes cervical radiculopathy and axillary nerve involvement.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Hand-behind-back and overhead reach markedly limited; dressing, grooming and side-sleeping affected; transfers independent. Outcome measures selected: SPADI (0–100, higher = worse), QuickDASH (0–100), NPRS (0–10) and goniometric passive ROM.

4. Gait analysis

Gait independent; transfers independent; no assistive device used.

5. Balance

Static and dynamic balance not documented in this case.

6. Hand function

Reaching overhead and taking the hand behind the back markedly limited; hooking the blouse and combing the hair are restricted by shoulder range rather than hand dexterity. No assistive device.

7. Coordination

Not documented in this case.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Coracoid pain testFirm thumb pressure over the coracoid, sides comparedMarked pain on the affected sidePositive in this patient (matches the palpated coracoid tenderness) — anterior capsular inflammation
Passive ROM patternPassive glenohumeral external rotation, abduction, internal rotationGlobal restriction, external rotation worstPositive — confirms capsular restriction
Drop arm testArm passively abducted to 90°, then lowered slowlyUncontrolled descentResult not stated in the case record; a positive test would suggest rotator cuff tear
Spurling's testCervical extension, lateral flexion and axial compressionArm pain reproducedResult not stated; absence of radicular symptoms and a clear neurological screen argue against cervical referral, which would need re-examination if positive
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Pain (6/10 at rest, 8/10 on movement)
  • Capsular restriction of glenohumeral ROM in the capsular pattern
  • Weak shoulder musculature (3+/5) with deltoid wasting

Functional limitations

  • Dressing and grooming (hooking blouse, combing hair)
  • Side-sleeping on the affected side

Disabilities

  • Reduced household and social participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to perform overhead and hand-behind-back activities of daily living secondary to pain and capsular restriction of the right glenohumeral joint (adhesive capsulitis).

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): reduce night pain from 6/10 to 3/10; gain 15° passive external rotation; independent in home stretches.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): pain ≤2/10; functional ROM (external rotation 60°, abduction 150°); SPADI reduced by 30%; independent dressing and grooming.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1, painful (weeks 1–2): hot pack 15 minutes, pendulum exercises, grade I–II mobilizations, TENS; sleep supine with a pillow under the arm. Stage 2, stiff (weeks 3–6): sustained grade III–IV posterior and inferior glenohumeral mobilizations; passive external rotation, abduction and internal rotation stretches. Stage 3, functional (weeks 7–12): elastic-band strengthening 3 × 10, closed-chain weight-bearing, functional reaching; progress stretch range by 5–10° weekly as pain allows.

14. Home programme

Passive ER, abduction and IR stretches held 30 s × 5, twice daily; home pulleys, wall climbing, towel stretch behind the back and rod exercises, 10 repetitions thrice daily; continue into stage 3 with elastic-band strengthening and functional reaching; sleep supine with a pillow under the arm.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Explain the adjunct therapies in managing chronic heel pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 2 — Management of pain: adjuvant methods

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Causes of chronic heel pain and mechanism of chronicity2
Biomechanical adjuncts: footwear, orthoses, taping, night splints2
Electrotherapy adjuncts: ultrasound, iontophoresis, shockwave2
Dry needling and soft-tissue adjuncts1.5
Exercise base, evidence (Rathleff) and conclusion2.5

aMechanism first: why does the heel stay painful for months?

Chronic heel pain (beyond 3 months) is most often plantar fasciopathy at the medial calcaneal tubercle, but the differential includes fat pad atrophy, calcaneal stress reaction, and Baxter's nerve entrapment — mention them and you separate yourself from the average script. Histology in chronic cases shows degenerative, mucoid change with fibroblast proliferation, not acute inflammation, so the word "fasciitis" is a misnomer for the chronic stage — treat it as a loading problem, not an inflammation problem.

bBiomechanical adjuncts

Off-load the origin of the fascia: soft heel cups or silicone heel pads for fat pad symptoms, prefabricated medial arch orthoses for the pronated foot, and firm-soled footwear — in India, flat chappals and hard bathroom tiles at home are common perpetuators worth asking about. Low-Dye taping supports the medial arch and gives immediate, measurable pain relief; if tape helps, an orthosis usually will. A night splint holding the ankle in about 5 degrees of dorsiflexion with toes dorsiflexed prevents the classic first-step morning pain by keeping the fascia lengthened overnight.

cElectrotherapy and shockwave adjuncts

Therapeutic ultrasound (1 MHz, around 0.5–1.0 W/cm²) over the calcaneal insertion is the traditional Indian OPD choice; evidence is modest, so frame it as a pain-relieving adjunct during the loading phase. Iontophoresis with dexamethasone gives short-term relief superior to placebo in some trials. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy is the best-evidenced of the passive adjuncts for chronic plantar fasciopathy — three sessions, roughly 2000 impulses — and is worth committing for recalcitrant cases.

dDry needling and soft-tissue work

Trigger points in gastrocnemius-soleus and the plantar intrinsic muscles refer to the heel and maintain the pain; dry needling or ischemic compression of the gastroc-soleus complex plus stretching of the triceps surae reduces fascial strain at the calcaneal origin. This link between calf tightness and heel pain is a favourite viva question.

eThe base under the adjuncts: exercise and evidence

Adjuncts palliate; loading cures. Progressive eccentric loading — heel drops off a step — has been the standard, and Rathleff and colleagues showed that high-load strength training (weighted heel raises with a towel under the toes, every second day for 3 months) produced markedly better results than stretching alone at 3 and 12 months. Conclusion: correct footwear and taping to off-load, shockwave or dry needling for pain, and a progressive high-load strengthening program as the definitive base.

Fig 2 — Strength training is the base; taping, shockwave and needling sit on top of it, never instead of it.
Examiner's tip: spend two lines on differential diagnosis before jumping to treatment — fat pad atrophy is worsened by stretching and steroid injection, and missing it costs the answer its clinical realism.

Sources

  1. Rathleff MS et al. High-load strength training versus stretching for chronic heel pain (BJSM / RSM series).
  2. Chui K et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.

On the evaluation form — Q2: Chronic heel pain (plantar fasciopathy)

I. Subjective examination

A 48-year-old male shopkeeper whose work involves standing 10–12 hours daily (BMI 29) presents with seven months of right heel pain. Chief complaint: classical first-step pain on waking and after sitting. Symptom analysis — site: right heel; onset: insidious; duration: seven months; type: sharp on first steps, dull by evening; severity: NPRS 7/10 on first steps; aggravating factors: first steps after rest, prolonged standing; relieving factors: not reported. Red-flag screen: no night pain and no numbness. Vital signs normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Pes planus with arch collapse on weight bearing and calcaneal valgus; type of gait: antalgic.

On palpation. Point tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle and over the proximal plantar fascia; tight gastrocnemius-soleus complex (increased deep tissue tension).

1. Motor assessment

Ankle dorsiflexion 5° with the knee extended. MMT: plantarflexors and invertors 4/5; hallux flexors 4/5. Functional strength: single-leg heel raises 8 (fewer than the expected 20). Achilles reflex intact. Girth symmetrical.

2. Sensory assessment

Plantar sensation intact; tarsal tunnel Tinel's test negative — excludes tarsal tunnel syndrome, and with an intact Achilles reflex excludes S1 radiculopathy.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Standing tolerance 30 minutes; painful first steps limit occupational walking. Outcome measures selected: NPRS (0–10) for first-step pain, LEFS (0–80, higher = better) and the Foot Health Status Questionnaire (foot-specific quality of life).

4. Gait analysis

Antalgic gait with reduced push-off on the right.

5. Balance

Single-leg balance normal.

6. Hand function

Not relevant to this case.

7. Coordination

Not documented in this case.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Windlass testGreat toe passively dorsiflexed, loading the fasciaHeel pain reproducedPositive in this patient — confirms plantar fasciopathy (consistent with medial calcaneal point tenderness)
Silfverskiöld testDorsiflexion with the knee extended, then flexedLimited only with the knee extendedPositive — isolated gastrocnemius tightness (consistent with the documented 5° dorsiflexion with knee extended)
Heel squeeze testCalcaneus compressed between the palmsFocal bony painResult not stated in the case record; a positive test would raise suspicion of calcaneal stress fracture
Navicular drop testNavicular height sitting versus standingDrop ≥10 mmFindings consistent with the observed arch collapse and calcaneal valgus — excessive pronation; numerical drop not recorded
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Insertional heel pain
  • Restricted ankle dorsiflexion
  • Weak foot intrinsics

Functional limitations

  • Painful first steps
  • Poor standing tolerance

Disabilities

  • Difficulty sustaining shop work
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to stand and walk for occupational demands secondary to insertional plantar-fascia pain with restricted ankle dorsiflexion.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): first-step pain from 7/10 to 4/10; gain 5° dorsiflexion; stand 60 minutes.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): pain ≤2/10 on morning steps; 15 heel raises; full shop duties; LEFS up ≥9 points.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): ice massage 5–10 minutes after work, contrast bath, ultrasound 1 MHz over the fascial origin, IFT for analgesia. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): plantar fascia stretch (ankle dorsiflexed, toes extended, 30 s × 3, thrice daily); eccentric heel drops off a step 3 × 15 daily; heel raises over a towel roll 3 × 8–12 on alternate days. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): towel curls, short-foot holds 10 s × 10, progressive loading, graded return to prolonged standing.

14. Home programme

Morning arch ball-rolling; night splint if morning pain persists; silicone heel cups; weight-management advice; continue the stretching and eccentric regimen above daily.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. How do you determine the methods to promote physical activity in musculoskeletal conditions?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 3 — Functional training and physical activity promotion

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Why physical activity matters in MSK conditions1.5
Assessment of current activity, readiness and barriers2
Prescription: WHO 2020 guidelines and FITT framework2
Behaviour change methods matched to readiness2.5
Monitoring, progression, relapse planning and conclusion2

aMechanism first: why inactivity is the disease

In every musculoskeletal condition — osteoarthritis, low back pain, rheumatoid arthritis — pain triggers a downward spiral of avoidance, deconditioning, weight gain and more pain: the fear-avoidance cycle. Physical activity is therefore not a health footnote but the primary disease-modifying intervention. The question asks how you determine the method, so your answer must be a decision process, not a shopping list.

bStep 1 — assess the person, not just the joint

Quantify current activity (steps per day, minutes of moderate activity per week, a simple activity diary or IPAQ-short), then grade readiness to change using the transtheoretical model — precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance. Next, list the barriers honestly: pain and fear, fatigue, comorbidity, and the Indian realities — heat, traffic, unsafe walking roads, the belief that "rest is best" after joint pain, and women's household time constraints. The barrier profile selects the method.

cStep 2 — prescribe against a standard

Anchor the target to the WHO activity guidelines (2020): 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week in bouts that can be as short as a few minutes, muscle-strengthening on two or more days, and for older adults, balance training on three or more days. Critically, WHO states that some activity is better than none — start where the person is. Build the FITT plan: frequency, intensity (Borg rating of perceived exertion 11–13, or the talk test — able to talk, not sing), time and type. Walking is the cheapest and most culturally acceptable aerobic mode in India; yoga doubles as flexibility and balance training.

dStep 3 — match the behaviour change method to readiness

For someone in precontemplation, education about pain and deconditioning (not scare tactics) plus motivational interviewing — open questions, reflective listening, rolling with resistance — moves them to contemplation. In preparation, set SMART goals with the patient ("30-minute walk before work, five days a week") and write them down. In action, use graded activity, self-monitoring (pedometer or phone step counter), feedback and social support — walking groups, family involvement. In maintenance, plan for relapse: pain flares are setbacks, not failures.

eStep 4 — monitor, progress, and conclude

Review every 2–4 weeks: recheck steps, symptoms (pain during and 24 hours after activity should settle to baseline), and confidence. Progress intensity and duration by roughly 10% per week when symptoms allow. Conclusion: the method is determined by assessing activity status and readiness, matching the behaviour-change technique to the stage, prescribing to the WHO standard with FITT, and monitoring — the therapist is a coach, not a machine operator.

Fig 3 — A four-step ladder: assess, match, prescribe, monitor. Drawing the ladder itself answers "how do you determine".
Examiner's tip: the verb in this question is "determine" — marks sit in the decision logic (readiness staging, barrier analysis), not in listing exercise types.

Sources

  1. WHO. Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 10th ed.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. What alternative intervention would you suggest for lateral elbow pain, based on biomechanical concepts, for a patient who has already undergone conventional physiotherapy treatment?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 3 — Biomechanical concepts in rehabilitation

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Why pain persists after conventional treatment — pathomechanics1.5
Biomechanical analysis: kinetic chain, grip, tool and technique2
Mulligan mobilization-with-movement plus taping2
Neurodynamic intervention for the radial nerve2
Eccentric Flexbar (Tyler twist) and evidence1.5
Conclusion1

aMechanism first: why did conventional treatment fail?

Lateral epicondylalgia ("tennis elbow", and in India far more often a housewife's or mechanic's elbow from repetitive wringing and wrenching) is an overload tendinopathy of the extensor carpi radialis brevis at its origin. If ultrasound, friction massage, stretching and counterforce bracing have failed, three causes stand out: the load keeps coming back through faulty mechanics; cervical or radial nerve involvement is feeding the lateral elbow pain; and the tendon has never been properly strengthened. Your alternative intervention must attack these.

bBiomechanical analysis of the load path

Work along the kinetic chain: wrist position during grip (a flexed wrist during gripping spikes ECRB demand), grip size and tool handle diameter, technique in the patient's actual occupation or sport — racket grip and backhand mechanics, or in the kitchen, knife-sharpening and wet-clothes wringing. Correct the movement that loads the tendon, or every treatment below is temporary.

cMulligan mobilization-with-movement

A lateral glide of the ulna (or a squeeze of the forearm) applied while the patient makes a fist or grips pain-free gives an immediate increase in pain-free grip strength. Reapply for three sets of ten or more, then tape the forearm to sustain the glide — classically left on for two days without exercises (Mulligan). The immediate-on, immediate-off pain relief is the biomechanical signature that distinguishes MWM from passive modalities.

dNeurodynamics — the missing link

Lateral elbow pain can be a cervical referral or a radial nerve sensitization that no amount of local elbow treatment will fix. Screen the cervical spine and conduct a neurodynamic test; if radial nerve bias tests are positive, treat with sliders (gentle alternating elbow extension with wrist flexion, keeping tension "on-off" without stretching the nerve) as described by Butler and Jones and Shacklock. This is the classic "alternative intervention" the examiner has in mind for a resistant case.

eRe-load the tendon: Flexbar Tyler twist

Finish with eccentric training using the crooked Flexbar — the Tyler twist, performed with the unaffected arm assisting — which in a randomized trial beat standard eccentric wrist-extension exercise for pain and strength. Progress resistance over 4–6 weeks, then return the patient to sport or work with the corrected technique. Conclusion: resistant lateral elbow pain needs a biomechanical diagnosis — correct the load path, mobilize with movement, treat the nerve, then re-load the tendon.

Fig 4 — One elbow, four targets: load path, joint glide, nerve, tendon. Each gets one intervention in the answer.
Examiner's tip: the phrase "already undergone conventional physiotherapy" is the cue to look outside the elbow — cervical and radial nerve screening earns the discriminating marks.

Sources

  1. Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System.
  2. Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics.
  3. Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient.

On the evaluation form — Q4: Lateral elbow pain (lateral epicondylalgia)

I. Subjective examination

A 40-year-old right-dominant male machine operator and weekend cricketer presents with five months of right lateral elbow pain. Chief complaints: pain worse on gripping spanners and lifting a full bottle (coffee-cup sign); weak grasp. Onset: after intensified batting practice. Symptom analysis — site: right lateral elbow; onset: post-training, no acute trauma; duration: five months; severity: NPRS 6/10 with gripping; aggravating factors: gripping and lifting; relieving factors: not reported. II. Objective examination

On observation. No swelling; the arm is carried slightly flexed.

On palpation. Tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and the common extensor origin (extensor carpi radialis brevis); cervical spine non-tender.

1. Motor assessment

Wrist and elbow ROM full. MMT: wrist extensors 4/5 with pain on resistance. Resisted grip isometrically painful; grip strength approximately one-third less than the left, worse with the elbow extended. Brachioradialis reflex normal. Girth symmetrical.

2. Sensory assessment

Sensation intact in the radial territory, including the C6 dermatome; radial nerve non-tender on palpation.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Mobility normal; limitation is confined to gripping tools, turning keys and the batting grip. Outcome measures selected: NPRS (0–10) with gripping; PRTEE (0–100, higher = greater pain and disability); grip dynamometry in kg.

4. Gait analysis

Gait and mobility normal.

5. Balance

Not documented in this case.

6. Hand function

Reaching unaffected; grasping and releasing limited by painful grip — difficulty gripping spanners, turning keys, holding a full bottle and the batting grip. No assistive device.

7. Coordination

Not documented in this case.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

Decreased ability to grip and lift secondary to lateral epicondylalgia of the right common extensor origin.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain with gripping from 6/10 to 3/10; grip strength up 10%; brace worn at work.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): pain ≤1/10 with daily gripping; grip within 10% of the left; PRTEE halved; full work and batting duties.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): isometric wrist extension held 45 s × 5, three to four times daily, pain kept ≤3/10; ice after work; padded gloves. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): eccentric wrist extensor training — lift the wrist up with the other hand and lower slowly over 3–4 s; 3 sets of 15 daily. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): concentric-eccentric and functional loading — wrist deviations, wrist curls, pronation-supination with a rod; return to batting.

14. Home programme

Daily isometrics or eccentrics as above; brace during gripping tasks; self-massage over the tender point twice daily.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. How do you distinguish and prioritize the various external application techniques for correction of forward neck posture?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 4 — External applications in musculoskeletal rehabilitation

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Mechanism of forward head posture and its consequences1.5
Kinesiology taping — rationale and method2
Rigid taping / postural braces — rationale and limits2
Priority logic and patient selection2.5
Evidence and conclusion2

aMechanism first: what is forward neck posture?

Forward head posture is part of upper crossed syndrome: deep neck flexors and lower scapular stabilizers become inhibited and elongated while upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals and pectoralis minor tighten. For every inch the head translates forward, the load on the cervical extensors multiplies, producing chronic upper back and neck ache, suboccipital headaches and rounded shoulders. External applications do not strengthen anything — they provide proprioceptive cueing, brief support, or correction of the scapular position while the exercise program does the real work.

bDistinguishing the techniques

Kinesiology taping is elastic (up to about 140% stretch) and works by proprioceptive input and light tissue lift, not by holding the head back. Apply an inhibition-facilitation pair: a vertical strip over the upper trapezius with light tension (10–15%) from insertion to origin, and facilitation strips over the deep cervical flexor region or a Y-strip along the thoracic spine. The patient feels a gentle "reminder" when the head drifts forward. Rigid (sports or zinc oxide) taping mechanically pulls the scapulae into retraction and holds the correction, but irritates skin within 3–4 days and cannot be worn in Indian heat and sweat through a full work week. Postural braces — figure-of-eight elastic supports with a thoracic strap — hold the shoulders back externally; they transfer the work to the garment, weaken the scapular muscles if overused, and are best reserved for short high-load exposure such as long two-wheeler commutes or a week of examination invigilation.

cPrioritizing: a decision rule worth writing

Priority one is always the active program — deep neck flexor training (craniocervical flexion, 10 repetitions of 10-second holds), scapular retraction and thoracic extension — because posture is a habit of muscle, not of strap. Priority two is kinesiology tape as a wearable cue for 3–5 days at a time during retraining; it is comfortable in our climate, tolerates bathing, and reinforces the correction between sessions. Priority three is rigid taping for short, defined periods when stronger cueing is needed. Braces come last and only as a time-limited bridge, never as the treatment. Contraindications across all of them: skin allergy, loss of sensation over the taped area, and open wounds.

dEvidence and conclusion

Studies of taping combined with exercise in forward head posture show better reduction of pain and neck disability than exercise alone in the short term, but tape without exercise does not hold its gain — exactly what the mechanism predicts. Conclusion: distinguish the techniques by mechanism (elastic cue versus rigid hold versus brace), and prioritize them in inverse proportion to how much work they do for the patient: the more the device works, the less the patient's muscles do.

Fig 5 — Priority ladder climbs from exercise at the base to brace at the top of the drawing's list — the device works more as you go up, and that is exactly why you use it less.
Examiner's tip: the phrase "distinguish AND prioritize" wants two things — a comparison of mechanisms, then an explicit order with justification. Scripts that only describe taping techniques score half.

Sources

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  2. Chui K et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation.
  3. OSHA. Computer Workstations eTool.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain the cognitive-behavioural methods in the treatment of post-operative knee arthroplasty.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 4 — Cognitive-behavioural methods in rehabilitation

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Why cognition matters after knee arthroplasty — fear-avoidance model1.5
Pain neuroscience education and expectation setting2
Graded activity and pacing2
Relaxation, imagery and coping skills1.5
Goal setting, self-efficacy and evidence (Abbott NESD trial)2
Conclusion1

aMechanism first: the pain in the brain, not just the knee

After total knee arthroplasty, outcome is decided as much by beliefs as by the implant. Kinesiophobia — fear of movement — feeds the fear-avoidance cycle: pain is interpreted as damage, activity is avoided, quadriceps atrophy and stiffness set in, and the avoided movement hurts more when finally attempted. Catastrophizing ("my new knee has failed") and low self-efficacy predict slower recovery of function. Cognitive-behavioural methods target exactly these modifiable thoughts.

bPain neuroscience education

Before and after surgery, teach the patient that pain during graded rehabilitation is load-sensitivity, not tissue damage: a graph of expected recovery over 6–12 weeks, shown pre-operatively, sets realistic expectations and reduces catastrophizing. Explain that post-operative swelling and warmth for some weeks are normal biological healing, not infection — a fear that brings many Indian patients back to the outpatient department unnecessarily.

cGraded activity and pacing

Replace "avoid and rest" with time-contingent quotas: a walking and exercise plan set by time, not by pain, progressed weekly. Pacing teaches the boom-and-bust patient — who cleans the whole house on a good day and is bed-bound for two after — to split tasks into sustainable units. Each success resets the belief "I cannot", and the graded staircase becomes behavioural proof against the fearful thought.

dRelaxation, imagery and coping skills

Diaphragmatic breathing and progressive muscle relaxation (adapted around the operated limb) lower sympathetic arousal and pain amplification; guided imagery of walking without a limp is used before practice sessions. Coping skills include self-talk restructuring and planning for flare-ups: a written flare-up plan (reduce activity by a third, do not stop, use ice and breathing) prevents the flare from becoming a relapse into avoidance.

eGoal setting, self-efficacy and evidence

Set SMART goals the patient chooses (climb the temple steps by week 8, sit cross-legged for meals if the surgeon permits), review them weekly, and attribute success to the patient's own effort — that is how self-efficacy is built. The strongest supporting evidence is the NESD trial of Abbott and colleagues: pre-operative education combined with neuromuscular exercise before knee arthroplasty improved post-operative outcomes. Conclusion: CBT methods do not replace range-of-motion and strengthening after arthroplasty — they decide whether the patient actually performs them.

Fig 6 — Fear-avoidance cycle on the left, graded staircase on the right; the arrow between them is your entire answer in one stroke.
Examiner's tip: every CBT method you name must be tied to the arthroplasty context (quota-based walking, flare-up plans, SMART goals like sitting cross-legged) — generic psychology definitions alone cap you at half marks.

Sources
