Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Bloom's Taxonomy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 6 — professional practice, pedagogy and entrepreneurship: Bloom's taxonomy and intended learning outcomes

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Original 1956 taxonomy: the six cognitive levels2.5
Revised 2001 taxonomy and the knowledge dimension2.5
Affective and psychomotor domains1.5
Application: writing ILOs and assessments2.5
Conclusion: link to Miller's pyramid1

aWhat a taxonomy of learning is, and the 1956 original

A taxonomy is a classification that orders things by complexity, and Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives (Bloom and colleagues, 1956) orders cognitive learning outcomes from simple recall to the highest forms of thinking. The original six levels, each requiring those below it: knowledge (recall facts — name the ulnar nerve roots), comprehension (explain in your own words), application (use the rule in a new patient), analysis (break a gait pattern into its deviations), synthesis (assemble a treatment plan), and evaluation (judge which plan is best, and defend the choice). Two claims matter for teaching: the hierarchy is cumulative — a student cannot analyze what they do not understand — and it pushes teachers to aim above the recall level where most exams quietly live.

bThe revised taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001)

The revision, led by Krathwohl and Anderson, renamed the levels as verbs and swapped the top two: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create — creation now sits at the apex. Its deeper change is that it is two-dimensional: the cognitive process dimension is crossed with a knowledge dimension of four types of content — factual (terminology, details), conceptual (classifications, principles), procedural (techniques, methods), and metacognitive (knowledge of one's own thinking, and of oneself as a learner). A learning outcome is therefore a cell in a grid: "design (create) a graded eccentric loading programme (procedural)" is a different cell from "list the contraindications (factual, remember)", and postgraduate physiotherapy training lives almost entirely in the right-hand, higher cells.

cThe other two domains

Cognitive is only one of Bloom's three domains. The affective domain (Krathwohl's hierarchy: receiving, responding, valuing, organizing, characterizing) tracks how attitudes form — the student who first attends to patient counselling, then practises it, then values it, until professional empathy is character. The psychomotor domain (Simpson's and Harrow's versions: perception, set, guided response, mechanism, complex overt response) is where manual skills progress from clumsy imitation to automatic mastery — obviously the physiotherapist's home domain. A complete lesson plan touches all three: the student must know, must care, and must do.

dApplication — writing ILOs and honest assessments

This is where the taxonomy earns its syllabus place. Intended learning outcomes should be written with observable verbs at the intended level: "list" and "define" sit at remember; "differentiate" at analyze; "construct" or "justify" at create and evaluate — while verbs like "know", "understand" and "appreciate" are unmarkable because nobody can observe them. Assessment must then align with the outcome (constructive alignment): an ILO promising analysis cannot be tested by a recall MCQ, and a viva that only asks "define TENS" has silently lowered the level of the whole course. Use the grid as a checklist when preparing a class: name the cell you are aiming at before writing the slide.

eConclusion — Bloom meets Miller

For clinical competence, Bloom's cognitive domain pairs naturally with Miller's pyramid of assessment: knows (the base, Bloom's remember), knows how (apply and analyze), shows how (psychomotor domain under observation) and does (performance in real practice). Conclusion: Bloom's taxonomy is the operating system of physiotherapy education — it decides what we ask in vivas, what our MCQs actually test, and whether we are training recallers of electrotherapy lists or clinicians who can create and defend a treatment decision.

Fig 9 — the revised pyramid (note the 2001 swap: create at the apex), flanked by the four knowledge dimensions and Miller's assessment ladder. One sketch covers the whole answer.
Examiner's tip: quote one physiotherapy-specific verb pair at each level (define SPADI at remember, justify the treatment plan at evaluate) — examiners marking a pedagogy paper reward the ability to use the taxonomy, not to recite its ladder.

Sources

  1. Anderson LW, Krathwohl LH, et al. A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives. New York: Longman; 2001.
  2. Bloom BS, et al. Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, Handbook I: The Cognitive Domain. New York: David McKay; 1956.
  3. Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Acad Med 1990;65:S63-7.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Describe the different methods used in strength training.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4 — exercise physiology and prescription: strength training methods

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Isometric and isotonic (concentric and eccentric) methods2.5
Isokinetic and plyometric methods2.5
Dosage: intensity, sets, repetitions, frequency, progression2.5
Special regimes: variable resistance, circuit training, periodisation1.5
Clinical application and Indian context, conclusion1

aIsometric and isotonic methods

Classify by what happens to muscle length and joint angle. In isometric training the muscle develops tension without changing length — the joint does not move; the strength gain is angle-specific (plus a small spill-over of roughly 10 to 20 degrees either side), so several angles must be trained. It is the method of choice when movement is prohibited or painful: post-operative limbs, painful arthritic joints, and in the classic setting of a patient in a cast — brief maximal holds, for example a six-second contraction repeated several times at multiple angles. In isotonic (dynamic) training the joint moves: the concentric phase shortens the muscle to lift, the eccentric phase lengthens it under load to lower. Eccentric loading produces greater force per unit of activation and better hypertrophy stimulus, at the price of delayed-onset muscle soreness — which is exactly why it is both the tool of choice in tendinopathy rehabilitation (heavy slow resistance, eccentric decline protocols) and something to grade carefully in the untrained.

bIsokinetic and plyometric methods

Isokinetic training keeps limb velocity constant while the machine accommodates resistance moment to moment, so the muscle works maximally through the whole range — free weights are hardest only where leverage is worst. Computerised dynamometers (Cybex, Biodex) also quantify torque, making this the reference standard for strength testing as well as a training mode, across a spectrum of angular velocities. Plyometric training works the stretch-shortening cycle: a rapid eccentric pre-load stores elastic energy, and the immediate concentric recoil spends it — depth jumps, bounding, medicine-ball throws. It trains power rather than pure strength, demands a strength base and sound landing mechanics first, and belongs to late-stage athletic rehabilitation.

cDosage — where prescription marks live

Every method is a vehicle; the dose is the engine. Intensity: a novice begins around 60 to 70 per cent of one repetition maximum, advanced lifters train at 80 per cent and above. Volume: about 8 to 12 repetitions per set for general strengthening (heavier loads, fewer repetitions for pure strength; lighter loads to muscular failure for hypertrophy), typically 2 to 4 sets per muscle group. Rest: 2 to 3 minutes between sets for strength work. Frequency: 2 to 3 sessions per week per muscle group, because the muscle grows between sessions, not during them. And every plan runs on progressive overload — small systematic increases in load, volume or frequency as adaptation allows — paired with the principle of specificity: you get precisely what you train.

dSpecial regimes

Variable-resistance equipment (cam-and-lever machines) varies resistance to match the natural strength curve through the range. Circuit resistance training strings stations together with short rests for combined strength and conditioning in limited time. Bodyweight and elastic-resistance training deliver progressive overload without a gym — the practical backbone of Indian home programmes. Periodisation structures training into phases (hypertrophy, strength, power, deload) so peak performance arrives at the right competition or season, and the same logic phases a rehabilitation programme from control, to capacity, to power.

eClinical application and conclusion

Prescription is a matching exercise: post-operative knee — isometric quadriceps setting, progressing to eccentric work; anterior knee pain — closed-chain weight-bearing work; older adults — power training, because the ability to react quickly fades faster than strength and predicts falls; metabolic risk — the Misra JAPI 2009 consensus for Asian Indians explicitly prescribes muscle-strengthening activity on most days as part of daily physical activity, not an optional extra. Conclusion: there is no best method — there is a best match between method, stage of healing, and goal, held together by measurable dosage and progressive overload.

Fig 10 — the four-method grid with use-cases and one dosage line beneath. In a 10-mark answer this figure is the skeleton the paragraphs hang on.
Examiner's tip: whichever method you describe, end its paragraph with "so it is used when...". A method without a clinical indication is trivia; a method matched to a patient phase is prescription — and that is the difference the marks table is measuring.

Sources

  1. McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA, et al. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  3. Misra A, Chowbey P, Makkar BM, et al. Consensus statement for diagnosis of obesity, abdominal obesity and the metabolic syndrome for Asian Indians. J Assoc Physicians India 2009;57:163-70.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper I

QP 8129 · 28-May-2024 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1History taking

  • History generates hypotheses; objective exam tests them.
  • OPQRST: onset, provocation, quality, radiation, severity, timing.
  • Red flags: night pain, weight loss, fever, carcinoma, trauma, neuro deficit, bladder-bowel.
  • Record in ICF: body function, activity, participation, environment, personal.

2Instrumentation techniques

  • Chain: power supply to oscillator/timer to pulse shaper to output amplifier to isolation to patient.
  • Difference: therapeutic chain sends energy to patient; EMG chain takes signal away, differential amplifier with high CMRR cancels 50 Hz.
  • Needle EMG filter band roughly 10 Hz to 10 kHz; gain in µV per division.
  • Safety: macroshock vs microshock; applied parts B/BF about 100 µA, CF about 10 µA.

3MSK adaptations to training

  • Order: skill, then neural drive (weeks 2-8), then hypertrophy (8+), matrix last (months).
  • Type IIx shifts to IIa with any regular training.
  • Wolff's law: bone along lines of strain; cartilage eats cyclic compression.
  • Detraining unwinds fastest first: drive and capillaries within weeks.

4Muscle plasticity with ES

  • Stimulated recruitment: non-selective, spatially fixed, temporally synchronous — reversed size principle, fatigues fast.
  • Chronic 10-20 Hz for weeks transforms fast to slow (Salmons and Vrbova, 1969).
  • Dose: 30-50 Hz, 200-400 µs, ramped, 1:5 on-off; denervated muscle needs millisecond pulses.
  • Electrode over motor point: most contraction for least current.

5Probability and normal distribution

  • Probability 0 to 1; classical (equally likely), empirical (long-run frequency), subjective (belief).
  • Addition rule subtracts the overlap; independent events multiply.
  • Normal: µ and σ only; mean = median = mode; total area 1; asymptotic tails; inflection at µ ± 1σ.
  • 68.27 — 95.44 — 99.73 per cent within 1, 2, 3σ; Z = (X - µ)/σ.

6Instrumentation of NMES

  • Blocks: PSU, oscillator + timer, pulse shaper (µs, waveform), output amp (mA, ramp), isolation + current limit, electrodes at motor point.
  • Charge-balanced biphasic pulses prevent electrolytic burns.
  • Worked dose: 45 Hz, 300 µs, ramp 2 s, 10 s on : 50 s off, 12-15 contractions, 3 times weekly.
  • Contraindications: pacemaker, pregnancy over uterus, DVT, malignancy, insensate skin.

7Testing of hypothesis

  • Steps: state H0/H1, set α 0.05, choose test, compute, decide.
  • Type I = reject true H0 (α, false positive); Type II = keep false H0 (β, false negative); power = 1 - β, target 80 per cent.
  • P-value: probability of data this extreme or more if H0 true — never "probability H0 is true".
  • One-tailed only if the direction was declared in advance.

8SPADI psychometrics

  • 13 items: 5 pain + 8 disability, each 0-10; total ÷ 130 × 100 = 0-100.
  • Reliability: alpha 0.86-0.96; ICC 0.84-0.95.
  • MCID about 8-13 points; MDC95 about 18 points — change below MDC is noise.
  • Validated Indian versions: Hindi (2011) and Tamil (2012).

9Bloom's taxonomy

  • 1956: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, evaluation.
  • 2001: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create (create on top).
  • Knowledge dimension: factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive.
  • Miller: knows, knows how, shows how, does; write ILOs with observable verbs.

10Strength training methods

  • Isometric (angle-specific, post-op), isotonic (concentric/eccentric, tendon rehab), isokinetic (fixed velocity, testing), plyometric (stretch-shortening, power).
  • Dose: 60-70% 1RM novice, 8-12 reps, 2-4 sets, rest 2-3 min, 2-3 days per week.
  • Principles: progressive overload + specificity.
  • Misra 2009: strengthening exercise is prescription for Asian Indian metabolic risk.
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the factors affecting mobility during aging.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 4a — Biomechanics across the lifespan: aging

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Meaning of mobility; why aging changes it1
Articular factors: cartilage, capsule, synovium2
Muscular factors: sarcopenia, dynapenia, stiffness2
Neural and sensory factors: reaction time, proprioception, balance2
Other factors: pain, fear of falling, deconditioning, comorbidity, skin/footwear2
Clinical application and conclusion1

aWhat mobility means — and why age attacks it

Mobility is the capacity to change and control joint position and to move the body through space — a joint-range, strength, and motor-control package. Aging does not damage one system; it quietly taxes all four pillars at once: articular, muscular, neural, and behavioural. The examiner wants you to say this framing sentence before listing factors, because it shows you understand the integrated nature of the problem.

bArticular and connective-tissue factors

Articular cartilage thins and loses water and proteoglycans, so its shock-absorbing capacity falls; joint surfaces that once glided now protest. The joint capsule and ligaments become fibrotic and less extensible through cross-linking of collagen, so capsular restriction reduces range of motion, especially at the shoulder and hip. Synovial fluid volume and viscosity change, reducing lubrication. The net result: stiffer joints with less terminal range, and a slower response to load.

cMuscular factors

The headline term is age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Muscle mass declines roughly 3 to 5 percent per decade from the third decade, accelerating after the seventh, so that an average 80-year-old retains only about 80 percent of young-adult mass. Crucially, strength and power fall two to five times faster than mass — this quality loss is called dynapenia — because of preferential atrophy of fast type II fibres and reduced neural drive. Loss of power (force times velocity) matters most for mobility tasks: rising from a chair, climbing a bus step, catching a trip. Tendons also stiffen and lose elasticity, and their reduced compliance lowers the energy returned during gait, raising the metabolic cost of walking. Sustained connective-tissue loading produces time-dependent creep, and aged tissue recovers it more slowly, so posture-related deformities and stiffness accumulate.

dNeural and sensory factors

Reaction time lengthens, motor-unit firing rates fall, and there is a progressive loss of motor units with reinnervation that leaves larger, clumsier units. Proprioceptive acuity declines at the joint and muscle-spindle level, vestibular hair cells degenerate, and vision loses acuity and contrast sensitivity. Standing balance therefore deteriorates, postural sway increases, and protective stepping reactions slow — which is why falls, not stiffness, are the first presenting complaint in many older Indian patients who walk barefoot on wet floors.

eBehavioural and systemic factors

Pain from osteoarthritis reduces voluntary movement; fear of falling produces self-imposed inactivity; deconditioning then accelerates sarcopenia — a vicious cycle. Comorbidities (diabetic neuropathy, stroke, cardiopulmonary limitation), medication effects, decreased skin elasticity, foot deformities, and unsafe footwear (chappals rather than supported shoes) all chip away at mobility. Bone loss (osteopenia/osteoporosis) makes falls costlier, which feeds the fear again.

Fig 1 — Draw three inputs (joint, muscle, nerve) funnelling into one output box (mobility down, falls risk up) with the inactivity feedback loop. This shows the examiner systems-level thinking in ten seconds.
Examiner's tip: the phrase "strength is lost two to five times faster than mass — dynapenia" is a marks magnet. Also mention power (not just strength) for chair-rise and fall-recovery; most answers stop at mass.

Sources

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — biomechanics of aging chapters.
  2. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — aging, sarcopenia and exercise in older adults.
  3. Hislop, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing — strength changes with age.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe the role of fascia in the musculoskeletal system.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 1c — Basic concepts: fascia

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition and classification (superficial, deep, visceral)2
Mechanical role: envelope, compartmentalization, transmission of force2.5
Elastic storage and movement efficiency1.5
Sensory/proprioceptive role1.5
Clinical application: scarring, fibrosis, stretching, myofascial pain2.5

aWhat fascia is

Fascia is the three-dimensional continuous web of connective tissue — mostly collagen with elastin and a hydrated ground substance rich in hyaluronan — that invests every muscle, organ, nerve and vessel. Classically: superficial fascia (subcutaneous, carries fat and vessels), deep fascia (dense envelopes such as fascia lata, crural fascia, thoracolumbar fascia), and visceral fascia. Modern terminology treats it as one interconnected tensional network rather than isolated sleeves.

bMechanical roles: envelope, compartment and transmitter

First, it packages: separating muscles into compartments, allowing glide between them through sliding layers, and retaining muscle shape so fibres contract efficiently without bulging sideways. Second, it is a dynamic skeleton for force: because connective tissue links muscle to tendon, bone and neighbouring muscle, tension generated in one belly is distributed laterally to its neighbours — myofascial force transmission. This means force reaches the skeleton by paths other than the classic origin-insertion tendon line, which partly explains why isolated single-muscle exercises still load wide regions.

cElastic storage and whole-body continuity

The fascial network acts as a biological spring. In walking and running, the fascia lata and the plantar fascia, together with the Achilles tendon and thoracolumbar fascia, store and release elastic energy, so muscle fibres can contract almost isometrically while the spring oscillates — economical movement. The continuity across the back line and spiral lines is the anatomical basis for whole-body "chains" used clinically, and tensegrity describes how local tension is spread globally through this continuous web.

dSensory role

Fascia is one of the richest sensory organs of the body: it is densely innervated by free nerve endings and mechanoreceptors (Ruffini, Pacinian, interstitial receptors), and contains contractile myofibroblasts. It contributes substantially to proprioception and interoception, and its nociceptors are implicated in myofascial pain and the tenderness of myofascial trigger points.

eClinical application

When fascia is injured or immobilized, hyaluronan thickens and layers lose their glide — fibrosis and adhesion follow surgery, burns or prolonged bed rest, limiting range and raising injury risk. Treatment follows logically: gentle sustained stretching and movement to restore glide (the basis of yoga-like and slow-load approaches popularized by fascial fitness research), manual therapy to free adhesions, and early postoperative movement to prevent sticky layers. Scars act as irritable anchors in the tensional web; releasing them can change distant mobility.

Fig 2 — Two muscles in one fascial web: cross-hatched connecting layers, a side-arrow for lateral force transmission, plus a circle for its sensory role. Four strokes, full concept.
Examiner's tip: structure the answer as "structure — mechanics — sensation — clinic". Quote Schleip's finding that fascia is richly innervated and can actively contract via myofibroblasts; most students still describe it as inert packing, and correcting that earns easy marks.

Sources

  1. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — fascia and connective tissue structure.
  2. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — connective tissue mechanics.
  3. Schleip — fascial research, Fascial Fitness articles, Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Elaborate on the kinetics and kinematics of the shoulder following rotator cuff repair.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6c — Mechanics and pathomechanics: shoulder

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Surgical background, healing biology and protection rationale2
Kinematics: joint motion changes, scapulohumeral rhythm, stiffness3
Kinetics: force couples, deltoid-cuff interaction, compression3
Rehabilitation implications and conclusion2

aBackground: what was repaired and what must be protected

A rotator cuff repair re-approximates torn cuff tendon (most often supraspinatus) to the greater tuberosity, by anchors and sutures. The repaired tendon-to-bone interface is weakest early: healing passes through inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases, and tendon strength does not approach normal for months. Every kinematic and kinetic statement below flows from this one biological fact — the repair must be moved enough to prevent stiffness but not loaded enough to fail.

bKinematics after repair

Kinematics is the geometry of motion, and it changes in three ways. First, passive range is deliberately restricted in the early phase — abduction and external rotation are the guarded arcs because both maximally strain the supraspinatus footprint. Second, scapulohumeral rhythm is altered: pain, inhibition and cuff deficiency increase scapular upward rotation and the use of scapulothoracic substitution, so the patient "hikes" the shoulder to reach overhead; the normal 2:1 glenohumeral-to-scapular ratio becomes more scapular. Third, postoperative stiffness is the signature complication — capsular contracture reduces glenohumeral rotation, and internal-rotation deficits shift mechanics further. Because the deltoid is preserved and active while the cuff is protected, the joint's instantaneous centre of rotation can translate upward if the cuff's stabilizing pull is late to return.

cKinetics after repair

Kinetics is the study of forces. Normal shoulder function depends on a transverse and coronal force couple: in the coronal plane, deltoid's upward pull is balanced by the inferior stabilizing pull of the intact cuff (especially subscapularis anteriorly and infraspinatus posteriorly), which compresses the humeral head into the glenoid — concavity compression. Immediately after repair the cuff side of the couple is surgically silenced, so unopposed deltoid force would drive superior humeral head translation and impingement of the repair under the acromion. The subscapularis and infraspinatus, if intact, must therefore be protected but activated early, since they supply the "seatbelt" that keeps the head centred. Passive forces also matter: immobilization shortens the capsule, and friction at the repaired footprint raises the torque needed for motion.

dRehabilitation implications and conclusion

Rehabilitation is applied kinetics and kinematics: early gentle passive motion to glide the surfaces and limit adhesion (unless the tear was massive, where conservative immobilization may be chosen), avoidance of active abduction against gravity in the first weeks, progressive activation of the scapular stabilizers to restore rhythm, and later resisted external rotation and scapular retraction before deltoid-dominant lifting. Conclusion: after repair the shoulder moves differently (kinematics) and is loaded differently (kinetics) because a healing, temporarily non-contractile cuff lets deltoid dominate; successful therapy restores rhythm first and the force couple second.

Fig 3 — Circle for the humeral head, one upward arrow (deltoid), two converging green arrows (cuff compression into the glenoid). Label it "coronal force couple" — that label alone is worth a mark.
Examiner's tip: open with "the repair must be moved but not loaded" and the whole answer writes itself. Distinguish kinematics (motion geometry, rhythm, stiffness) from kinetics (forces, couples, compression) in your subheadings — examiners specifically check whether you know the difference.

Sources

  1. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — shoulder complex mechanics.
  2. Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — rotator cuff rehabilitation.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — post-repair protocols and force couples.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe the various physiological adaptations seen in muscles during endurance training.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 5a — Physiological basis of movement: exercise and training

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition of endurance training1
Peripheral adaptations: mitochondria, capillaries, myoglobin, enzymes3
Muscle fibre adaptations2
Metabolic and substrate adaptations2
Central adaptations and functional conclusion2

aDefinition

Endurance training is repeated, sustained, predominantly aerobic exercise — typically large-muscle rhythmic activity at moderate intensity performed three to five times a week for weeks. The muscles adapt to delay fatigue: they learn to generate the same force for longer, using oxygen more efficiently and sparing their limited carbohydrate fuel.

bPeripheral (muscular) adaptations — the marks-rich core

The dominant change is mitochondrial biogenesis: mitochondrial volume density rises by roughly 25 to 100 per cent with training — in humans largely enlargement of existing mitochondria rather than new ones — driven by PGC-1alpha signalling, so aerobic ATP production capacity rises. Capillary density increases (more capillaries per fibre, smaller diffusion distances), improving oxygen and substrate delivery and metabolite removal. Myoglobin content rises, storing and ferrying oxygen inside the fibre. Oxidative enzymes of the Krebs cycle, electron transport chain and beta-oxidation pathways increase in activity, so fat — an abundant fuel — is oxidized faster. The net result: a rightward shift of the lactate threshold, meaning the same work is done with less lactate accumulation and less fatigue.

cMuscle fibre adaptations

Type I (slow oxidative) fibres hypertrophy modestly and become even more oxidative; type IIa fibres shift their myosin heavy-chain profile toward a more oxidative type IIa phenotype (with possible IIx-to-IIa conversion), so the fast population becomes fatigue-resistant. There is little wholesale conversion of type II to type I in humans, and no dramatic hypertrophy — that is the resistance-training answer, not the endurance one. Intramuscular triglyceride storage increases as a local fuel depot.

dMetabolic and substrate adaptations

Trained muscle spares muscle glycogen by oxidizing more free fatty acids at any given submaximal intensity; the "crossover" shifts so carbohydrate is preserved for later effort. Resting glycogen storage capacity itself increases, phosphocreatine depletion at a given load is less, and buffering and lactate-shuttle capacity improve so lactate can be cleared and used as fuel by other fibres and the heart.

eCentral and functional adaptations

Although the question is about muscle, one line on the whole-body context earns completeness: stroke volume rises, resting and submaximal heart rate fall, and muscle blood flow extraction (arteriovenous oxygen difference) improves. Functionally, the trained muscle can sustain walking, cycling or occupational activity longer, fatigue resistance being the single most practical outcome for physiotherapy patients in cardiac, pulmonary and deconditioned populations.

Fig 4 — One big fibre box, six blue dots for mitochondria, three parallel lines for capillaries, and an arrow labelled "lactate threshold shifts right". Thirty seconds to draw, and it carries the answer's whole logic.
Examiner's tip: the commonest error is writing hypertrophy and neural-gain adaptations from strength training. State explicitly: "endurance training increases quality (oxidative machinery), not bulk." Quote PGC-1alpha once, then stop — depth beats name-dropping.

Sources

  1. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — sports physiology and muscle adaptation.
  2. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — endurance training adaptations.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — aerobic endurance training principles.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the changes in the mechanics of the elbow following fixed flexion deformity of the elbow.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6c — Mechanics and pathomechanics: elbow

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Normal elbow mechanics recap2
Effect on joint kinematics and carrying angle2
Functional losses of movement and reach2
Compensatory movements and adjacent-joint overload2.5
Physiotherapy significance and conclusion1.5

aNormal mechanics recap

The elbow is a trochleoulnar (hinge) plus radiohumeral (pivot) joint: flexion-extension occurs at the ulnohumeral articulation, pronation-supination at the proximal radioulnar joint. The flexion axis runs through the epicondyles; full extension ends in a slight valgus carrying angle — roughly 11 degrees in men and 13 degrees in women — which lets the forearm clear the hip in carrying objects. Flexion is guided by the coronoid and olecranon fitting the trochlea, giving the joint its intrinsic bony stability.

bKinematic changes with fixed flexion deformity

A fixed flexion deformity (FFD) means the joint cannot reach terminal extension — the olecranon is blocked by anterior capsular contracture, biceps tightening, or bony impingement (as in malunited distal humerus fractures, rheumatoid arthritis, or post-burn scar contracture common in Indian practice). The functional arc of motion shifts upward: total range is preserved in many cases but is displaced into flexion. The close-packed, locked position of full extension is lost, so the arm that would have transmitted load through a congruent, maximally contact-distributed joint now loads the posterior trochlea and radial head even at rest. The carrying angle is effectively reduced or abolished in extension because there is no extension; the deformity is often accompanied by pronation contracture, eating into the roughly 100-degree functional pronation-supination arc (about 50 degrees each way, Morrey).

cFunctional losses

Functionally, roughly 100 degrees of flexion-extension (from about 30 to 130 degrees) carries most daily activity, so a small FFD of 15 to 20 degrees is surprisingly well tolerated. What matters is reach: the patient cannot push open a door, cannot reach the far end of a table, cannot do a press-up or support body weight on an extended limb, and cannot put the hand flat under the thigh when sitting. Reaching the back pocket or combing hair is affected only when flexion contracture is combined with pronation loss.

dCompensations and overload

Compensation comes from the shoulder (increased abduction and medial rotation to make the hand meet the midline or the table) and the wrist (hyperextension to flatten the hand). These substitutions overload adjacent structures: the shoulder abductors fatigue, and the wrist is forced into end-range postures. The elbow itself now moves through its flexed arc against contracted soft tissue, so the extensor mechanism (triceps) works at a shortened, mechanically disadvantaged length, and the joint reaction force is directed through a smaller contact area posteriorly — encouraging cartilage wear over time.

ePhysiotherapy significance and conclusion

Assess and record the FFD with a goniometer and the functional arc, then decide: postural and night extension splinting, prolonged low-load stretch, joint mobilizations (especially posterior glides to regain extension), and management of the cause (scar release in post-burn patients, pain control in arthritis). Conclusion: FFD does not merely subtract degrees — it relocates the entire arc, removes the locked extended position for weight-bearing, changes the carrying angle and joint reaction forces, and shifts work to shoulder and wrist, and therapy must address all of these.

Fig 5 — Two bones at an open angle, the elbow circle, an arc labelled "30 degrees lost", and a small arrow showing where extension should lie. The examiner instantly sees you understand arc relocation.
Examiner's tip: write the sentence "the arc does not shrink, it shifts." Then give the functional arc values (30-130 degrees does most daily tasks) — numbers anchor an otherwise descriptive answer and show clinical sense.

Sources

  1. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — elbow complex mechanics.
  2. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — elbow and forearm joints.
  3. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — elbow contracture assessment.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Describe the various changes seen in forward head posture on the body.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 7b — Posture: abnormal postures and deformities

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition and causes1.5
Cervical spine changes: segmental alignment, curves2.5
Muscular imbalance: upper crossed syndrome2
Remote effects: respiration, shoulder, TMJ, headache2
Assessment and management2

aDefinition and causes

Forward head posture (FHP) is an anterior translation of the head relative to the trunk, so the external auditory meatus falls ahead of the shoulder instead of aligning with it. It rides on thoracic kyphosis, and its causes are our daily furniture: prolonged smartphone and laptop use, poor bench and pillow ergonomics, and weak endurance of the deep cervical flexors. Every centimetre of forward translation adds effective load on the cervical extensors, multiplying the moments the neck must sustain.

bChanges in the cervical spine

The spine adapts in a see-saw: upper cervical segments extend (the head must stay level to look forward, hence upper cervical extension) while lower cervical segments flex. The natural cervical lordosis first accentuates, then with disc degeneration and posterior soft-tissue creep may flatten or reverse. Sustained flexion loads the cervical discs posteriorly, stretches the posterior ligaments and capsular structures, and shortens the anterior structures. The craniovertebral angle decreases, and the suboccipital region is held in chronic extension, compressing the upper cervical facet joints and the trigeminocervical nucleus territory.

cMuscular changes — the imbalance pattern

FHP is the facial expression of upper crossed syndrome: tightness of the upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals and pectorals; weakness and inhibition of the deep neck flexors (longus colli, capitis) and the lower and middle trapezius with serratus anterior. The scapulae abduct, tilt anteriorly and elevate — a protracted, rounded-shoulder thorax. Trigger points flourish in the upper trapezius and levator because they hold the head statically for hours.

dRemote effects on the body

The rounded chest restricts rib excursion, so breathing becomes more apical and accessory-muscle driven, reducing chest-wall expansion. Subacromial space narrows with scapular protraction and downward rotation, predisposing to shoulder impingement. The protracted mandible stresses the temporomandibular joint, encouraging disc displacement and bruxism. Sustained suboccipital extension and upper cervical facet loading refer pain via the trigeminocervical complex into tension-type headaches. The whole kinetic chain leans: increased thoracic kyphosis, lumbar compensation, and a higher energy cost of upright posture. Swallowing and voice are subtly affected in severe cases.

eAssessment and management

Assess by plumb-line and craniovertebral angle from a lateral photograph, pectoral and suboccipital length, deep-neck-flexor endurance (chin-tuck hold), and scapular position. Treatment is the mirror image of the cause: lengthen the tight (pectoral, upper trapezius, suboccipitals), strengthen the weak (deep flexors, lower trapezius, serratus anterior), and re-engineer the environment — screen at eye level, lumbar support, and regular postural resets.

Fig 6 — A dashed vertical plumb line, a head circle sitting in front of it, a curved neck, and two boxes: "tight" and "weak". This IS the upper-crossed pattern drawn honestly in under a minute.
Examiner's tip: the phrase "upper cervical extension with lower cervical flexion — so the eyes stay level" is what separates an A-grade answer from a list of complaints. Always end with the trigeminocervical link to headaches; it is a favourite viva follow-up.

Sources

  1. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — posture and spinal curves.
  2. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — posture impairment syndromes and Janda's crossed syndromes.
  3. Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — shoulder girdle and posture relationships.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe the role of equilibrium following ankle injuries.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6d — Mechanics and pathomechanics: ankle injuries and balance

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Equilibrium and postural control framework2
The ankle as a sensory and mechanical organ of balance2.5
Deficits after ankle injury: receptors, sway, instability2.5
Assessment of balance after injury1
Balance training and conclusion2

aWhat equilibrium means

Equilibrium is the state in which the body's centre of mass stays over its base of support. Postural control achieves it by integrating three sensory inputs — somatosensory (joint and muscle receptors, richest at the ankle), vestibular, and visual — and by grading three motor strategies: the ankle strategy for small slow sways on a firm wide surface, the hip strategy for larger disturbances, and the stepping strategy when the base is exceeded. Static equilibrium holds a position; dynamic equilibrium maintains control during movement.

bThe ankle as the organ of balance

In standing, the ankle is the fulcrum of the inverted pendulum of the body. Mechanically, its ligaments and the calf-peroneal muscle group correct each sway in the sagittal and frontal planes; sensorily, the ankle ligaments, capsule and muscle spindles deliver the earliest warning that the ground relationship has changed. The lateral ligament complex in particular carries mechanoreceptors that fire at the end-ranges where a sprain actually happens.

cWhat injury does to equilibrium

A lateral ankle sprain tears ligament and with it the mechanoreceptors, degrading joint position sense and reflex latency. The classical chain: damaged receptors give degraded afferent input, delayed or reduced protective reflexes, increased postural sway especially with eyes closed (sensory reweighting onto vision), recurrent episodes of the ankle "giving way", and finally chronic ankle instability. Freeman described this as articular reflex failure; later work confirmed increased sway and poor single-leg balance in unstable ankles, including deficits on the uninjured side, implying a central reweighting component. Strength loss of the peroneal muscles compounds the mechanical side, and every re-sprain re-damages the afferent field.

dAssessment

Assess single-leg stance time with eyes open versus closed (a large eyes-closed drop flags sensory reliance), the Star Excursion Balance Test or SEBT for dynamic reach, joint position sense reproduction, and peroneal strength and reaction time. Instrumented force plates quantify sway and time-to-boundary in research settings, but clinical tests detect the same signal.

eTraining and conclusion

Balance training is the treatment and the prevention: progressive single-leg work on unstable surfaces, wobble-board and perturbation training, hopping and sport-specific agility. In a classic randomized trial of acute sprains, supervised rehabilitation emphasizing balance training cut re-injury at one year from about 29 percent to 7 percent, and systematic reviews report roughly a one-third reduction in sprains among athletes. Conclusion: after ankle injury, restoring equilibrium — not merely range and strength — is the difference between recovery and a lifetime of a "weak ankle".

Fig 7 — A dot (centre of mass) on a line (body) over a small ankle circle on a base line, with two curved sway arrows. Add the words "inverted pendulum" and "damaged receptors" and the mechanism is complete.
Examiner's tip: quote the Holme 1999 trial numbers (re-injury 29 percent without balance training versus 7 percent with) — one number pair turns a descriptive answer into an evidence-based one. Mention Freeman by name for the mechanoreceptor concept.

Sources

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — postural equilibrium.
  2. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — ankle complex and stability.
  3. Freeman and Wyke — articular reflexes at the ankle joint, 1967 (primary).
  4. Holme et al 1999, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports — supervised rehabilitation after ankle sprain (primary).
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. A 50-year-old man is unable to dorsiflex his right foot following an intramuscular injection in his right gluteal region. Describe his pathological gait.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 8b — Gait: abnormal and pathological gait

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Localization and nature of the lesion (sciatic, peroneal division)2
Gait deviations across the gait cycle (foot slap, foot drop)3
Compensations (steppage, circumduction, trunk lean)2
Energy cost, consequences and differential features1.5
Physiotherapy significance and conclusion1.5

aThe lesion

A gluteal-region intramuscular injection that immediately produces dorsiflexion loss has injured the sciatic nerve — the classic injection palsy of Indian outpatient practice. The sciatic nerve runs through the middle of the buttock deep to piriformis; a needle placed medial or inferior to the safe upper-outer quadrant strikes it. Within the nerve the common peroneal division is lateral, less protected by connective tissue and relatively tethered, which is exactly why the peroneal division is injured far more often than the tibial division. This man therefore most likely has a peroneal-division lesion: loss of the ankle dorsiflexors and evertors (tibialis anterior, extensors, peroneals), with relative sparing of plantar flexion and inversion — a picture of steppage gait. Sensory loss affects the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot; pain and paraesthesia in a sciatic distribution are common early.

bGait deviations through the cycle

At initial contact the affected foot, hanging in equinovarus, cannot be held in neutral, so it strikes either flat and slaps — foot slap as eccentric control of dorsiflexors is lost — or lands toes-first with the forefoot. During loading response the ankle remains plantarflexed, so the tibialis anterior silence removes the first rocker shock absorption and the stance limb accepts weight abruptly. In mid-stance and terminal stance the ankle stays in relative equinus; push-off is only mildly weak if the tibial division is spared, but ankle stability is poor on uneven ground. The characteristic problems are in swing: with no dorsiflexors the foot would drag, so toe clearance is the patient's single biggest engineering problem, solved by compensation.

cCompensations

The textbook compensation is exaggerated hip and knee flexion of the swing limb to lift the dropped foot high — steppage gait, often with the classical foot slap on descent. Alternative or additional patterns include circumduction (swinging the leg outward in an arc), hip hiking (elevating the pelvis on the swing side), and contralateral vaulting (rising on the sound toes to create clearance). Watch an Indian patient walking on a wet floor in chappals and you will see trunk lean toward the sound side and widened base as well — safety overrides elegance.

dConsequences and differential points

Clearance strategies raise the metabolic cost of walking and can overload the hip and lumbar spine. Persistent equinus predisposes to ankle plantar-flexion contracture, calf tightness and, if sensory loss is significant, unnoticed injuries and ulceration over the dorsum of the foot. On examination, look for gluteal and hamstring weakness if the whole sciatic nerve is involved (then knee flexion is weak too), a diminished or intact Achilles reflex depending on tibial sparing, and confirm with nerve conduction studies, which typically show the peroneal division far more affected.

ePhysiotherapy significance and conclusion

Early management: an ankle-foot orthosis or dorsiflexion spring splint to hold the foot neutral in swing and give lateral stability in stance, gait training with the orthosis, electrical stimulation and strengthening of any partially active dorsiflexors, tendon-transfer considerations in permanent lesions, stretching to prevent equinus contracture, sensory protection education, and careful follow-up — many injection palsies show partial spontaneous recovery over months. Conclusion: this is a preventable, iatrogenic high peroneal-pattern sciatic lesion producing foot drop; its gait is the body's intelligent solution to one missing function — ankle dorsiflexion — and the physiotherapist restores clearance with an orthosis while awaiting and supporting nerve recovery.

Fig 8 — A horizontal timeline arrow with three boxes: foot slap at contact, abrupt loading in stance, hip-and-knee hyperflexion in swing, plus a caption listing the substitute clearances. This maps deviation to phase, which is what a 10-marker demands.
Examiner's tip: candidates lose marks by narrating anatomy without connecting to gait phases. For every deviation, force the sentence pattern "because X muscle is silent at Y phase, the patient does Z." Mention the AFO explicitly — it is the management action the examiner is silently waiting for.

Sources

  1. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — pathological gait analysis.
  2. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — nerve injuries and gait.
  3. Saunders, Inman and Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — the major determinants of gait (primary).
  4. Reviews of sciatic nerve injection injury (Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine / International Journal of Surgery case reports, primary).
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe the changes in male and female body structure and composition.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 2a — Anthropometry: body composition and sex differences

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Overall size and proportion differences2
Body composition: fat mass versus fat-free mass3
Skeletal and pelvic differences2
Hormonal basis of the differences1.5
Functional and clinical significance1.5

aSize and proportions

On average, men are taller (roughly 12 to 13 centimetres globally) and heavier, with broader shoulders and narrower hips; women have a lower shoulder-to-hip ratio, a relatively wider pelvis, shorter limbs relative to trunk, and more subcutaneous fat distributed in the gluteofemoral (pear) pattern versus the male abdominal (apple) pattern. The female centre of gravity sits lower, and the carrying angle of the forearm is about 2 degrees greater in women.

bBody composition: fat versus lean

The essential difference is in the two-component model. Women carry substantially more body fat: healthy young women average roughly 20 to 30 percent fat against 12 to 20 percent in men, and essential fat is about 12 to 15 percent in women versus about 3 to 5 percent in men — the female body banks fat for reproductive function. Conversely, fat-free mass — muscle, bone, water — is absolutely and relatively greater in men: men have about 40 percent more muscle mass in the upper body and 25 to 33 percent more in the lower body, larger muscle fibre cross-sectional areas (especially type II), greater bone mineral density and less total body water percentage-wise. Men therefore generate higher absolute strength and power; when strength is expressed per kilogram of lean mass the gap narrows considerably, which is the examiner's favourite nuance.

cSkeletal and pelvic differences

The female pelvis is adapted for childbearing: a wider and shallower pelvis, rounder inlet, broader subpubic angle (80 to 85 degrees versus 50 to 60 degrees in men), and a greater inclination of the femur with a larger Q angle at the knee — the mechanical link to the higher female incidence of patellofemoral pain and anterior cruciate ligament injury. Men have larger, denser, more robust long bones with more prominent muscle attachments; women have lighter bones and, after menopause, accelerated bone loss with higher osteoporosis and fracture risk.

dHormonal basis

Testosterone drives male muscle mass, haemoglobin concentration and visceral fat deposition; oestrogen directs female fat to the gluteofemoral depot, supports bone density, and its menopausal withdrawal reverses both fat distribution and bone protection. This is why the sex differences in strength are largely, though not completely, hormonal.

eFunctional and clinical significance

Functionally, male anatomy favours absolute power; female anatomy favours endurance and flexibility (greater joint laxity). Clinically, the physiotherapist reads these tables with care: female Q angle and ligament laxity inform knee rehabilitation, gluteofemoral fat and the lower centre of gravity alter balance training, female lower lean mass means lower absolute strength benchmarks and slower basal metabolic rates, and postmenopausal bone loss demands early weight-bearing and resistance exercise. Sex-specific normative values — never unisex ones — should be used when interpreting skinfold, body mass index and strength data.

Fig 9 — Two stacked bars: the male bar mostly green (lean) with a thin yellow cap; the female bar with a taller yellow cap. One arrow says "more fat-free mass". Any examiner marking composition can mark this figure in five seconds.
Examiner's tip: always include the two-component model (fat mass + fat-free mass = body mass) before giving numbers, and finish with "per kilogram of lean mass the strength gap narrows" — that one sentence shows you think, not memorize. The Q-angle link to the female knee converts this from anatomy to physiotherapy.

Sources

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — anthropometry and sex differences.
  2. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — body composition, metabolism and hormonal regulation.
  3. ACSM's Resource Manual — body composition assessment and normative values.
  4. American Health Foundation roundtable, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition — healthy body fat percentages (primary).
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Describe the effects of thermal agents on soft tissue repair.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 10a — Biophysical effects of physical agents: thermal agents

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Phases of soft-tissue healing2
Effects of superficial heat2
Effects of cryotherapy2
Effects of deep heating (ultrasound)2
Phase-wise clinical application and conclusion2

aThe healing phases first

Soft tissue repair runs through three overlapping phases: the inflammatory phase (roughly days 0 to 6: haemostasis, vasodilation, exudation, phagocytosis), the proliferative phase (weeks 1 to 3 or so: fibroblast proliferation, collagen synthesis, angiogenesis, granulation), and the remodelling phase (months up to a year: collagen reorganization along lines of stress, gradual strength gain to perhaps 80 percent of original). Every thermal agent earns its place by speeding, slowing or reshaping one of these phases.

bSuperficial heat

Heating to 40 to 45 degrees Celsius produces vasodilation and increased blood flow, raising oxygen and nutrient delivery and accelerating metabolic rate locally — helpful for resolution in the late inflammatory and proliferative phases. It increases collagen extensibility, so heated tissue stretches further with less risk — the basis of heating before stretch in contracture and scar work. It decreases pain (gate control plus later endorphin effects), reduces muscle spasm and decreases joint stiffness; useful in subacute and chronic low back pain, before mobilization. Applied in the acute inflammatory phase it would worsen oedema and pain, which is the classic caution.

cCryotherapy

Cold is the acute-phase agent. It causes vasoconstriction, limiting bleeding and oedema formation in the first 24 to 48 hours; it reduces metabolic rate and secondary hypoxic injury; it slows nerve conduction velocity, raising the pain threshold and providing analgesia; and it reduces muscle spasm by cooling muscle spindles. Applied correctly — with protection of the skin and careful timing — it shortens the painful acute window, and early controlled motion on a numb, less swollen joint begins healing in a better mechanical environment. Cold should not be used over ischaemic tissue or poor circulation, and excessive duration risks nerve injury (watch the ulnar nerve at the elbow and the peroneal nerve at the fibular head).

dDeep heating: therapeutic ultrasound

Ultrasound (typically 1 megahertz for 3 to 5 centimetres depth) heats collagen-rich tissue selectively — tendon, ligament, joint capsule — from within. It increases extensibility for stretching of dense connective tissue, raises blood flow, and (at non-thermal intensities) promotes cellular activity: proposed stimulation of fibroblast proliferation and protein synthesis, aiding the proliferative and early remodelling phases. It should be avoided over acute inflammation, malignancy, the pregnant uterus, growth plates and cemented implants.

ePhase-wise clinical application and conclusion

The examination answer is a timetable: cold in the inflammatory phase, heat and gentle ultrasound in the proliferative phase, and heat plus deep heating before stretching and strengthening in remodelling. Combined with early graded movement — the real driver of organized collagen — thermal agents manage the environment while mechanotransduction directs the repair. Conclusion: thermal agents do not heal tissue themselves; cold buys time in the acute phase by controlling oedema and pain, and heat plus deep energy later increase circulation and extensibility so that movement can do its work — they are assistants to, not substitutes for, therapeutic exercise.

Fig 10 — A timeline arrow with three phase boxes, each tagged COLD or HEAT, and a curve showing collagen strength rising over months. The one-line caption is the entire clinical message of this answer.
Examiner's tip: structure the whole answer around the three healing phases and you cannot drift. The sentence "thermal agents manage the environment; movement directs the repair" is a memorable closer. Learn the contraindication trio for each agent — viva examiners love asking heat over acute inflammation and cold over ischaemic skin.

Sources

  1. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — thermal agents and tissue healing.
  2. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — physical agents in rehabilitation.
  3. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — local blood flow and temperature regulation.
  4. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — connective tissue injury and repair.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper II

QP 8130 · 30-May-2024 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Aging and mobility

  • Muscle mass: 3-5% lost per decade from the 30s; strength and power fall 2-5 times faster than mass (dynapenia).
  • Four pillars shrink together: joint (cartilage, capsule), muscle (sarcopenia), nerve (reaction time, proprioception), behaviour (fear of falling).
  • Power loss matters most for chair-rise and fall recovery — mention it for extra marks.

2Fascia

  • One continuous collagen-hyaluronan web: packages, transmits force laterally (myofascial force transmission), stores elastic energy.
  • Richest sensory organ — mechanoreceptors plus myofibroblasts; source of myofascial pain.
  • Treat the glide, not just the muscle: slow stretch, movement, scar release.

3Shoulder after cuff repair

  • Protect the healing tendon-bone interface: moved, not loaded.
  • Kinematics: guarded abduction and external rotation, altered scapulohumeral rhythm (more scapular), stiffness is the big complication.
  • Kinetics: deltoid unopposed upward versus cuff compression — concavity compression; restore rhythm first, force couple second.

4Muscle in endurance training

  • Mitochondria 2-3 times more, capillary density up, myoglobin up, oxidative enzymes up.
  • Type I hypertrophy modest; IIx toward IIa; no big bulk — quality, not size.
  • Glycogen sparing, lactate threshold shifts right; fatigue resistance is the outcome.

5Elbow fixed flexion deformity

  • The arc does not shrink, it shifts into flexion; carrying angle effectively lost.
  • Functional arc 30-130 degrees does most tasks; small FFD tolerated, but no pushing, no weight-bearing lock, no flat reach.
  • Compensation: shoulder and wrist — they overload. Treat with extension splinting, low-load stretch, posterior glides.

6Forward head posture

  • Upper cervical extension with lower cervical flexion, so the eyes stay level; craniovertebral angle decreases.
  • Upper crossed syndrome: tight upper trapezius, levator, suboccipitals, pecs; weak deep neck flexors, lower trapezius.
  • Remote effects: apical breathing, impingement, TMJ stress, tension-type headache via trigeminocervical nucleus.

7Equilibrium after ankle injury

  • Three inputs (somatosensory, vestibular, visual) plus three strategies (ankle, hip, stepping); body is an inverted pendulum on the ankle.
  • Torn ligament means torn mechanoreceptors — Freeman: articular reflex failure, sway up, eyes closed worse, chronic instability.
  • Balance training cut re-injury from 29% to 7% (Holme 1999) — quote it.

8Injection foot drop

  • Sciatic nerve, peroneal division (lateral, less protected): dorsiflexors and evertors out; plantar flexion relatively spared.
  • Contact: foot slap or toe strike; stance: abrupt loading; swing: steppage — hip and knee hyperflexion.
  • Alternatives: circumduction, hip hiking, vaulting; manage with AFO, stimulation, contracture prevention.

9Male versus female structure

  • Fat: women 20-30% versus men 12-20%; essential fat 12-15% versus 3-5%; fat-free mass higher in men.
  • Upper body muscle about 40% more in men; strength gap narrows per kilogram of lean mass.
  • Pelvis: subpubic angle 80-85 degrees versus 50-60; larger Q angle links to female knee problems.

10Thermal agents and repair

  • Three phases: inflammatory days 0-6, proliferative weeks 1-3, remodelling months to a year.
  • Cold in inflammation: vasoconstriction, less oedema, analgesia, slower nerve conduction.
  • Heat 40-45 degrees later: blood flow, collagen extensibility before stretch; ultrasound heats deep collagen. Match agent to phase; movement directs the repair.
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall.
