  14. Schleip R. Fascial fitness articles, Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies (primary).
Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the various special tests used for pain around the elbow.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2 — Screening: shoulder and upper extremity (elbow region)

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Lateral epicondylalgia tests (Cozen, Mill, chair, Maudsley)2.5
Medial epicondylalgia tests (reverse Cozen, golfer's elbow tests)1.5
Ligament stability testing (varus/valgus, moving valgus stress)2
Nerve provocation tests (Tinel at cubital and radial tunnels)1.5
Interpretation, clusters and validity1.5
Clinical application and conclusion1

aWhy the elbow needs a test battery, not one test

Pain around the elbow comes from four possible sources: the wrist extensor common flexor origin (lateral epicondylalgia), the wrist flexor origin (medial epicondylalgia), the collateral ligaments, and the three nerves that wrap the joint (ulnar, radial, median). So the examiner first localises by palpation, then confirms with resisted tests that load the tendon, stress tests that load the ligament, and provocation tests that load the nerve. Mechanism first: every test below simply reproduces the patient's pain by putting tension or contraction through the structure suspected.

bLateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow) tests

In Cozen's test the patient makes a fist, forearm pronated; the examiner stabilises the elbow, palpates the lateral epicondyle with one thumb and resists wrist extension — with radial deviation (Dutton lists the elbow extended; flexed ~90° is the common Indian convention) — with the other hand. Sharp pain over the lateral epicondyle is positive — the extensor carpi radialis brevis origin is loaded under resistance.

In Mill's test the arm is held with elbow extended, forearm pronated; the examiner passively flexes the wrist with the elbow extended and forearm pronated (some add slight ulnar deviation). Pain at the lateral epicondyle indicates a positive test because the common extensor origin is stretched, not contracted.

The chair (lift) test: the patient lifts a chair with the hand gripping its back, elbow extended, forearm pronated — reproduction of lateral elbow pain is positive. Maudsley's test resists extension of the middle finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint; pain at the lateral elbow suggests extensor origin involvement or radial tunnel irritation. Mill's and Cozen's are also often listed with a resisted-grip test: grip strength measured with elbow extended versus flexed drops notably in tennis elbow.

Fig 1 — Cozen's test drawn as a flow: position, resistance, and where the pain must land. Drawing the palpating thumb on the epicondyle earns the interpretation mark.

cMedial epicondylalgia (golfer's elbow) tests

Reverse the logic. Resisted wrist flexion with the elbow extended and forearm supinated, palpating the medial epicondyle, reproduces pain at the common flexor origin (reverse Cozen's). Passive wrist extension with elbow extension stretches the flexor origin (reverse Mill's). Always compare grip strength and note that medial symptoms also raise ulnar nerve and medial collateral ligament in the differential — that is why the next two groups of tests follow.

dLigament stability tests

Valgus stress with the elbow flexed to about 25 degrees and the humerus in external rotation tests the medial (ulnar) collateral ligament — flexion relaxes the joint’s bony locking; varus stress in the same position tests the lateral collateral ligamentts the lateral ulnar collateral ligament and may produce posterolateral rotatory instability. The moving valgus stress test — applying a valgus load while the elbow moves from flexion toward extension — reproduces the patient's medial pain in the arc of about 120 to 70 degrees. For posterolateral rotatory instability use the push-up or chair rise test with forearm supinated, and the lateral pivot-shift apprehension test. Mentioning the 30-degree position (isolating the anterior band, relaxing the capsule) is what converts a list into an answer.

eNerve provocation tests

Tinel's sign is percussed at the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle — tingling radiating into the ulnar two fingers suggests ulnar nerve irritation. A positive Tinel over the radial tunnel region (3-4 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle) with a positive Maudsley's test points to radial tunnel syndrome rather than tennis elbow — the classic examiner trap. Elbow flexion test (sustained maximal flexion, forearms supinated and wrists extended, for three to five minutes) provokes ulnar symptoms; the upper limb tension test biases the nerve bed.

fInterpretation and clinical application

No single elbow test is definitive, so interpret a cluster: palpation point plus two concordant resisted or stretch tests plus functional provocation (gripping a jar, lifting a bucket in the Indian household context). Lateral pain with a normal neck screening but positive Cozen's and Mill's supports local epicondylalgia; add sensory testing and cervical screening to exclude C6-C7 referral. The conclusion of the answer should say: localise by palpation, confirm by loading the tissue, clear the joints above and below, and screen the nerves — that is the examiner's expected final line.

Examiner's tip: write each test as position + force + positive finding + structure loaded. Four tests written that way score more than ten names alone.

Sources

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  2. Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.

On the evaluation form — Q1: Elbow pain (lateral / medial epicondylalgia with ligament & nerve screening)

I. Subjective examination

A 34-year-old right-dominant male, computer operator and club badminton player, presents with aching pain just distal to the lateral elbow for four months, radiating along the dorsum of the forearm; 7/10 at worst on NPRS. History of onset: no trauma, but a recent increase in practice hours. Symptom analysis — site: just distal to the right lateral elbow, radiating to the dorsal forearm; duration: four months; aggravating factors: gripping, lifting, typing with the wrist extended and backhand strokes; relieving factors: rest. Red-flag screen: no night pain and no neck symptoms. Vital signs: BP 122/80 mmHg, PR 78/min, afebrile.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Mild wasting of the right wrist-extensor mass; no oedema, scar or carrying-angle deformity; the elbow is carried in about 70° flexion.

On palpation. Tenderness 5–10 mm distal to the lateral epicondyle over the common extensor origin, milder over the flexor origin; joint line and olecranon non-tender; increased tissue tension over the extensor mass; no spasm, swelling or crepitus.

1. Motor assessment

AROM full except pain at end-range wrist extension; PROM full with a painful stretch end-feel in Mill's position. MMT: wrist extensors 4/5 with pain. Grip dynamometry 25–30% weaker on the right. Resisted isometrics painful for wrist and middle-finger extension. Reflexes intact and symmetric. Girth 1 cm less at 10 cm below the lateral epicondyle.

2. Sensory assessment

Light touch and pinprick intact in the C5–T1 dermatomes; no paraesthesia; neck movements do not reproduce the elbow symptoms (rules out cervical referral).

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Difficulty with pouring, lifting a pressure cooker, typing beyond 20 minutes, wringing clothes and carrying groceries; unable to grip firmly at work. Outcome measures selected: Numerical Pain Rating Scale (0–10); Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE) — condition-specific scale for pain and function in epicondylalgia; QuickDASH (0–100, higher = greater disability); Patient-Specific Functional Scale (0–10); dynamometry for grip strength; MRC grading 0–5.

4. Gait analysis

Gait normal.

5. Balance

Not documented in this case.

6. Hand function

Reaching, grasping, releasing and firm gripping are limited by elbow pain — pouring, wringing clothes, carrying groceries and a firm working grip are affected. No assistive device used.

7. Coordination

Not documented in this case.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Cozen's testStabilise the elbow; the patient makes a fist and pronates; resist wrist extensionSharp pain at the lateral epicondylePositive in this patient (matches pain on resisted wrist extension) — lateral epicondylalgia (extensor carpi radialis brevis)
Mill's testPronate the forearm, fully flex the wrist, extend the elbowPain over the lateral epicondylePositive in this patient (matches the painful stretch end-feel in Mill's position) — lateral epicondylalgia
Maudsley's testElbow extended; resist middle-finger extensionPain over the lateral epicondylePositive in this patient (matches painful resisted middle-finger extension) — extensor origin involvement; differentiates radial tunnel
Golfer's elbow test (reverse Cozen's)Forearm supinated, wrist flexed; resist wrist flexionPain over the medial epicondyleResult not stated in the case record (only milder flexor-origin tenderness on palpation); if positive, indicates medial epicondylalgia
Elbow valgus stress testElbow flexed 20–30°; apply a valgus forcePain or medial gappingResult not stated in the case record; if positive, indicates medial (ulnar) collateral ligament sprain
Elbow varus stress testElbow flexed 20–30°; apply a varus forcePain or lateral gappingResult not stated in the case record; if positive, indicates lateral collateral ligament sprain
Moving valgus stress testValgus force while moving the elbow from flexion to extensionPain near 120° flexionResult not stated in the case record; if positive, indicates MCL injury (thrower's elbow)
Elbow flexion testMaximal flexion, forearm supinated, wrist extended, for 1–3 minutesTingling in the ulnar distributionResult not stated in the case record (no paraesthesia reported); if positive, indicates cubital tunnel syndrome
Tinel's at the elbowPercuss over the cubital tunnel / radial tunnelDistal tingling along the nerveResult not stated in the case record; if positive, indicates ulnar or radial nerve irritation
Upper limb tension tests (ULTT)Sequential tensioning of the median / radial / ulnar nervesSymptoms altered by neck side-flexionResult not stated in the case record; if positive, indicates a neurogenic contribution to the elbow pain
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Extensor-origin pain
  • Painful, weak grip
  • Reduced load tolerance

Functional limitations

  • Gripping, lifting, typing, racquet sport

Disabilities

  • Reduced work productivity and sports participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to grip and perform repetitive upper-limb tasks secondary to lateral epicondylalgia.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): reduce pain from 7/10 to 3/10 on NPRS; activity modification and ergonomic advice; independent isometric home programme.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): pain 0–1/10; strength within 10% of the uninvolved side; PRTEE reduced by at least 50%; return to typing and graded badminton.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): relative rest, electrotherapy for pain, isometrics, ice after activity. Stage 2 (weeks 2–6): progressive isotonic and eccentric wrist extensor work, soft-tissue mobilisation, Mulligan mobilisation-with-movement, stretching, desk ergonomics. Stage 3 (weeks 6–12): functional and sports-specific loading, scapular conditioning, graded racquet drills.

14. Home programme

Isometric holds; eccentric wrist extension with a light dumbbell or rice-bucket gripping; self-stretch; ice; review at 2 weeks.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe the various steps involved in the decision-making process in physiotherapy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 3 — Decision making, direct access and autonomous practice

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition and why structured decision making matters1
Modes: analytic, intuitive/pattern recognition, narrative1.5
Steps of the patient management cycle (examination to outcome)4.5
Factors influencing decisions and common biases1.5
Application example and shared decision making1.5

aWhat decision making means in physiotherapy

Decision making in physiotherapy is the deliberate process of collecting and weighting clinical information to answer four questions: what is wrong (diagnosis), what can physiotherapy change (prognosis), which intervention is most likely to change it (selection), and is it actually changing (re-examination). Under direct access the physiotherapist is the first contact, so the process must also decide when to treat and when to refer — that is the Paper III angle examiners look for.

bModes of clinical decision making

The analytic (hypothetico-deductive) mode is slow, conscious and hypothesis-testing — the novice's route and the route for complex patients. Intuitive or pattern-recognition mode is fast, built on experience, efficient but prone to bias. Narrative reasoning listens to the patient's illness story and goals. Experts blend all three, but the written answer must present the structured cycle as the backbone.

cThe steps of the process

Step 1, examination: gather demographic data, history and systems review, then select tests and measures. Step 2, evaluation: interpret the data — cluster findings, compare sides, weigh the findings against hypotheses. Step 3, physiotherapy diagnosis and problem list: label the movement or functional impairment (for example, painful resisted wrist extension with grip weakness), prioritise problems that matter to this patient. Step 4, prognosis: estimate achievable improvement and time frame, and set SMART goals with the patient. Step 5, intervention selection: choose techniques that match the impairments, the stage of healing, the evidence and the patient's preferences, in agreed doses. Step 6, re-examination: measure immediate effects (pain relief after a trial technique, range change after mobilisation) and progress at each visit. Step 7, modify or progress, and decide discharge when goals are met or plateau reached. The loop closes: re-examination feeds new examination data.

Fig 2 — The decision cycle as a loop with re-examination feeding back into examination; a single diagram that answers the whole question.

dFactors that influence the decision

Patient factors (age, comorbidity, occupation, expectations, finances), clinician factors (knowledge, skill, experience, biases such as anchoring on the first impression, confirmation bias and availability bias), environmental factors (equipment, caseload, time, referral access) and research evidence. Acknowledge that in Indian settings, travel distance, payment out of pocket and family involvement shape follow-up and goal decisions — examiners reward this grounding.

eApplication and shared decision making

Close with a worked mini-example: a 45-year-old teacher with subacromial pain — history suggests stage 2 impingement, tests confirm a painful arc and positive empty-can; goals are overhead writing and sleeping; intervention is scapular and rotator cuff loading; re-examination at two weeks uses the SPADI score and the painful arc. Shared decision making means the patient chooses between options with the clinician's guidance — and documentation of each step protects the autonomous practitioner.

Examiner's tip: marks sit in the verbs — collect, evaluate, diagnose, prioritise, prognose, select, re-examine, modify. Seven verbs, seven sentences, full marks.

Sources

  1. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 5th ed. FA Davis.
  2. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Write in detail about the postoperative management following both-bone fracture of the upper limb (radius-ulna fracture).

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5 — Assessment of fractures, pre- and post-operative management

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Injury, fixation and pre-operative assessment baseline1.5
Phase 1 (0-2 weeks): protection, oedema, distal and adjacent motion2
Phase 2 (2-6 weeks): graded active motion of forearm and wrist2.5
Phase 3 (6-12 weeks): strengthening and functional retraining2
Complications to monitor1.5
Discharge criteria and conclusion0.5

aThe injury and what surgery achieved

A both-bone forearm fracture disrupts the ring formed by the radius, ulna and interosseous membrane — the hinge that lets us pronate and supinate. Open reduction and internal fixation with plates and screws (dynamic compression plating) restores anatomy and is usually rigid enough to permit early controlled motion, which is the single most important sentence in this answer: rehabilitation after ORIF of the forearm is motion-first, because crossed synostosis and stiffness are the enemies.

bPhase 1 — days 0 to 14: protect and prevent

Assess first: neurovascular status (radial and ulnar pulses, median, radial and ulnar nerve territories), wound condition, pain by VAS, oedema by circumference or figure-of-eight, and the six Ps of compartment syndrome — pain out of proportion, pallor, paraesthesia, pulselessness, paralysis, pressure. Treatment: elevation above heart level, cryotherapy, active finger and thumb exercises every waking hour, tendon glides, shoulder and elbow active range within the surgeon's protocol, gentle pain-free wrist motion if allowed, and education on sling use and sleeping position. No loading, no resistance, no passive stretching of the incision.

cPhase 2 — weeks 2 to 6: recover the arcs

With the wound healed and callus beginning, progress active elbow flexion-extension, wrist flexion-extension and — the functional gold of the forearm — pronation and supination, first gravity-eliminated (elbow at side, doing doorknob turns), then against gravity. Add scar mobilisation once suture lines are mature, heat before sessions, and graded grip work with putty only if the fracture pattern and surgeon permit. Re-measure every visit: goniometric arcs, oedema, pain with the patient-rated scales. Expect roughly half to two-thirds of full arcs by six weeks; document why if not.

dPhase 3 — weeks 6 to 12 and beyond: load and function

Once radiological union signs appear (usually 8-12 weeks), begin progressive resisted exercise — theraband wrist and elbow work, weighted pronation-supination with a hammer or wiper bar, isometric gripping, then eccentric wrist extensor loading relevant to work. Functional retraining mirrors the Indian patient's life: carrying a water bucket, wringing a mop, riding a two-wheeler, lifting a child, keyboard or field work. Plyometric and return-to-sport stages follow for athletes; heavy manual workers may need 4-6 months.

Fig 3 — A four-phase timeline over one axis with the monitor strip below; examiners award the phase boundaries and the safety bar.

eComplications to watch and record

Compartment syndrome (most dangerous early), re-fracture after plate removal, radioulnar synostosis (especially proximal-third and head-injury patients), malunion with loss of the interosseous space and therefore loss of supination, non-union, superficial or deep infection, nerve injury (posterior interosseous), complex regional pain syndrome, and distal radioulnar joint instability. Each complication changes the plan — synostosis needs prolonged motion work or surgical excision; CRPS needs desensitisation and graded exposure, not force.

fConclusion and discharge criteria

Discharge when pronation-supination and wrist arcs are functional for the patient's tasks (as a working benchmark, about 50 degrees each way of pro-sup covers most daily activity), grip within about 80 percent of the other side, and the patient is independent in a home programme. State that progress is always paired with radiological union, never ahead of it.

Examiner's tip: the phrase "guided by radiological union and surgeon protocol" plus the six Ps earns the safety marks that most candidates miss.

Sources

  1. Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL. Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures. Lippincott.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 5th ed. FA Davis.

On the evaluation form — Q3: Postoperative management following both-bone forearm fracture (radius–ulna, post-ORIF)

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 26-year-old right-hand-dominant labourer. Chief complaints: elbow, forearm and wrist stiffness and inability to use the hand at work. History: fall onto the outstretched hand causing a closed both-bone forearm fracture, treated by open reduction and internal fixation with plates 10 days ago; the surgeon now permits gentle active movement. No other past medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history is given. Symptom analysis: site — elbow, forearm, wrist and surgical scars; onset — after surgery 10 days ago; type — stiffness with pain over the scars; severity — 4/10 on the NPRS; aggravating and relieving factors not specified. Pain evaluation: post-surgical pain over the scars, 4/10 on the NPRS. Red-flag screen: vitals stable and afebrile; no warmth or discharge from the scars; serial neurological checks planned to detect iatrogenic nerve palsy. Vital signs: stable, afebrile.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Well-healed radial and ulnar surgical scars; diffuse forearm and hand oedema; forearm carried in mid-prone; mild disuse wasting of the biceps and the intrinsic muscles; gait normal; no bony contour irregularity other than the surgical sites.

On palpation. Minimal tenderness over the scars; no warmth or discharge; no crepitus or abnormal mobility over the fracture site (stable fixation); reduced skin mobility over the scars.

1. Motor assessment. AROM per protocol: elbow flexion 15–110°, extension −15°, pronation 40°, supination 35°, and half-range wrist movements; gentle PROM shows soft end-feels from oedema. MMT: elbow 4/5, wrist and hand 3+ to 4/5. Reflexes intact. Muscle girth measured 2 cm below the lateral epicondyle for serial charting; the fracture site is stable to gentle stress.

2. Sensory assessment. Light touch and pinprick intact in the superficial radial, median and ulnar nerve territories (checked serially for iatrogenic palsy); no wrist drop or clawing; Tinel's sign negative along the scars; monitor for sympathetic signs of complex regional pain syndrome.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Independent in self-care using the left hand; unable to lift, twist a doorknob or wring clothes with the right hand; sling worn outdoors. FIM review shows minimal assistance for upper-body bathing and dressing. Outcome measures: NPRS (0–10); QuickDASH (0–100, higher = greater disability); Patient-Specific Functional Scale (0–10); serial girth for oedema; goniometry; MRC scale 0–5.

4. Gait analysis. Gait normal.

5. Balance. Not affected in this upper-limb presentation; not formally assessed.

6. Hand function. Limited on the right — unable to lift, twist a doorknob or wring clothes; self-care and work tasks performed with the left hand; no assistive device for the hand.

7. Coordination. Not formally assessed at this stage.

8. Investigations

Serial radiographs reviewed by the surgeon documenting fixation and fracture union; radiographic union guides progression to resisted loading and return to heavy labour.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Squeeze test (result not documented)Compress the radius and ulna together at mid-forearm, away from the fracture sitePain along the interosseous membraneInterosseous membrane injury / incomplete union
Piano-key test (result not documented)Translate the ulnar head dorsally and releasePainful, excessive rebound of the ulnar headDistal radioulnar joint instability
Press (chair-lift) test (result not documented)Patient presses the palm on the chair seat to risePain over the DRUJDRUJ involvement
Elbow varus / valgus stress (result not documented)Gentle varus and valgus stress at 20–30° flexionPain or laxityAssociated collateral ligament injury
Tinel's at the scar (negative in this patient)Percussion along the scars and nerve coursesDistal tinglingNeuroma or post-surgical nerve irritation
Resisted pronation / supination (result not documented)Isometric resistance to forearm rotation away from the fracture sitePain over the shaftsBone stress; correlate with radiographs
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Post-surgical pain (4/10 over the scars)
  • Elbow–forearm–wrist stiffness
  • Forearm and hand oedema
  • Weak grip and forearm rotation
  • Scar adhesion

Functional limitations:

  • Cannot eat with the right hand, lift or twist

Disabilities:

  • Off work as a labourer
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to perform hand-intensive occupational and self-care activities secondary to post-ORIF elbow–forearm–wrist stiffness, oedema and weakness.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain reduced to 2/10; oedema within 1 cm of the left side; elbow flexion ≥120°, extension within 5° of full, 60° pronation and supination; independent home programme.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): full functional ROM; MMT 5/5; grip within 10% of the uninvolved side; QuickDASH improved ≥15 points; graded return to heavy labour by 12 weeks subject to radiographic union.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (0–3 weeks): elevation and retrograde massage for oedema; gentle AROM of the elbow, forearm, wrist and fingers within limits; isometrics; wound care. Stage 2 (3–6 weeks): progressive AROM and gentle PROM; forearm rotation with a rod; putty and graded weights; scar mobilisation; sustained stretches. Stage 3 (6–12 weeks): progressive resisted exercise; lifting and twisting function; work-conditioning.

14. Home programme

Hourly short exercise sessions; putty squeezing; self-assisted rotation; scar massage once healed; no lifting heavier than a kettle until cleared.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Write in detail about various investigations used for spinal cord injuries.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4 — Investigations, imaging and electrodiagnosis in diagnosis

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
ASIA/ISNCSCI neurological examination and classification2.5
MRI — role and findings1.5
Radiographs and CT1
Myelography1
Somatosensory and motor evoked potentials, EMG1.5
Urodynamics, autonomic and laboratory studies; conclusion2.5

aThe ASIA exam — the investigation that classifies everything else

The International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury, examined in detail, is the bedrock. Sensory testing: light touch and pin prick graded 0-2 over 28 dermatomes each side, plus deep anal pressure. Motor testing: the 10 key myotomes (C5 elbow flexors, C6 wrist extensors, C7 elbow extensors, C8 finger flexors, T1 finger abductors; L2 hip flexors, L3 knee extensors, L4 ankle dorsiflexors, L5 long toe extensors, S1 ankle plantarflexors) graded 0-5, plus voluntary anal contraction. From these derive the neurological level of injury, and the AIS grade: A complete (no sacral sparing S4-5), B sensory incomplete, C motor incomplete with less than half of key muscles below the level grade 3 or more, D motor incomplete with at least half grade 3 or more, E normal. The 2019 revision refined the zone of partial preservation — it can now be recorded for incomplete injuries lacking sacral motor or sensory function — and introduced a star-tagging system for non-SCI-related deficits. Spinal shock is tracked clinically; return of the bulbocavernosus reflex signals its end and makes the exam reliable.

bMRI — the cord itself

MRI is the investigation of choice for cord parenchyma: it shows cord contusion, oedema, haemorrhage, compression by disc, bone fragment or haematoma, and ligamentous injury. Length of haemorrhage and length of oedema on T2 carry prognostic weight — haemorrhage predicts poorer motor recovery. It also picks up underlying pathology such as tumour, syrinx or demyelination. Contraindications are pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants.

cRadiographs and CT — the bone and the canal

Plain films in the trauma series (lateral cervical spine first) screen alignment and fractures. CT with reformats is superior for fracture morphology, canal encroachment, and surgical planning, and is now the primary screening modality in most trauma protocols. Together: MRI tells you about the cord, CT tells you about the column.

Fig 4 — All investigations converge on the ASIA classification, which drives prognosis and rehabilitation; MRI for the cord, CT for the bone, evoked potentials for conduction.

dMyelography

Contrast injected into the thecal sac outlines the cord and nerve roots on X-ray/CT; it is reserved for patients in whom MRI is contraindicated or unavailable — still relevant in Indian district practice where MRI access may be limited. It shows canal obstruction, root avulsion, and arachnoiditis; complications include post-lumbar-puncture headache and, rarely, seizure.

eElectrophysiology

Somatosensory evoked potentials stimulate a peripheral nerve (typically tibial or median) and record cortical responses, testing the dorsal column pathways — useful in spinal shock to demonstrate conduction, intra-operatively to monitor the cord, and prognostically (a preserved SSEP early on favours motor recovery). Motor evoked potentials test the corticospinal tract, complementing SSEPs. Needle EMG and nerve conduction distinguish a superimposed peripheral nerve or root injury from cord pathology and detect neurogenic bladder candidates for intervention.

fUrodynamics and the remaining studies

Urodynamics — cystometry with uroflowmetry and leak point pressures — characterises the neurogenic bladder (areflexic versus hyperreflexive, dyssynergic), guides clean intermittent catheterisation and guards the upper tracts from high-pressure storage. Digital rectal examination assesses anal tone and the bulbocavernosus reflex; the ASIA autonomic standards document records sudomotor and cardiovascular function. Bone mineral density scans surveil disuse osteoporosis, and blood work (creatinine for renal surveillance, vitamin D, haemoglobin) completes the picture. Conclusion: imaging grades the injury structurally, the ASIA exam grades it functionally, electrophysiology gives conduction and prognosis, and urodynamics protects the kidneys — each answers a question the others cannot.

Examiner's tip: write out the ten key muscles and the AIS A-E definitions verbatim — these are the two lists this question is really set for.

Sources

  1. American Spinal Injury Association. International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI), 2019 revision.
  2. McKinnis LN. Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging. FA Davis.
  3. Greenspan A, Beltran J. Orthopaedic Imaging: A Practical Approach. Lippincott.

On the evaluation form — Q4: Acute spinal cord injury (investigations-focused assessment)

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 32-year-old construction worker. Chief complaints: inability to move the lower limbs and loss of sensation below the chest; urinary retention with a catheter in situ. History: fall from scaffolding 24 hours ago; mechanism of injury was an axial load plus flexion; immediate paraplegia and sensory loss below the chest. Past medical history: no comorbidities. Symptom analysis: site — below the chest; onset — immediate at the time of injury; duration — 24 hours; type — sensorimotor loss below the neurological level during spinal shock; severity — complete loss of voluntary motor control below the level. Red-flag screen: major trauma with suspected spinal instability — strict spinal precautions maintained; neurogenic shock on vital signs. Vital signs: BP 96/60 mmHg (neurogenic shock picture), PR 52/min, SpO2 96%, temperature 35.8°C.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Supine on a spine board with a cervical collar, sandbags and tape; reduced chest expansion with abdominal breathing; no pressure sores yet.

On palpation. Midline tenderness with a step-off at the thoracolumbar junction; rectal examination for tone and voluntary contraction.

1. Motor assessment. ASIA motor examination: the 10 paired key myotomes (C5–T1 and L2–S1) graded 0–5 per the ISNCSCI standard; currently grade 0 in all lower-limb myotomes. Bulbocavernosus reflex absent (spinal shock); deep tendon reflexes and the abdominal and cremasteric reflexes absent below the level. Serial MMT every 24 hours; ROM of all limbs for contracture prevention.

2. Sensory assessment. The 28 key sensory points (dermatomes) on each side tested for light touch and pinprick on a 0–2 scale; sensory level, deep anal pressure and sacral sparing (S4–S5) documented; AIS grade A–E assigned.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Acute-phase function is respiratory (incentive spirometry, vital capacity), skin integrity and passive mobility; the patient is unable to move in bed or transfer and requires total assistance acutely. FIM (18 items, scored 18–126) documents the baseline for transfers, locomotion and self-care. Outcome measures: ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS grades A–E) — the international classification standard; ASIA motor and sensory scores; FIM (18–126) for independence; Spinal Cord Independence Measure (SCIM) — a condition-specific daily-function measure for SCI; serial ISNCSCI worksheets, then weekly.

4. Gait analysis. Non-ambulatory in the acute phase; gait assessment deferred.

5. Balance. Not assessed acutely; seated balance for ≥1 hour is a defined rehabilitation goal.

6. Hand function. The upper limbs lie above the sensory level; formal hand function assessment is deferred in the acute phase.

7. Coordination. Not formally assessed during spinal shock.

8. Investigations

(i) AP and lateral spine radiographs as the initial screen; (ii) MRI — the investigation of choice for cord parenchyma, haematoma, disc and ligament injury; (iii) CT for fracture morphology and surgical planning; (iv) serial ASIA examination daily during spinal shock; (v) urodynamics once stable; (vi) blood counts, electrolytes and renal function; (vii) DVT surveillance with Doppler as indicated; (viii) pulmonary function tests for cervical injuries; (ix) urinary cultures.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
ASIA / ISNCSCI exam (performed — motor and sensory levels and AIS grade charted serially)Standardised motor and sensory charting with anal contraction and deep anal pressureSensory and motor levels; AIS grade A–EClassifies completeness and prognosis of the cord lesion
Bulbocavernosus reflex (positive finding present — absent contraction in this patient)Pinch or catheter-tug at the glans; observe the anal sphincterAbsent contractionSpinal shock; reappearance marks its end
Anal wink (sphincter reflex) (positive finding present — absent contraction in this patient)Prick the perianal skinAbsent contractionConus / sacral reflex arc involvement
Plantar (Babinski) response (result not documented)Stroke the lateral soleGreat toe extensionCorticospinal (UMN) lesion above S1
Rectal tone & voluntary anal contraction (positive finding present — lax tone, no voluntary squeeze in this patient)Digital rectal examinationLax tone, no voluntary squeezeConus medullaris / sacral sparing assessment
Clinico-radiological correlation (MRI findings not reviewed at this assessment)Correlate the neurological level with MRI signal changeCord haemorrhage or transectionPoorer prognosis than contusion-only patterns
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Loss of motor control and sensation below the neurological level
  • Neurogenic bladder and bowel
  • Spinal shock
  • Risk of pressure ulcers, DVT and autonomic dysreflexia

Functional limitations:

  • Unable to move in bed or transfer

Disabilities:

  • Total assistance required acutely
11. Functional diagnosis

Inability to perform mobility and self-care tasks secondary to acute spinal cord injury.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): maintain skin integrity and full PROM; prevent respiratory and thrombotic complications; daily neurological documentation; bowel–bladder programme; assisted log rolling.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): innervated muscles to MRC grade ≥3; seated balance ≥1 hour; family-trained passive movements; wheelchair mobility and transfers; measurable FIM gains.

13. Treatment plan

Acute: spinal precautions; chest physiotherapy (deep breathing, incentive spirometry, assisted cough); passive movements twice daily; two-hourly log-roll turning; ankle pumps with medical thromboprophylaxis; bowel–bladder schedule; family education. Rehabilitation: strengthening of innervated muscles; mat activities; transfer and wheelchair training; tilt-table standing; orthotic assessment for incomplete lesions; home accessibility advice — caregiver training is central to Indian family-based rehabilitation.

14. Home programme

Family and caregiver training in assisted log rolling, two-hourly turning with skin inspection, passive movements and the bowel–bladder schedule; continuation of deep-breathing exercises as taught.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe screening of the knee following posterior cruciate ligament injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2 — Screening: lower quadrant (knee)

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Anatomy, mechanism and presenting features1
Posterior drawer test: technique, grading, accuracy3
Posterior sag sign1.5
Quadriceps active test1.5
Differentiating combined injuries (dial, varus, gait)1.5
Interpretation, functional screening and conclusion1.5

aMechanism first: why the tibia falls backwards

The posterior cruciate ligament is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation at 90 degrees of flexion — the strongest ligament in the knee. It tears either by a direct blow to the anterior tibia (dashboard injury, or falling onto a flexed knee with the foot plantarflexed) or by hyperextension. Classic presentation: vague posterior aching, swelling that is mild compared with ACL tears, and difficulty with descending stairs and deceleration — the quadriceps works harder to hold the tibia forward.

bPosterior drawer — the gold standard

Patient supine, hip flexed 45 degrees, knee flexed 90 degrees, foot stabilised on the plinth (the examiner may sit lightly on the foot); hamstrings must be relaxed — palpate them. Thumbs sit on the joint line feeling the step-off between the medial tibial plateau and the medial femoral condyle; the normal plateau sits about 1 cm anterior to the condyle. A posteriorly directed force is applied to the proximal tibia. Grading: grade I — 0-5 mm translation, plateau still anterior to the condyle; grade II — 5-10 mm, plateau flush with the condyle; grade III — more than 10 mm, plateau drops behind the condyle, and suspect an associated posterolateral corner injury. The test is the most accurate for PCL diagnosis, with reported sensitivity near 90 percent and specificity near 99 percent; always compare with the other knee because congenital laxity exists. Repeat in internal and external rotation: increased laxity in external rotation points to the posterolateral corner.

Fig 5 — Three panels of tibia position against the femoral condyle; drawing the step-off and the three word-pictures (anterior, flush, behind) is exactly what the marking scheme wants.

cPosterior sag sign (Godfrey test)

With the hips and knees flexed to 90 degrees, legs supported at the heels, look from the side: gravity makes the tibia visibly drop backwards on the affected side, flattening the normal step-off contour. It can be reinforced by a gentle anterior push that reduces the tibia with a visible shift. Around 79 percent sensitivity and essentially 100 percent specificity are reported — a highly specific screening sign that is simply observation, so always look before you touch.

dQuadriceps active test

Knee at 90 degrees, foot flat; ask the patient to slide the foot gently down the plinth (or isometrically extend the knee against the examiner's hand). In a PCL-deficient knee the quadriceps contraction pulls the posteriorly subluxed tibia visibly anterior — the relocation is the positive. Sensitivity is modest (about half of proven tears) but specificity is high (about 97 percent), and it demonstrates the dynamic compensatory role of the quadriceps, which is the rationale for quadriceps-dominant rehabilitation.

eScreening for combined injuries

A grade III drawer is rarely isolated. The dial test at 30 and 90 degrees — more than about 10 degrees of excess external rotation at 30 degrees only suggests an isolated posterolateral corner; at both 30 and 90 degrees suggests PCL plus posterolateral corner. Varus stress and reverse pivot shift, gait observation for varus thrust, and hyperextension recurvatum complete the screen. Remember the trap: a posteriorly subluxed tibia makes a routine anterior drawer look falsely positive — reduce the sag first, then test the ACL.

fInterpretation, functional screening and conclusion

Cluster the posterior drawer, sag sign and quadriceps active test with the mechanism and functional history. Screen quads and hamstring strength, step-down control, and use the knee outcome scales from Paper III Unit 6. Conclude: isolated grade I-II injuries do well with quadriceps-focused rehabilitation; grade III or combined injuries need orthopaedic referral — that referral sentence is the examiner's favourite closing line.

Examiner's tip: the three word-pictures — anterior, flush, behind — for drawer grades I, II, III. And never forget "compare with the other knee".

Sources

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  2. Rubinstein RA Jr et al. The accuracy of clinical examination in PCL injuries. Am J Sports Med. 1994.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. Lippincott.

On the evaluation form — Q5: Posterior cruciate ligament injury (dashboard injury)

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 29-year-old car driver. Chief complaints: right posterior knee pain with a feeling of the shin sinking backward, and a limp while walking. History: head-on collision 5 days ago in which the right knee struck the dashboard; immediate posterior knee pain; walks with a limp. No other past medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history is given. Symptom analysis: site — posterior aspect of the right knee; onset — immediate, at the dashboard impact; duration — 5 days; type — dull pain behind the knee; severity — 5/10 on the NPRS; aggravating factors — descending stairs, kneeling and deep squats; relieving factors — rest and ice; no locking. Red-flag screen: no red-flag features documented. Vital signs: stable.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Mild posteromedial swelling; posterior sag of the tibia visible at 90°; antalgic, quadriceps-avoidance gait on stairs; watch for serial vastus medialis wasting.

On palpation. Tenderness along the posterior joint line and popliteal fossa; small non-ballottable effusion; no spasm or warmth; posterior tibial sag palpable on comparison.

1. Motor assessment. AROM: flexion 0–125° with end-range pain; extension painful in the last 10°. PROM: posterior glide increased. MMT: quadriceps 4/5 (inhibition), hamstrings 4+/5, hip and ankle muscles 5/5; resisted isometrics painful for the quadriceps at 60–90°. Reflexes intact; thigh girth equal; limb lengths equal.

2. Sensory assessment. Light touch and pinprick intact in the L3–S2 dermatomes; the common peroneal nerve is specifically tested around the fibular neck, because PCL injuries with posterolateral corner involvement can stretch it; foot dorsiflexion and eversion strong.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Descending stairs, squatting and prolonged sitting are limited; driving and sport are reduced; step-down and single-leg half-squat testing deferred acutely. Outcome measures: KOOS (0–100 per subscale, higher = better); Oxford Knee Score (0–48, higher = better function); WOMAC (0–96, higher = greater disability); NPRS (0–10); Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS 0–80, higher = better); instrumented arthrometry (KT-1000) where available.

4. Gait analysis. Antalgic gait with quadriceps avoidance on stairs.

5. Balance. Single-leg stance time reduced on the right; Star Excursion Balance Test reach reduced in the posterior directions.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this lower-limb presentation.

7. Coordination. Not formally assessed at this visit.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Posterior drawer test (result not documented)Supine, hip 45°, knee 90°, foot stabilised; posterior force on the proximal tibiaPosterior tibial displacement, graded 1+ (<5 mm), 2+ (5–10 mm), 3+ (>10 mm)Gold standard for PCL injury; grade guides management
Posterior sag (Godfrey) sign (positive — sag visible and palpable in this patient)Supine, hips and knees held at 90°, legs supportedVisible posterior sag of the tibiaPCL tear
Quadriceps active test (result not documented)Seated, knee at 90°; patient actively slides the foot forwardPosteriorly subluxed tibia visibly reducesPCL insufficiency
Dynamic posterior shift test (result not documented)Hip and knee moved passively from 90–90 toward extensionClunk as the tibia reduces near extensionPCL tear
Dial test at 30° and 90° (result not documented)Prone, knees 30° then 90°; externally rotate both feet>10° difference at 30° only = posterolateral corner; at both = PCL + PLCDistinguishes isolated PCL from combined injury
Reverse Lachman (result not documented)Knee flexed 20–30°; posterior force on the tibiaExcessive posterior translationPCL laxity
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Posterior knee pain
  • Posterior tibial laxity
  • Quadriceps weakness
  • Dynamic instability on stairs

Functional limitations:

  • Descending stairs, squatting and prolonged sitting

Disabilities:

  • Reduced driving and sport
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to perform stair descent, squatting and single-leg loading secondary to PCL insufficiency.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain reduced from 5/10 to 2/10; full pain-free extension; quadriceps isometric activation with electrical stimulation; independent crutch walking and home programme.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): quadriceps 5/5 with girth within 1 cm; controlled single-leg squat and step-down; KOOS and LEFS within 10 points of age norms; clinical stability 0–1+; return to driving and recreational sport.

13. Treatment plan

Acute (0–2 weeks): relative rest; extension brace for comfort in grade 2–3; cryotherapy; isometric quadriceps (avoid early isolated hamstring work — the hamstrings pull the tibia posteriorly); patellar mobilisations. Subacute (2–6 weeks): closed-chain strengthening — mini-squats 0–45°, step-ups, high-seat cycle, proprioceptive drills. Advanced (6–12 weeks): single-leg strengthening, plyometric and quadriceps-dominant sport drills, stair-descent retraining; reconstruction reserved for grade 3 or combined PCL–posterolateral corner injuries.

14. Home programme

Quad sets, straight-leg raises, heel slides, step-ups, single-leg balance; review 2-weekly.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Describe in detail the assessment following Symes amputation.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5 — Amputations: assessment and prosthetic prescription

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
The level, surgical essence and advantages of Symes amputation2
Residual limb (stump) assessment2.5
Proximal segment, spine and general assessment1
Prosthetic considerations and prescription logic2
Gait analysis with and without prosthesis1.5
Complications, functional outcomes and conclusion1

aWhat a Symes amputation is, and why it is loved

A Symes amputation is a disarticulation at the ankle joint with removal of the malleoli, the heel pad sutured over the end of the tibia to create a durable, end-bearing stump. Its advantages: virtually full end bearing (the heel pad is made for load), an intact long tibial lever arm with preserved knee and good muscle control, self-suspension from the bulbous distal end, a shorter but fully end-bearing limb (a leg-length discrepancy is expected), lower energy cost of walking than transtibial amputation, and — uniquely — the patient can hobble short distances on the bare stump (a real advantage for night bathroom use in Indian homes). Disadvantages to mention: the bulbous end is cosmetically bulky in a prosthesis, and heel pad migration can occur.

bResidual limb assessment

Assess in the examiner's order — look, feel, measure, move. Shape: the classical Symes stump is bulbous with a narrow shaft above; note any dog-ears or prominences that the socket must accommodate. Skin and heel pad: intact plantar skin, no breakdown or wart-like cysts on the end; check whether the pad is stable over the tibia or migrates on weight bearing (pinch and glide it distally). Scars: posterior heel-flap scar placement and maturity. Circulation and sensation: palpable pulses proximal and at the flap margins, protective sensation of the pad — critical for an end-bearing limb. Measurements: residual length from medial tibial plateau to end, circumference at defined levels, and comparison with the sound side; the bulbous diameter determines prosthetic design. Palpate the bony end for tenderness and heterotopic bone. Volume stability: oedema versus mature stump — sockets are prescribed on mature volume.

cProximal segment and whole patient

Because the knee is intact, the big wins are hip and quadriceps power, full knee range, and absence of hip flexion contracture; assess manually and functionally (sit-to-stand). Balance, upper limb strength for aids, cardiovascular endurance, vision, and the systemic disease that caused the amputation (diabetes control, Hansen's disease status) frame the prognosis. Document the pre-prosthetic stage: stump conditioning, shrinker socks, walking with crutches.

Fig 6 — Stump silhouette on the left with the three assessment boxes on the right; the look-feel-measure-move order is what examiners tick off.

dProsthetic considerations

The bulbous end must pass through a narrow shank, so socket designs manage this: posterior-opening or medial-window sockets (Canadian type), expandable-wall closed sockets, or bivalve designs. The socket gives total contact, distributes load between the end-bearing pad and the proximal tibia, and the bulbous flare provides suspension; a suprapatellar strap is added when the flare is insufficient. Because the space between stump end and floor is small, a thin SACH or solid-ankle cushioned foot is standard — few modern Symes prostheses use articulated ankles. Check in with the prosthetist's goals: end bearing, suspension during swing, rotation control, cosmesis (the unavoidable compromise).

eGait analysis

With the prosthesis: near-normal gait is expected because limb length is preserved and the knee is intact; look for shortened stance phase, reduced push-off, vaulting on the sound side, and early knee flexion issues. Check socket pistoning (pad migration or volume loss), pressure areas over the malleolar remnants, and stairs, slopes and floor sitting — cross-legged sitting and squatting matter to the Indian patient. Without the prosthesis: short-distance bare-stump walking is one of the level's unique advantages, assess skin tolerance for it.

fComplications, outcomes and conclusion

Watch for heel pad migration, skin breakdown and cysts, stump overgrowth in children, and wound failure in dysvascular or diabetic patients. Reported outcomes are strong: roughly four in five adults walk with their prosthesis, energy cost is close to normal, and most need minimal therapy. Conclude: the assessment revolves around the end-bearing pad and the intact knee — protect the first and strengthen the second.

Examiner's tip: the five advantages — end bearing, long lever, self-suspension, near-normal energy, bare-stump standing — is a guaranteed marks list. Write it.

Sources

  1. Maxey L, Magnusson M. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. Mosby.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 5th ed. FA Davis.
  3. Kanas JL, Stevens PM. Syme ankle disarticulation: prosthetic management. Atlas of Amputations and Limb Deficiencies. AAOS.
  4. Chui J et al. Syme amputation: a systematic review. Foot Ankle Int. 2018.

On the evaluation form — Q6: Assessment following Symes amputation

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 44-year-old farmer. Chief complaints: stump pain, walking only with crutches (no prosthesis yet) and difficulty sitting on the floor. History: right Symes amputation (ankle disarticulation with heel-pad preservation) 6 weeks ago after a farm-thresher crush injury; non-painful phantom toe sensations. Past medical history: type 2 diabetes, controlled. Symptom analysis: site — right stump (with phantom sensations in the toes); onset — since surgery 6 weeks ago; type — stump pain with non-painful phantom sensations; severity — stump pain 4/10 on the NPRS; aggravating and relieving factors not specified. Red-flag screen: no red-flag features documented; the sound foot is monitored for diabetic complications. Vital signs: stable.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Well-healed bulbous stump with a retained heel pad; healthy scar; mild distal oedema after dependency; sound left foot inspected for callosities and diabetic skin changes.

On palpation. Mild tenderness over the stump end; heel pad mobile and well centred over the tibial end (critical for end-bearing); scar mobility adequate; no neuroma nodule or warmth; calf bulk 1 cm less on the right.

1. Motor assessment. ROM: right knee and hip full and pain-free. MMT: knee extensors 4+/5, knee flexors 4+/5, hip flexors and abductors 4+/5 (disuse weakness); sound limb 5/5. Reflexes intact; no clonus. Serial stump girth measured from the tibial tuberosity; functional limb length recorded for prosthetic prescription.

2. Sensory assessment. Light touch and pinprick over the stump (tibial and sural nerve territories); phantom sensation documented; Tinel's percussion for neuroma; the sound foot is screened with a 10 g monofilament and a 128 Hz tuning fork given the diabetes.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Ambulates with axillary crutches, non-weight-bearing; transfers independent; difficulty sitting on the floor; stairs with supervision. Outcome measures: NPRS (0–10) for stump and phantom pain; Patient-Specific Functional Scale (0–10); Locomotor Capabilities Index — an amputee-specific measure of basic and advanced walking ability; Timed Up and Go; serial stump girth for volume; 6-minute walk test for prosthetic endurance; post-fitting Timed Up and Go, 2-minute walk test, prosthetic gait observation and FIM (18–126) for overall independence.

4. Gait analysis. Axillary-crutch gait, non-weight-bearing; prosthetic gait observation planned after fitting.

5. Balance. Single-leg (sound-limb) stance 20 seconds; sound-limb balance training is part of the programme.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not formally assessed at this stage.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Heel-pad (end-bearing) assessment (heel pad mobile and well centred; only mild distal tenderness in this patient)Graded axial compression of the stump endPain or lateral shift of the padPoor end-bearing tolerance; defer or grade weight-bearing
Tinel's over the distal stump (no neuroma nodule palpated; percussion response not documented)Grid-pattern percussion over the stump endFocal sharp shooting tinglingNeuroma or nerve-ending irritation
Scar mobility (pinch-roll) (negative — scar mobility adequate)Lift and roll the skin over the scarTethered, painful skinAdherent scar needing mobilisation
Stump attitude check (no contracture documented; position monitored as a risk)Observe the stump position supine and standingFlexion–abduction contractureHip contracture risk; needs positioning and stretching

10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Stump pain
  • Deconditioned hip and knee musculature
  • Phantom sensation
  • Risk of flexion–abduction contracture
  • Non-prosthetic status

Functional limitations:

  • Cannot walk bipedally or sit on the floor

Disabilities:

  • Unable to return to farm work
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to ambulate and perform standing occupational activities secondary to Symes amputation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): stump pain reduced to 1–2/10; full pain-free hip and knee ROM with contracture-prevention stretching; stump conditioning begun; independent crutch gait indoors.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): full-time prosthetic use; gait without aids on level ground; hip and knee strength 5/5; continuous 500 m walk; return to modified farm duties.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (pre-prosthetic): stump conditioning and desensitisation (tapping, towel rubbing), shrinker sock, prone lying and hip extensor stretching, progressive resisted strengthening, sound-limb balance, scar massage, crutch gait, phantom-limb education. Stage 2 (prosthetic training): temporary then definitive prosthesis; progressive weight-bearing; gait re-education from parallel bars to level surfaces, stairs, donning/doffing and skin hygiene. Stage 3 (community/vocational): uneven-ground mobility, energy conservation for farm work, foot-care education for the sound limb given the diabetes.

14. Home programme

Daily stump washing and inspection, shrinker wear, strengthening and desensitisation.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe the role of demographic data and history taking in assessment.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 1 — Introduction to assessment: demographic data and history

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Demographic variables and their diagnostic/prognostic value3
Chief complaint and history of present illness (pain analysis)2
Past, drug, family, social and occupational history1.5
Red flag screening within history1.5
Indian context, documentation and link to clinical reasoning2

aDemographic data: the diagnosis before the examination

Age tells you the probability of pathology — osteochondritis in the young, osteoarthritis after fifty, osteoporotic fracture in the postmenopausal woman, tendon degeneration in mid-life. Sex modifies probabilities again: osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis, fibromyalgia in women; ankylosing spondylitis in young men. Occupation predicts the tissue: a farmer's knee, a tailor's shoulder, a software engineer's cervical pain, a construction worker's low back with a flexion-loading history. Hand dominance localises the symptomatic limb and sets functional expectations. Residence and socioeconomic status shape diagnosis (brucellosis and tuberculosis of the spine in endemic areas — spinal tuberculosis is still India's commonest spine pathology) and modify the plan (travel distance, ability to attend, home help). Religion, habits like tobacco and alcohol, marital status and family structure inform support and consent. Marital status, literacy and language also decide how the plan will be explained — the examiner wants you to use demographics, not just list them.

bChief complaint and history of present illness

Begin with the patient's own words for the main complaint and its duration. Then dissect each symptom along the standard ladder — onset (sudden or gradual, trauma), character and distribution, aggravating and relieving factors, timing and diurnal pattern, associated features like stiffness, swelling, paraesthesia, and the effect of treatment so far. Pain is analysed by site, character, severity on a VAS, radiation, temporal pattern and behaviour with posture and activity; night pain and rest pain are flagged immediately. The pattern is a diagnostic shortcut: inflammatory pain is worse at rest and in the second half of the night with morning stiffness over an hour; mechanical pain worsens with load and eases with rest.

Fig 7 — The history funnel: demographics in, working hypothesis out; the red-flag gate before any hands-on testing.

cPast, drug, family and social history

Past medical history (diabetes, tuberculosis, malignancy, previous surgery), past physiotherapy and its result; drugs (steroids and osteoporosis, anticoagulants and bleeding risk, analgesic dependence); family history (rheumatological disease, ankylosing spondylitis, haemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell in central India); social and occupational history (workload, posture, sports, sleep surface — a thin cotton mattress on the floor versus a hard cot changes spine advice).

dRed flags inside the history

Screen every musculoskeletal history for red flags: unexplained weight loss, night pain unrelieved by position, fever, loss of bladder or bowel control, saddle anaesthesia, progressive neurological deficit, history of carcinoma, and trauma in the osteoporotic or anticoagulated patient. A positive red flag changes the whole day — stop, document, refer. In the Indian context, chronic low back pain with evening fever and weight loss must raise spinal tuberculosis.

eDocumentation and the link to reasoning

The history is where shared goals are set — ask what the patient expects and what function they must recover (fetching water, sitting cross-legged for meals, riding a scooter). Record in standard formats (SOAP or the departmental assessment sheet) so the data can steer hypothesis testing: the history chooses the tests, the tests confirm or reject, and both together set the treatment. A well-taken history shortens examination, avoids unnecessary investigations, and is the single cheapest diagnostic instrument available.

Examiner's tip: do not list "age, sex, occupation" — state what each one rules in or out. Value, not vocabulary.

Sources

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function: A Comprehensive Analysis. FA Davis.
  3. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe various outcome measures used for knee pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 6 — Functional assessment, outcome scales and ICF

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Why outcome measures; psychometric properties and ICF mapping1.5
WOMAC1.5
KOOS1.5
Lysholm and Tegner scales2
Kujala patellofemoral score1
VAS, Knee Society Score and selection of the right tool2.5

aWhy we measure, and what a good measure must do

An outcome measure converts the patient's knee into a number we can track across visits and report to surgeons, insurers and researchers. A usable instrument needs reliability (same score on repeat testing), validity (measures what it claims), responsiveness (detects real change) and interpretability — the minimal clinically important difference, which for KOOS subscales is roughly 8 to 10 points. Map each tool to the ICF: impairment-level measures like VAS, activity-level measures like WOMAC and KOOS, participation-level measures like the Tegner activity scale. That single sentence ties this question to the Paper III Unit 6 framework.

bWOMAC — the osteoarthritis classic

The Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index: 24 items in three domains — pain (5 items), stiffness (2 items) and physical function (17 items) — scored 0-100 where higher means worse. Validated in knee osteoarthritis, available in translated Indian-language versions, responsive to change. Its limits: no sport or quality-of-life domain, ceiling effects in younger or higher-function patients, and poor performance in patellofemoral problems.

cKOOS — the expanded successor

The Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score: 42 items across five subscales — symptoms, pain, activities of daily living, function in sport and recreation, and knee-related quality of life — each scored 0-100 where higher means better (note the reversal from WOMAC; examiners love this trap). It captures the young athletic patient where WOMAC ceilings out, making it the preferred measure after ACL reconstruction and for sports injuries.

dLysholm score and the Tegner activity scale

The Lysholm knee scoring scale, originally for ligament injuries and later broadened, is a knee-specific 8-item questionnaire — limp, support, locking, instability, pain, swelling, stair climbing, squatting — scored 0-100, higher is better. It is short, so it suits busy Indian OPDs, but it has a ceiling in high-functioning athletes. It pairs with the Tegner activity level scale, which grades current and pre-injury activity from 0 (sick leave, desk work) to 10 (competitive sports at national level): together they answer two different questions — how the knee feels and what the patient can do.

Fig 8 — Item counts on one bar chart with the scoring-direction note beneath; that note is the mark most candidates lose.

eKujala score — the patellofemoral tool

The Kujala Anterior Knee Pain Scale: 13 items covering limp, walking, stairs, squatting, running, jumping, prolonged sitting, pain and swelling, all weighted to patellofemoral complaints, scored 0-100 with higher being better. It is the instrument of choice for patellofemoral pain and patellar instability studies.

fGeneric anchors and the complete toolkit

The Visual Analogue Scale (0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable) or its numeric cousin is the universal impairment measure — quick, repeatable, but one-dimensional. The Knee Society Score (Insall, 1989) combines a knee score (pain, range, stability, alignment — clinician-rated) with a functional score (walking, stairs), originally built for total knee arthroplasty follow-up. Selection logic closes the answer: osteoarthritis or post-arthroplasty means WOMAC or KSS; sports injury or young active knee means KOOS with Lysholm-Tegner; patellofemoral pain means Kujala; and every patient gets a pain scale plus objective measures (goniometry, manual muscle testing, timed walk or stair tests) — because patient-reported and performance-based numbers together tell the whole story.

Examiner's tip: score direction and item counts are the discriminating marks: WOMAC 24, KOOS 42, Lysholm 8, Kujala 13 — and opposite directions of "better".

Sources

  1. Bellamy N et al. Validation study of WOMAC. J Rheumatol. 1988.
  2. Roos EM et al. KOOS — Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther / JBJS. 1998.
  3. Lysholm J, Gillquist J. Evaluation of knee ligament surgery results. Am J Sports Med. 1982.
  4. Tegner Y, Lysholm J. Rating systems in the evaluation of knee ligament injuries. Clin Orthop. 1985.
