Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe screening of the ankle following ankle subluxation.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2 — Screening: lower quadrant (ankle and foot)

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Ligament anatomy and mechanism of subluxation1.5
History and observation1.5
Anterior drawer test of the ankle2
Talar tilt (inversion stress) test1.5
Syndesmosis, medial and associated-structure screening1.5
Functional tests, outcome measures and conclusion2

aAnatomy and mechanism: what a subluxation tells you

An ankle subluxation — a momentary partial dislocation, almost always the talus shifting under the tibiofibular mortise during an inversion or eversion episode — means the restraining ligaments failed: the anterior talofibular ligament (weakest, fails first in inversion), the calcaneofibular ligament (next, crosses both the tibiotalar and subtalar joints), and the posterior talofibular ligament (last). Repeated subluxation equals chronic instability, so screening asks three questions: which ligaments are loose, what else is injured, and can the dynamic stabilisers compensate.

bHistory and observation

Mechanism (inversion-plantarflexion for lateral), previous episodes — the single strongest predictor of chronic instability — inability to bear weight, swelling and bruising pattern, and functional giving way on uneven ground or stairs. Observe swelling, ecchymosis over the lateral ligaments, hindfoot alignment, arch posture, and gait (antalgic, avoidant push-off). Palpate systematically: distal fibula, ATFL and CFL course, base of the fifth metatarsal (avulsion), anterior syndesmosis, deltoid, and the proximal fibula — a Maisonneuve pattern referred up the leg.

cAnterior drawer test — the ATFL test

Patient sitting with leg hanging, ankle relaxed in about 10 to 20 degrees of plantarflexion; the examiner stabilises the tibia with one hand and grips the calcaneus with the other, drawing the hindfoot forward while the talus is distracted from the mortise. Excessive anterior translation with a soft end-feel compared with the other side indicates ATFL insufficiency. Best after five to seven days, once acute spasm has settled; a side-to-side difference of about 3 mm or more on stress imaging is the laboratory counterpart, and manual grading is subjective — hence always compare with the uninjured ankle.

Fig 9 — Lateral ligament map with the two stress-test arrows; knowing ATFL fails first and CFL second turns a drawing into marks.

dTalar tilt (inversion stress) test

Stabilise the tibia and calcaneus together, then invert (adduct) the talus in the mortise — a comparison test for the CFL and subtalar restraint. Increased tilt with a soft end-feel against the other side indicates lateral ligament laxity; pure talar tilt also loads the subtalar joint, so attribute carefully. Both tests can be done with an arthrometer or stress ultrasound/radiographs for objectivity when surgery is contemplated.

eClearing the rest of the ring

After a subluxation the examiner must clear the neighbours: the squeeze test (compress the calf mid-shaft; pain distally at the syndesmosis is positive) and external rotation test (dorsiflex the ankle and externally rotate — syndesmotic pain) rule out a high sprain; deltoid palpation and eversion stress rule out the medial side; the Ottawa ankle rules guide radiography (malleolar or midfoot bone tenderness plus inability to bear four steps); the Thompson test clears the Achilles; and the neurovascular check (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial pulse, sensation) is mandatory after any subluxation episode.

fFunctional screening and conclusion

Test what the instability actually steals: single-leg balance with eyes open and closed, the Star Excursion Balance Test, hopping and figure-of-eight running, stair descent. Quantify with the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool or FAAM for outcome tracking. Conclude the screening by grading: mechanical laxity (positive stress tests) plus functional instability (positive balance and giving-way) with muscle weakness means a structured proprioceptive-peroneal rehabilitation programme; bony avulsion, syndesmotic injury or neurovascular deficit means immediate referral. That closing sentence is what a 10-mark answer is judged by.

Examiner's tip: "compare with the other ankle" after each stress test, and never forget the pulses — the viva question hiding at the end of this paper.

Sources

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  2. Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. Lippincott.

On the evaluation form — Q9: Recurrent ankle instability / subluxation

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 21-year-old female college basketball player. Chief complaints: repeated giving way of the right ankle on uneven ground with the joint slipping out and back; persistent lateral swelling; apprehension on landing and cutting; walks with slight antalgia on uneven ground. History: three right-sided inversion sprains in 14 months, the latest 3 weeks ago. No other past medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history is given. Symptom analysis: site — anterolateral aspect of the right ankle; onset — after the initial sprain 14 months ago, recurrent since; duration — current episode 3 weeks; type — sharp pain; severity — 3/10 on the NPRS; aggravating factors — uneven surfaces, jumping and flat unsupportive chappals; relieving factor — taping. Red-flag screen: no red-flag features documented. Vital signs: normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Mild anterolateral swelling with resolving ecchymosis; slight pes planus with dynamic valgus on single-leg stance; the patient watches her foot during stance (visual dependency of chronic instability).

On palpation. Tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament, milder over the calcaneofibular ligament; the fifth metatarsal base, syndesmosis and medial structures are non-tender; no effusion or crepitus.

1. Motor assessment. AROM full, with pain at end-range inversion; dorsiflexion 5–10° less than on the left side. PROM: increased inversion laxity. MMT: peroneals 4/5 (the key finding in chronic instability); other muscles 5/5. Resisted isometrics painful for eversion. Ankle jerk intact; calf girth 1 cm less on the right.

2. Sensory assessment. Light touch and pinprick intact in the L4–S1 dermatomes, including the peroneal territories; ankle position sense commonly impaired after repeated sprains; eyes-closed single-leg stance reduced on the right — the proprioceptive deficit central to functional instability.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Running, cutting, jumping and landing are limited; single-leg hop is limited by apprehension; the LEFS documents the overall activity limitation. Outcome measures: Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool — a condition-specific questionnaire for chronic ankle instability; Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) with ADL and sport subscales; NPRS (0–10); LEFS (0–80); Patient-Specific Functional Scale (0–10); single-leg stance time and Star Excursion Balance Test as performance measures.

4. Gait analysis. Slight antalgia on uneven ground; dynamic valgus on stair descent.

5. Balance. Eyes-open single-leg stance normal; eyes-closed single-leg stance clearly reduced; Star Excursion Balance Test reach reduced posteromedially and anteriorly.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not separately tested; the proprioceptive and balance deficits above are the relevant coordination-related findings.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Anterior drawer test (result not documented)Ankle relaxed in about 20° plantarflexion; stabilise the tibia, translate the talus anteriorlyExcessive anterior translation or soft end-feelAnterior talofibular ligament laxity
Talar tilt (inversion stress) test (positive — increased inversion laxity on PROM in this patient)Ankle neutral; stabilise the leg, invert the hindfootExcessive inversion laxity versus the sound sideCalcaneofibular ligament laxity / subluxation
Squeeze test (negative — syndesmosis non-tender)Compress the fibula against the tibia at mid-calfPain over the syndesmosisSyndesmotic (high ankle) injury
External rotation (Kleiger) test (negative — no syndesmotic or medial joint pain)Stabilise the leg, externally rotate the foot with the knee at 90°Syndesmotic or medial joint painSyndesmosis injury, possible deltoid involvement
Thompson / Simmonds test (result not documented)Prone; squeeze the calfNo plantarflexionAchilles rupture (exclude in ankle trauma)
Cotton test (result not documented)Anteroposterior drawer with the ankle in neutralIncreased translation with a mushy end-feelGeneralised talar instability
Single-leg balance, eyes closed (positive — clearly reduced on the right)Timed unilateral stance, eyes closedReduced time or increased sway versus the leftProprioceptive deficit of functional instability
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Anterolateral ligament laxity with recurrent subluxation
  • Peroneal weakness
  • Impaired proprioception and balance
  • Dorsiflexion tightness

Functional limitations:

  • Running, cutting, jumping and landing

Disabilities:

  • Reduced basketball and college outdoor participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to perform running, cutting and single-leg stability tasks secondary to chronic ankle instability.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain reduced from 3/10 to 1/10; swelling controlled; peroneal isometric activation; eyes-closed single-leg balance progressing toward 30 seconds.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): peroneal strength 5/5; Star Excursion Balance Test within 5–10% of the left side; confident hop, side-hop and cutting; full return to basketball with preventive bracing.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): relative rest; balance retraining from single-leg stance to eyes-closed and foam surfaces; peroneal isometrics; taping. Stage 2 (weeks 2–4): elastic-band peroneal strengthening, wobble-board balance, calf stretching, reactive peroneal drills, hopping in place. Stage 3 (weeks 4–8): plyometrics, agility ladder, cutting and landing mechanics, uneven-surface training, sport reintegration with a semi-rigid orthosis. Stage 4 (weeks 8–12): full return with a twice-weekly prevention programme and footwear advice (supportive shoes rather than loose sandals).

14. Home programme

Band eversion, single-leg balance progressions, heel raises off a step; surgery is considered only after failed 3–6-month rehabilitation.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Write in detail about clinical reasoning in manual therapy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4 — PT diagnosis, special tests and red flags; Unit 3 — decision making

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition, dual-process theory and reasoning modes1.5
Hypothesis-oriented examination2.5
Schools of thought in manual therapy2.5
Red flags and differential screening1.5
Re-assessment and treatment-based classification1.5
Expert versus novice reasoning; conclusion0.5

aWhat clinical reasoning is

Clinical reasoning is the thinking process that converts patient data into decisions — diagnosis, prognosis and intervention. Modern understanding is dual-process: System 1 is fast, automatic pattern recognition born of experience; System 2 is slow, deliberate, analytic hypothesis testing. The novice must live in System 2 deliberately; the expert runs System 1 and audits it with System 2 when the pattern does not fit. In manual therapy, reasoning decides not only which technique, but whether manual therapy belongs in the plan at all.

bHypothesis-oriented examination

The Jones model structures the examination around hypotheses generated from the very first history sentence. From the referral, demographics and opening complaint the clinician frames candidate hypotheses across categories: the pain source (pathology, tissue), movement impairment, contributing factors (biomechanical, psychosocial), precautions and contraindications, prognosis, and management. Each question and each test then deliberately seeks information that confirms or rejects a hypothesis, and the therapist reweights with every finding. In manual therapy this shows as: does the movement reproduce the pain (a concordant sign), does repeated movement centralise or abolish it, which direction of mobilisation changes it immediately. Hypothesis orientation is what separates an examination from a checklist.

cSchools of thought and their reasoning fingerprints

The Maitland concept (Australian) is hypothesis-driven, movement-based, with Maitland's famous dictum that the therapist needs a hypothesis only until the next piece of data arrives; grades I-IV of oscillation are chosen by irritability and stiffness versus pain. The McKenzie method (mechanical diagnosis and therapy) classifies by directional preference — derangement responds to repeated movements in one plane, dysfunction to end-range loading, postural syndrome to education. The Kaltenborn-Evjenth/OMPT tradition reasons by arthrokinematics and grades of translation to restore roll-glide. Paris's reasoning emphasises segmental dysfunction and soft-tissue signs. The modern synthesis (Jones and Rivett) makes reasoning itself explicit: narrative, diagnostic, procedural, interactive, collaborative and predictive reasoning streams run in parallel during one consultation.

Fig 10 — The reasoning cycle with the red-flag gate at the top; the loop from re-assessment back to cues is the sentence that earns full marks.

dRed flags and the reasoning to refer

Before any mobilisation, reasoning screens for red flags: unexplained weight loss and night pain, fever, history of malignancy, sphincter disturbance or saddle anaesthesia, progressive neurological deficit, trauma in the osteoporotic, anticoagulated or pregnant patient, upper cervical ligament laxity (RA), and vascular claudication. Manual therapy is contraindicated or requires modification in osteoporosis, acute fracture, inflammatory flare, hypermobility and vertebrobasilar insufficiency for cervical techniques. The clinician's reasoning must distinguish nociceptive mechanical pain from systemic or visceral mimicry — in the Indian clinic, spinal tuberculosis and malignancy present late, so vigilance is high.

eRe-assessment: the manual therapist's stethoscope

Immediate re-assessment after a treatment trial is the core manual-therapy reasoning skill: the pre-post comparison of the concordant sign — pain on movement, range, or the patient's functional task. Improvement validates the hypothesis and the technique; no change rejects it and redirects the reasoning. Sustained reassessment over visits separates real progress from short-term analgesic effects, and treatment-based classification systems (for example, the Pittsburgh low-back classification) formalise this logic into subgroups: mobilisation responders, specific-exercise responders, centralisation, control-dysfunction groups.

fExpert versus novice, and the honest conclusion

Experts reason by organised patterns, tolerate uncertainty, self-monitor for bias, and change course early; novices gather indiscriminately and anchor on first impressions. Clinical reasoning in manual therapy, concluded properly, is not the decoration of technique selection — it is the safety system that decides who should be mobilised, who should be exercised, and who should be sent to a surgeon today.

Examiner's tip: name Jones, Maitland, McKenzie and Kaltenborn in one paragraph with one reasoning idea each, then close with "immediate re-assessment validates every hypothesis". That paragraph alone is a third of the marks.

Sources

  1. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  3. Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper III

QP 8131 · 03-Jun-2024 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Elbow special tests

  • Cozen's = resisted wrist extension, pain at lateral epicondyle
  • Mill's = passive stretch (elbow ext, forearm pronated, wrist flexed)
  • Reverse both for golfer's elbow (medial)
  • Valgus at ~25 deg = MCL; varus = LUCL
  • Tinel cubital tunnel = ulnar; Maudsley = radial tunnel trap

2Decision-making steps

  • Examine, evaluate, diagnose, prioritise, prognose (SMART), intervene, re-examine, modify
  • Novice = analytic; expert = pattern recognition + audit
  • Bias list: anchoring, confirmation, availability

3Both-bone forearm fracture

  • ORIF plate = motion-first rehab
  • Phase 1 (0-2 wk): protect, elevate, finger/shoulder AROM, watch 6 Ps
  • Phase 2 (2-6 wk): elbow, wrist, pro-sup, scar mob
  • Phase 3 (6-12 wk): resistance; 3-6 months: work/sport
  • Enemies: stiffness, radioulnar synostosis, compartment syndrome, re-fracture after plate removal

4SCI investigations

  • ASIA: 10 key muscles 0-5, 28 dermatomes x 2 modalities 0-2, plus DAP and VAC
  • AIS A = no sacral sparing; C = less than half key muscles 3 or more; D = half or more
  • 2019 revision: ZPP now allowed in incomplete injuries; star tag for non-SCI deficits
  • MRI = cord (haemorrhage = poor prognosis); CT = bone and canal
  • Myelography when MRI contraindicated or unavailable
  • SSEP tests dorsal columns, gives prognosis; urodynamics protects the kidneys

5PCL screening

  • Posterior drawer at 90 deg = gold standard (about 90 percent sensitive, 99 percent specific)
  • Grade I anterior (0-5 mm), Grade II flush (5-10 mm), Grade III behind (over 10 mm + suspect PLC)
  • Sag sign: tibia drops by gravity; quadriceps active: tibia shifts forward on quad contraction
  • Dashboard mechanism; sag makes ACL drawer falsely positive — reduce first

6Symes amputation

  • Ankle disarticulation, malleoli removed, heel pad over tibia end
  • Advantages: end bearing, long lever, self-suspending, near-normal energy, bare-stump standing
  • Socket: posterior door or expandable wall; thin SACH foot
  • Assess: pad migration, bulbous diameter, knee ROM, quads strength

7Demographics and history

  • Every variable must rule something in or out (age, sex, occupation, dominance, locality)
  • Inflammatory pain: rest + second half of night + morning stiffness over 1 hour
  • Red flags: weight loss, night pain, fever, sphincter loss, saddle anaesthesia, progressive deficit
  • India context: spinal TB with evening fever and weight loss

8Knee outcome measures

  • WOMAC 24 items (5 pain, 2 stiffness, 17 function); high = worse
  • KOOS 42 items, 5 subscales; high = better
  • Lysholm 8 items x 100; Tegner 0-10 activity level; Kujala 13 items patellofemoral
  • KSS = knee score + function score (arthroplasty); VAS 0-10 for all

9Ankle after subluxation

  • Inversion order of failure: ATFL first, CFL second, PTFL last
  • Anterior drawer in 10-20 deg plantarflexion tests ATFL; talar tilt tests CFL
  • Squeeze + external rotation = syndesmosis; Ottawa rules for X-ray
  • Pulses and sensation after every subluxation episode

10Clinical reasoning in manual therapy

  • Hypothesis categories: pain source, movement impairment, contributing factors, precautions, prognosis, management
  • Schools: Maitland (movement, grades), McKenzie (directional preference), Kaltenborn (arthrokinematics), Paris (segmental)
  • Immediate re-assessment of the concordant sign = validate or reject the hypothesis
  • Red flag gate before any mobilisation

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. What is the importance of functional training in individuals with total hip replacement?

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 3 — functional training and physical activity promotion

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Rationale and goals of functional training after THR2
Assessment, precautions and early milestones2
Transfer, gait and stair training progression2
ADL retraining and joint protection2
Strengthening, balance, community reintegration and evidence2

aWhy functional training matters — the mechanism first

A total hip replacement removes the arthritic joint but the patient's real problem is functional: getting out of bed, walking to the bus, squatting to an Indian toilet, sitting cross-legged. Functional training is important because it converts surgical success into daily-life success. Mechanism: the operation restores a stable, pain-free lever; the muscles around it — gluteus medius, gluteus maximus, hip flexors — are weak and inhibited from months of limping and disuse. Abductor weakness leaves the patient with a positive Trendelenburg pattern until the posterior capsule precautions are deliberately trained around and the hip musculature re-educated. Functional training therefore targets the impairments while rehearsing the exact tasks the patient must perform at home.

bAssessment and early milestones

Assess on day one or postoperative day zero: active straight-leg raise, hip abduction and extension strength, quadriceps control, ability to shift in bed. Standard bedside markers are sitting over the edge of the bed by day zero or one, standing transfers, and walking with a frame by day one or two. Record pain (VAS), range, and a baseline functional score such as the Harris Hip Score or Oxford Hip Score so improvement is documentable.

cTransfer, gait and stair progression

Teach each task as a rehearsed sequence: bed mobility with log-rolling to the operated side being avoided in favour of the sound side, sit-to-stand with the operated leg forward, then walker, then crutches, then single stick held on the opposite hand. Progress from frame to stick only when abductor control allows a level pelvis. Stairs last, with the taught rhyme — good leg to heaven, bad leg to hell (up with the sound, down with the operated).

Fig 1 — Safe versus danger zone box after a posterior-approach THR. Reproducing this pair of boxes with the three danger positions earns the precautions marks fast.

dADL retraining and joint protection

Rehearse real tasks: raised chair and commode, long-handled reacher for dressing, sock aid, slip-on footwear, sleeping with a pillow between the knees. For the Indian context specifically address floor-level living: a Western-style raised seat for the initial weeks, graded squat training only after surgeon clearance, and a side-lying method for getting down to and up from the floor. This is where functional training earns its name — the therapy looks like the patient's life, not like a gym.

eStrengthening, balance and community reintegration

Progress from isometrics to open-chain abduction in side-lying, then closed-chain work: mini-squats within the safe range, step-ups, stationary cycling with a high saddle. Add balance boards and treadmill walking for endurance. By week six to twelve the goal is independent community ambulation, and long-term adherence to the WHO recommendation of 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity per week.

fEvidence and conclusion

Enhanced-recovery protocols with structured early mobilisation reduce hospital stay and complications without increasing dislocation; functional scores improve most when exercise is task-specific and progressive. Conclude: the implant restores the joint, functional training restores the person.

Examiner's tip: when a question says "importance", spend the first two marks on WHY (disuse weakness, fear, dislocation risk) before listing WHAT — students who list exercises without the mechanism lose the reasoning half.

On the evaluation form — Q1: Post-total hip replacement (functional training)

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 62-year-old woman. Chief complaints: post-operative hip pain and the need for help with transfers and toileting. History: post-operative day 3 after a cemented total hip replacement (posterolateral approach) for hip osteoarthritis. No other past medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history is given. Symptom analysis: site — operated hip; onset — after surgery 3 days ago; type and severity — pain 4/10 on the NPRS (0–10); aggravating and relieving factors not specified. Red-flag screen: no red-flag features documented. Vital signs: stable.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Operated limb held slightly abducted; mild trochanteric swelling; surgical dressing clean.

On palpation. Mild warmth only; no calf tenderness; reduced gluteal bulk.

1. Motor assessment. Hip flexion 70° and abduction 25°, within precautions. MMT (MRC 0–5): hip abductors and extensors 3/5, knee muscles 4/5. Thigh girth 2 cm less than on the other side.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation, distal pulses and foot movements normal — sciatic and common peroneal nerve function preserved.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Bed mobility with moderate assistance; sit-to-stand using a high chair. Outcome measures: Harris Hip Score (0–100), Oxford Hip Score (0–48), TUG and PSFS (0–10) recorded at baseline, 6 and 12 weeks.

4. Gait analysis. Walks 10 m with a frame, partial weight bearing.

5. Balance. Single-leg stance unsafe.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not formally assessed at this stage.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Trendelenburg test (not documented; single-leg stance currently unsafe)Stand on the operated leg for 30 secondsPelvis drops on the opposite sideGluteus medius weakness
Thomas test (result not documented)Supine; one hip flexed to flatten the lumbar spineOpposite heel lifts off the couchFixed hip flexion contracture
Leg-length measurement (result not documented)ASIS to medial malleolusMore than 1 cm differenceLimb-length imbalance
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Pain (4/10 on the NPRS)
  • Weak hip abductors and extensors
  • Restricted hip ROM

Functional limitations:

  • Dependent transfers
  • Non-functional gait

Disabilities:

  • Unable to manage home and community activities
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to perform transfers, ambulation and home and community activities secondary to post-operative pain, hip muscle weakness and restricted ROM following total hip replacement.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): independent bed mobility and transfers; walk 30 m with a walker; NPRS down to 2/10; hip abduction 4/5.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): community gait without an aid; Trendelenburg negative; Harris Hip Score gain of 20 points; stairs independently.

13. Treatment plan

Phase I (days 1–5): ankle pumps hourly; gluteal isometrics 5 × 10 twice daily; assisted abduction within limits; walker gait twice daily. Phase II (weeks 2–6): standing abduction 3 × 12, mini-squats 3 × 10, step-ups; progress walker to cane. Phase III (weeks 7–12): band-resisted abduction 3 × 15, single-leg stance 4 × 30 seconds, stairs. Precautions — posterolateral approach: no flexion past 90°, adduction past midline or internal rotation; anterior/anterolateral approach: avoid extension and external rotation beyond neutral.

14. Home programme

Daily exercise set; high chair and raised toilet seat for 6–8 weeks.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. What are the recent advances in electrotherapy management of above-knee amputation?

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 5 — evidence-based electrotherapy and recent advances

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Goals of electrotherapy after AKA and assessment of the stump2
Pain control: TENS for stump and phantom pain2
Oedema and stump conditioning: IFT, HVPC, NMES2
EMG biofeedback and myoelectric training2
Newer concepts: mirror therapy, graded motor imagery, phantom motor execution and evidence2

aGoals and assessment — set the stage first

After an above-knee amputation the physiotherapist's electrotherapy agenda has four targets: control residual-limb and phantom pain, shrink and condition the stump, prevent flexion contracture of the hip by keeping the residual muscles working, and prepare the patient for prosthetic control. Assess stump healing (semicircular grading of wound maturity), sensation, volume, hip range and strength before choosing any modality.

bPain control: TENS and interferential therapy

Conventional high-frequency TENS (40–80 Hz per DeLisa; 80–100 Hz in common practice, strong but comfortable) over the stump or proximal dermatomes is the workhorse for residual-limb pain, acting through segmental gating. For phantom limb pain, electrodes placed on the contralateral intact limb or over the stump can be tried, though recent evidence cautions us: the Cochrane review found no randomised trials of adequate quality to prove or refute TENS for phantom and stump pain, so it stays a safe, inexpensive option rather than a proven cure. Interferential current offers deeper comfortable stimulation for stump oedema-associated ache and can be combined with active muscle pumping.

cOedema, shaping and muscle conditioning

High-voltage pulsed current and interferential therapy assist in early postoperative oedema along with compression bandaging and stump shaping. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) over the residual quadriceps, hamstrings and adductors maintains muscle bulk and the muscle-tendon bed for later prosthetic suspension; it also produces the pumping action that reduces oedema. Functional patterns matter more than raw intensity — stimulate the patient into attempting the contraction simultaneously.

Fig 2 — Stump diagram with NMES electrode pair over the residual quadriceps and a TENS note card. Drawing the electrode placement is what separates a passing answer from a distinction answer.

dEMG biofeedback and myoelectric training

EMG biofeedback over the hip abductors and residual thigh muscles re-educates recruitment, reduces co-contraction and gives the patient a visible target. When a myoelectric or microprocessor-controlled prosthesis is planned, the same surface electrodes train graded, well-separated contraction of residual muscle groups — the bridge from therapy to prosthetic function.

eRecent advances — the genuinely new material

The important recent shift is from stimulation to re-training the brain's map of the missing limb. Mirror therapy and graded motor imagery (laterality recognition, imagined movements, then mirror work) now carry the strongest evidence for phantom pain prevention and relief. Phantom motor execution goes one step further: myoelectric pattern recognition decodes the patient's intended phantom movements from residual-limb EMG and drives a virtual limb on screen, typically fifteen sessions at two to three per week, with good reported reductions in phantom pain. Pair this with the surgical advance of targeted muscle reinnervation, which gives the prosthesis user intuitive control sites, and with home training now feasible through textile-electrode bands. Other additions: sensory desensitisation programmes, transcutaneous vagus or auricular stimulation as investigational options, and shockwave therapy for stump neuroma pain in selected cases.

fEvidence and conclusion

Grade your claims honestly: mirror therapy with graded motor imagery has the best non-drug evidence available, though Cochrane rates that evidence as low certainty; TENS for phantom pain lacks trial evidence but is safe and cheap; phantom motor execution shows promising phase-two data. Conclude: modern electrotherapy after AKA is less about the machine and more about neuromodulation — restoring the cortical representation of the limb.

Examiner's tip: the word "recent" is where marks hide. Every student writes TENS; only the well-read student writes graded motor imagery and phantom motor execution with session dosage. Do NOT claim TENS is proven for phantom pain — saying the Cochrane evidence is absent but the risk is nil shows maturity.

Sources

  1. Johnson MI et al. TENS for phantom pain and stump pain. Cochrane Database Syst Rev.
  2. Chui L et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation. Amputation chapters.
  3. Guideline on prevention and management of phantom limb pain, J Orthop Surg Res 2026.
  4. Pilot studies of phantom motor execution with textile-electrode systems, J Neuroeng Rehabil 2026.

On the evaluation form — Q2: Transfemoral amputation (phantom pain & stump electrotherapy)

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 48-year-old man. Chief complaints: shooting phantom pain, stump aching and poor sleep. History: right transfemoral amputation 8 weeks ago after a road accident. No other past medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history is given. Symptom analysis: site — phantom foot and stump; onset — since the amputation 8 weeks ago; type — shooting phantom pain with stump aching; severity — 6/10 on the NPRS (0–10), 5–8 episodes daily; aggravating and relieving factors not specified. Red-flag screen: no red-flag features documented; distal stump warmth noted and monitored. Vital signs: normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Stump oedematous and bulbous distally; scar well healed; hip held in slight flexion–abduction.

On palpation. Distal warmth; marked lateral tenderness (possible neuroma); reduced scar mobility.

1. Motor assessment. Hip flexion 100°, extension −15°. MMT: gluteus maximus and gluteus medius 3/5, quadriceps and hamstrings 4/5. Stump girth charted at 5 cm intervals.

2. Sensory assessment. Phantom sensation with telescoping; allodynia of the distal stump to light touch; sensation reduced near the scar.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Independent transfers and wheelchair mobility; crutch gait indoors; poor stamina; unable to tolerate a socket. Outcome measures: NPRS with a pain diary; PSFS (0–10) for prosthetic use and sleep; 6-minute walk test repeated after fitting.

4. Gait analysis. Crutch gait indoors.

5. Balance. Sound-limb stance 20 seconds.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not formally assessed at this stage.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Tinel's sign at the stump (lateral stump tenderness present; percussion response not documented)Percussion along the scar and distal stumpTingling radiates into the phantom footNeuroma — TENS and desensitisation target
Bony palpation (result not documented)Firm pressure over the femoral endSharp localised painProminent bony end or spur — refer
Weight-tolerance test (not documented; pylon standing planned in the treatment programme)Graded stump pressure, then pylon standingPain on loadingNot ready for prosthetic weight bearing
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Phantom pain
  • Stump hypersensitivity and oedema
  • Weak hip extensors and abductors

Functional limitations:

  • Cannot tolerate a socket

Disabilities:

  • Wheelchair-dependent for community mobility
11. Functional diagnosis

Inability to tolerate prosthetic socket wear and to achieve community ambulation secondary to phantom pain, stump hypersensitivity and hip muscle weakness.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): phantom pain reduced from 6/10 to 3/10 with TENS; stump tolerates towel rubbing 5 minutes twice daily; full hip extension.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): fewer than two phantom episodes daily; conical stump maintained in a shrinker; walk 200 m with a preparatory prosthesis.

13. Treatment plan

Electrotherapy (staged): conventional TENS (around 100 Hz, short pulse duration) 30–60 minutes, 2–3 sessions daily over the stump or the contralateral limb for phantom pain; IFT for stump aching; ramped NMES to the glutei 20 minutes daily. Weeks 1–2: figure-of-eight bandaging, shrinker, prone lying. Weeks 3–6: strengthening and mirror therapy 15 minutes twice daily. Weeks 7–12: pylon standing and prosthetic gait training.

14. Home programme

Self-bandaging, mirror therapy, prone lying 20 minutes twice daily, hip exercises 3 × 15, pain diary review.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe the physiotherapy interventions in correction of posture in scoliosis.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 3 — postural stability and corrective techniques

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition, mechanism and assessment including Cobb angle2
Physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises: Schroth principles3
Adjunct exercise: stretching, strengthening, core and breathing2
Postural re-education, bracing role and school screening2
Evidence and conclusion1

aMechanism and assessment

Scoliosis is a lateral curvature with vertebral rotation; in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis the deformity feeds itself — asymmetric loading by the Hueter-Volkmann principle slows growth on the concavity and accelerates it on the convexity, so early postural correction matters more than late. Assess with the Adam's forward-bend test (a rib hump on the convex side), scoliometer reading, and radiographic Cobb measurement of the curve: curves under 10 degrees are spinal asymmetry only, 10 to 20 degrees need exercise and observation, 20 to 40 to 45 degrees get bracing plus exercises, and beyond that surgery is discussed. Record curve flexibility on side-bending films.

bCorrection — scoliosis-specific exercises

The modern umbrella is physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises (PSSE), of which the Schroth school is the best known. Its correction block has three self-correction components in front of a mirror: elongation (de-rotation by making the spine longer, which unlocks the rotation), then sagittal correction, then frontal-plane correction — the therapist's hands guide the concavity open. This is followed by rotational angular breathing: direct the breath into the collapsed concave zones to de-rotate the ribs from inside while stabilising the corrected posture. Finally, muscle activation in the corrected position — the patient is trained to hold the corrected spine, not merely to do repetitions of generic exercise.

Fig 3 — Curved spine with the two Cobb lines and the angle between them, plus the Schroth correction block. The angle drawn between the most tilted end vertebrae is the single most quotable measurement in scoliosis.

cAdjunct exercise programme

Around the specific work, prescribe: stretching of the shortened concave-side musculature (quadratus lumborum, latissimus, hip abductors on the concavity), strengthening of the convex side and of the deep core with emphasis on the multifidus and transversus abdominis, symmetrical postural endurance work, and breathing exercises to restore thoracic expansion. Unstable-surface and body-weight training keep the programme honest and home-friendly.

dPostural re-education, bracing and screening

Mirror-aided auto-correction, sitting and bag-carrying advice for schoolchildren, and periodic review every four to six months during the growth spurt. When a brace is prescribed, physiotherapy continues inside it — exercises maintain trunk strength, prevent stiffness, and address brace-wear adherence psychologically; the SOSORT consensus recommends exercise as an adjunct, especially for mild and moderate curves, and during brace weaning.

eEvidence and conclusion

SOSORT-endorsed PSSE programmes have RCT support for reducing curve progression risk and improving cosmetic trunk appearance in mild curves; generic exercises alone do not. Conclude with the examiner's line: the curve is corrected in three dimensions — sagittal, frontal and transverse — by elongation, de-rotation and breathing, then stabilised by muscle, or the deformity wins.

Examiner's tip: never write "strengthen the convex side and stretch the concave side" alone — that earns half marks. Pair every adjunct with the three-dimensional self-correction and rotational breathing logic of PSSE, and quote the curve-degree thresholds 10, 20 and 45.

Sources

  1. SOSORT consensus guidelines on conservative scoliosis management.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Scoliosis and spinal deformity section.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Spinal posture chapter.

I. Subjective examination

On observation. Standing: right shoulder elevated, right rib hump, waist-crease asymmetry; C7 plumb line deviated from the gluteal cleft.

On palpation. Paraspinal fullness on the right (convex) side; no tenderness.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation, myotomes and abdominal reflexes normal — neurogenic scoliosis excluded.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Sits through 6 school hours with slouching. Outcome measures: Cobb angle and scoliometer angle of trunk rotation for follow-up; SRS-22 questionnaire (function, pain, self-image); PSFS (0–10).

4. Gait analysis. Gait normal.

5. Balance. Balance normal.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not formally assessed at this stage.

8. Investigations

Standing posteroanterior spine radiograph for Cobb angle measurement per the screening pathway; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Postural asymmetry with poor sitting endurance and self-image concerns secondary to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, with a risk of curve progression during the remaining growth.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): performs a daily 20-minute exercise set independently; correct sitting posture for 30-minute study blocks.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): no progression on serial readings; 3 × 15 independent self-correction; brace compliance 18–20 hours daily if prescribed.

13. Treatment plan

Phase I (weeks 1–4): mirror feedback of curve correction; active self-correction 5 × 10-second holds, 3 times daily; hamstring and hip-flexor stretches 2 × 30 seconds daily. Phase II (weeks 5–12) — scoliosis-specific exercise (SEAS/Schroth-based): elongation and de-rotation in sitting, side-lying over a roll and standing; rotational angular breathing 10 breaths × 3; core stabilization (dead bug, bird-dog 3 × 10). Phase III: swimming and graded strengthening.

14. Home programme

Daily 20-minute set, brace wear as advised, monthly scoliometer review.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Write the principles and concept of the McKenzie technique.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 4 — manual therapy schools including McKenzie

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Philosophy and assessment by repeated movements2
Classification into syndromes3
Centralisation and directional preference concept2
Treatment principles and force progression2
Evidence and conclusion1
★ Memory hook — McKenzie law: centralise = continue, peripheralise = stop. Three syndromes D-P-D: Derangement (directional preference), Postural (correction), Dysfunction (end-range stretch).

aPhilosophy — mechanical assessment first

Robin McKenzie's concept is that most spinal and extremity pain of mechanical origin behaves in a predictable, directional way: certain movements worsen it and the opposite movements abolish it. Assessment therefore uses repeated end-range test movements in a single direction — flexion in lying, extension in lying — observing the effect on the site of pain. The patient is assessed as a mechanical system, and the directional response found in the first session drives the entire treatment.

bCentralisation and directional preference

Centralisation of symptoms is the heart of the method: when repeated movement abolishes distal or peripheral pain and draws it proximally toward the midline, the movement is therapeutic and the prognosis improves. Peripheralisation — pain travelling further down the limb — is a stop signal. Directional preference is the movement direction that centralises or abolishes pain; it is diagnostic and therapeutic simultaneously.

cThe classification — three mechanical syndromes plus OTHER

Derangement syndrome: internal displacement of nuclear material; pain changes within a single session, flexion aggravates, rapid changes occur. Dysfunction syndrome: structurally shortened tissue stretched painfully; pain appears only at end range, does not centralise, improves over weeks. Postural syndrome: pain only from prolonged static loading of normal tissue, abolished by position change. OTHER (non-mechanical or chronic presentations such as CRPS, neural compromise) requires a different route — red flags and central sensitisation states, where McKenzie principles alone do not apply.

dTreatment principles

Treatment is patient-generated force first, therapist force only if needed — force progression goes from static positions (sustained) to dynamic movements, to patient overpressure, to clinician overpressure, to mobilisation and traction. Education is central: the patient learns which postures to adopt (lumbar lordosis) and which to avoid (slumped sitting, flexion in derangement), so self-management reduces recurrences. In dysfunction syndrome the principle inverts — the short tissue is stretched repeatedly at end range; in postural syndrome the cure is postural correction and endurance.

Fig 4 — The before-and-after centralisation box with the force-progression ladder beneath it. This one diagram carries the whole concept of the technique.

eMaintenance and prevention

Once symptoms centralise and abolish, the patient maintains the directional-preference exercise and the postural habit: lumbar support in sitting, regular breaks from flexion, and a home programme of the recovery-of-function movements in the lost direction, restoring full flexion gradually once the derangement is stable.

fEvidence and conclusion

Centralisation is a validated prognostic sign; McKenzie care shows short-term superiority over generic advice for acute low back pain and equals other active therapies long term. Conclude: assess by repeated movement, classify by behaviour, treat with the patient's own force in the preferred direction, and make the patient their own therapist.

Examiner's tip: the four syllabus words are centralisation, directional preference, classification and self-management — build each h4 around one of them and the examiner ticks in order.

Sources

  1. McKenzie R, May S. The Lumbar Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Spine chapter.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Intervention sections.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Write down the role of physiotherapy in management of glenohumeral dysfunction in swimmers.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 1 — interventions for muscle performance and neuromuscular control

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Mechanism of swimmer's shoulder and assessment2
Acute phase management2
Definitive phase: rotator cuff and scapular retraining3
Technique correction and training-load management2
Return-to-pool criteria and prevention1

aMechanism and assessment

Swimmer's shoulder is an overuse problem of the shoulder girdle during the pull-through and recovery phases of freestyle. During recovery and hand entry the shoulder rotates under load; combined external rotation and abduction compresses the posterior-superior labrum and rotator cuff — internal impingement — while micro-instability from capsular laxity and fatigue lets the humeral head migrate. Fatigued periscapular muscles produce scapular dyskinesis: a dropped, protracted scapula that closes the subacromial space. Assess with the swimming history (stroke, weekly distance, hand-entry pattern), painful arc and Neer or Hawkins tests, labral provocation tests, scapular observation in repeated elevation, and documented glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) with the side-lying comparison against total arc rotation.

bAcute phase

Relative rest from the aggravating volume, not total rest — swimmers decondition fast and can kick-train with a pull-buoy between the ankles. Modalities are optional adjuncts; the real work is pain-free maintenance of range, isometric cuff loading, and posture correction. Address the posterior capsule tightness with sleeper and cross-body stretches early.

cDefinitive phase — rebuild the power chain

Rehabilitate from inside out: rotator cuff strength with external rotation at 0 and 90 degrees abduction using elastic resistance, scapular control with retraction, low-row, prone Y-T-W and serratus wall slides, then closed-chain work and pyometric catching, and finally dry-land swim-specific strength — pull-ups, cable internal-rotation mimicking the pull-through. Correct GIRD to bring the total rotation arc to symmetry (sleeper stretch, cross-body adduction stretch and joint mobilisations in external rotation). Restore thoracic extension rotation for the breathing pattern and core strength to anchor the kinetic chain.

Fig 5 — The overhead arm at hand entry with the impingement zone marked, the rebuilding chain and the GIRD rule. Examining boards love the GIRD numbers 18 to 20 degrees of deficit.

dTechnique and load — the coach's chair

Physiotherapy in swimmers fails without technique analysis: correct thumb-entry to fingertip-first entry, avoid midline crossover, balance the bilateral breathing, increase body roll. Coordinate with the coach on training-load modification — cutting only the painful sets, keeping the aerobic base.

eReturn to sport and prevention

Return to full training when the shoulder is pain-free through the full arc, external-rotation strength approximates the sound side (within 10 percent), and the scapula stays controlled after a fatigue set. Prevention is a season-long programme of cuff and scapular strengthening, GIRD surveillance, and a progressive rather than sudden increase in weekly distance.

Examiner's tip: half of every swimmer's-shoulder answer is NOT in the shoulder — GIRD, scapular dyskinesis and thoracic-core links are what fetch the full ten. Also name the phase of the stroke (hand entry, pull-through) when you describe the mechanism; vague "overhead activity" is a half-mark sentence.

Sources

  1. Wilk KE, Brotzman SB. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. Shoulder chapters.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Shoulder chapter.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Shoulder section.

On the evaluation form — Q5: Swimmer's shoulder

I. Subjective examination

A 19-year-old state-level freestyle swimmer (training mileage 30 km weekly) reports anterolateral right shoulder pain of six weeks' duration, with no trauma. Site: anterolateral right shoulder. Onset: gradual. Duration: six weeks. Type: overuse pain, occurring in the catch and pull-through phases of the stroke and now also present at night. Severity: 5/10 on NPRS during training, 2/10 at rest. Aggravating factors: swimming (catch and pull-through phases), lying on the shoulder at night. Relieving factors: rest. No neck-driven symptoms; no fever, weight loss or other red-flag features reported. Vital signs not recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Rounded shoulders with a forward head; scapular dyskinesis with inferior-angle winging on wall push-ups.

On palpation. Tenderness over the greater tuberosity, the anterior joint line and the medial scapular border; tight pectoralis minor.

1. Motor assessment. Painful arc on abduction between 60° and 120°; glenohumeral internal rotation 25° less than on the left. MMT: supraspinatus, external rotators, serratus anterior and lower trapezius 4/5, with upper trapezius dominance.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation normal; cervical dermatomal and myotomal screen normal — no neck-driven symptoms.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Dry-land push-ups show scapular winging; the catch phase of swimming is painful; the swimmer avoids breathing on the right side. Outcome measures: SPADI (0–100), QuickDASH (0–100) sports module, PSFS (0–10) for swimming tasks, and weekly training distance.

4. Gait analysis. Not formally analysed — an isolated right shoulder condition with no lower-limb involvement.

5. Balance. Not affected; not formally assessed.

6. Hand function. No hand dysfunction reported; no assistive devices used.

7. Coordination. Scapulohumeral coordination disturbed, evidenced by scapular dyskinesis with winging on wall push-ups.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

  • Rotator cuff overload with a painful arc (60–120°)

11. Functional diagnosis

Right subacromial impingement with rotator cuff overload, glenohumeral internal rotation deficit and scapular dyskinesis, causing training intolerance in a competitive swimmer.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pain reduced from 5/10 to 2/10 during daily activities; pain-free sleep; internal rotation deficit under 10°.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Full 30 km/week training, pain-free; SPADI reduced by 30%; normal scapulohumeral rhythm; return to racing by week 12.

13. Treatment plan

Phase I (weeks 1–2) — relative rest: training mileage cut to 50%; avoid butterfly and paddles; ice after sessions; sleeper stretch 3 × 30 seconds daily. Phase II (weeks 3–5) — scapular retraining: scapular setting, wall slides and prone Y-T-W 3 × 12; side-lying external rotation to theraband 3 × 15 daily. Phase III (weeks 6–12) — rotator cuff and kinetic-chain strengthening; graded return to training with volume increased 10–15% weekly; stroke correction with the coach (high-elbow catch, body rotation).

14. Home programme

Daily 15-minute band and stretch routine; icing after heavy sets.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain the role of assistive devices in the workplace.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 6 — assistive devices at work and assistive technology

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Definition, classification and principles of prescription2
Ergonomic assessment matching device to job demand2
Low-tech workplace devices with examples2
High-tech assistive technology with examples2
Benefits, barriers and return-to-work evidence2

aDefinition and classification

An assistive device is any tool, product or technology that enables a person with an impairment to perform a task they would otherwise be unable to do, or to do it more safely. In the workplace they range along a spectrum: low-tech ergonomic aids (reachers, splints, adapted cutlery), mid-tech (ergonomic keyboards, voice-amplifiers, sit-stand desks, powered wheelchairs) and high-tech assistive technology (screen readers, voice-recognition software, environmental control units). Orthoses, prostheses and mobility aids used on the job are part of the same family.

bPrinciples — the assessment comes first

The device is prescribed only after an ergonomic job analysis: the physical demands of the post (lift, reach, keyboard hours, standing time), the environment, the impairment profile, and the worker's own goals. Match the device to the task, not to the diagnosis. Involve the worker in selection — a device the worker rejects is a device that will sit in a cupboard. Check safety, training time, maintenance and cost before finalising the recommendation.

cLow-tech devices — cheap and immediate

Examples that earn concrete marks: reachers and long-handled tools for limited mobility after back injury; adjustable chair with lumbar support and footrest for the desk worker with chronic low back pain; angled or split keyboards and vertical mice for carpal-tunnel and WRMSD presentations; standing desks and anti-fatigue mats; lifting aids such as hoists and transfer boards in hospitals; jar openers, one-handed boards and splints in food or assembly work; amplified phones and visual alarms for hearing impairment.

Fig 6 — Labelled ergonomic workstation with the assessment chain. Simple boxes with the device names beside the body part they protect are enough; the examiner wants names, not art.

dHigh-tech assistive technology

Voice-recognition software for the worker with severe WRMSD of the hand or high spinal involvement; screen readers, magnification and Braille displays for visual impairment; eye-gaze systems and environmental controls for severe motor loss; powered mobility with work-specific modifications; prosthetic myoelectric hands for amputees returning to office or technical work. In the Indian context, also mention accessibility under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016, which obliges employers to provide reasonable accommodation.

eBenefits, barriers and evidence

Benefits: earlier and safer return to work, retention of employment and income, reduced re-injury and compensation cost, improved productivity and morale. Barriers: cost, employer attitudes, lack of trial and training, poor follow-up. Evidence: provision of ergonomic devices with workplace assessment reduces WRMSD symptom progression and lost workdays compared to advice alone; work-hardening programmes that embed the actual devices and tasks of the job return more workers to sustained employment. Conclude: the device is the visible half — the assessment, training and follow-up are what make it work.

Examiner's tip: structure this answer as classify, assess, match, train, follow up — and give at least six named devices with one condition each. Generic phrases like "helps the worker" carry no marks.

Sources

  1. Maxey L, Magnusson P. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. Work and ADL chapters.
  2. Chui L et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Work conditioning section.

On the evaluation form — Q6: Worker with MSK disorder — workplace assistive devices

I. Subjective examination

A 42-year-old assembly-line worker reports low back pain of two years' duration and right wrist discomfort of four months' duration. Severity: mid-shift backache 5/10 on NPRS (0–10). Heavy lifting and repetitive gripping are difficult. There is recurrent sick leave. No rest or night paraesthesia; no red-flag features documented. Vital signs not recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Assessed at the workstation: stooped lifting, forward head posture, and sustained wrist extension while standing on concrete flooring.

On palpation. Lumbar paraspinal tenderness at L4–L5 and tenderness over the first dorsal compartment of the right wrist.

1. Motor assessment. Lumbar ROM full but painful at end-range flexion; core strength 4/5; right grip 30% weaker; forearm flexibility reduced.

2. Sensory assessment. Median, ulnar and radial nerve screens normal; no rest or night paraesthesia.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Lifts 8 kg with correct technique until mid-shift; wrist-intensive work tolerated for only 2 hours. Outcome measures: NPRS (0–10), ODI (0–100%), QuickDASH (0–100) work module, PSFS (0–10), and monthly sick-leave days.

4. Gait analysis. Not formally documented; gait not reported as affected.

5. Balance. Not documented.

6. Hand function. Repetitive gripping and wrist-intensive grasping/releasing on the line difficult, tolerated 2 hours only; no assistive devices in use at presentation.

7. Coordination. Not affected.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

No specific special test results were documented in the case record; the examination findings noted above (lumbar and first dorsal compartment tenderness, painful end-range lumbar flexion, grip weakness) stand as recorded.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Lumbar and forearm overload
  • Weak core and wrist stabilisers
  • Sustained end-range postures

Functional limitations

  • Limited lifting tolerance
  • Limited assembly/wrist work tolerance (2 hours)

Disabilities

  • Reduced productivity
  • Recurrent sick leave
11. Functional diagnosis

Work-related lumbar and forearm (first dorsal compartment) overload secondary to sustained end-range postures at the workstation, with reduced lifting and assembly tolerance.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Mid-shift pain reduced from 5/10 to 2/10 with workstation changes; independent correct lifting technique.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Full shift with pain below 2/10; lifts 12 kg using aids; ODI down 20 points; no MSK-related sick leave.

13. Treatment plan

Phase I (weeks 1–2): worksite visit — trolley, lumbar cushion, anti-fatigue mat; lifting and neutral-wrist training; 3 micro-break stretches every 30 minutes. Phase II (weeks 3–6): core stabilisation (plank 3 × 30 seconds, dead bug, bird-dog daily); eccentric wrist strengthening 3 × 15. Phase III (weeks 7–12): work hardening with graded tasks; resistance training twice weekly; device-compliance review.

14. Home programme

Daily stretch and band routine; continued device use at home.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. What are the tendon transfer techniques for median nerve injury? Add a note on physiotherapy management.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 4 — neurological concepts including tendon transfer and re-education

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Principles of tendon transfer2
Transfers for low median lesion — opposition loss3
Transfers for high median lesion2
Post-operative physiotherapy: splint and re-education2
Strengthening, outcomes and conclusion1

aPrinciples of tendon transfer

A tendon transfer re-routes the muscle-tendon unit of a working muscle to the insertion of a paralysed one. The classic requirements: the donor muscle must be expendable, of adequate strength (grade 4 plus) and similar amplitude; joints must be mobile and supple; the transfer should run a straight line in a single direction; and it should be synergistic with the movement it replaces. Correctable contractures and adequate soft-tissue cover come first — no transfer survives a stiff, scarred bed.

bLow median lesion — restoring opposition

A low median injury paralyses the thenar intrinsic muscles, so thumb opposition and abduction are lost, and sensation over the radial three and a half digits is absent. The standard transfers: the FDS of the ring finger (Royle-Thompson) routed subcutaneously to the abductor pollicis brevis insertion; the Camitz transfer, in which the palmaris longus with a strip of palmar aponeurosis is passed to the APB — quick, single-incision, and best in carpal tunnel thenar wasting; the extensor indicis proprius split and transferred to the first dorsal interosseous and APB for opposition plus pinch; and a slip of abductor digiti minimi (Huber) for thenar bulk in the visible thumb-position deficit. The goal is a thumb that can abduct, rotate and reach the fingers — the opponensplasty in one word.

cHigh median lesion — the added problems

Above the elbow, FPL and FDP to the index are lost too, so flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint and index distal joint go in addition to opposition and sensibility. Reconstruct: brachioradialis or extensor carpi radialis longus to FPL for thumb flexion; side-to-side tenodesis of the index FDP to the middle-finger FDP for index flexion; and the same opposition transfers as above, plus an FCR or ECRL addition when a strong donor is needed. Sensation can be improved by neurovascular island flaps in selected cases.

Fig 7 — Two arrows from palmaris longus and ring FDS converging on the APB insertion, with the high-lesion transfers in the side box. A wrist circle with two labelled arrows is a full-marks diagram.

dPhysiotherapy before and after surgery

Pre-operatively, maintain the prerequisites: full passive joint range, soft-tissue mobilisation for scar and oedema, strengthen the donor muscles consciously (the patient must be able to fire FDS or palmaris longis on command), and desensitise and protect the anaesthetic zones. Post-operatively the transferred tendon is protected in a thumb-spica splint for three to four weeks, then controlled mobilisation begins.

eRe-education and strengthening

The heart of physiotherapy: the transferred muscle still contracts in its old pattern, so re-education trains the new action — the patient flexes the ring finger (donor action) and simultaneously watches and feels the thumb abduct. Use biofeedback, mirror work and repeated attempted opposition until the movement becomes a single unconscious synergy. Then progress through graded resistance to functional pinch, precision grip and activities of daily living; sensory re-education for the median territory proceeds in parallel.

fOutcomes and conclusion

Well-selected opposition transfers achieve functional pinch in most hands, though power and fine sensory discrimination never equal the original. Conclude: surgery re-routes the tendon, physiotherapy rewires the movement — the transfer earns its function on the treatment table.

Examiner's tip: name the donor AND the insertion for each transfer (FDS of ring finger TO abductor pollicis brevis) — a transfer without its insertion is half a mark. And never forget the physiotherapy half of the question: splint, donor-contraction re-education, then strengthening.

Sources

  1. Saunders RJ. Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation. Nerve injury chapters.
  2. Cooper C. Fundamentals of Hand Therapy. Tendon transfer sections.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Peripheral nerve injuries.

On the evaluation form — Q7: Median nerve injury — tendon transfer

I. Subjective examination

A 24-year-old man, six weeks after a deep right forearm laceration (high median nerve injury), is unable to oppose the thumb and reports a clumsy grip with numbness and cold intolerance in the radial three-and-a-half digits. He is right-handed. Tendon transfer (ring-finger FDS to APB, brachioradialis to FPL) is planned. No red-flag features or vital signs documented.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Thenar flattening with an "ape hand" deformity; trophic skin changes over the affected digits.

On palpation. Well-healed, mobile scar; no other palpation findings documented.

1. Motor assessment. MMT (MRC 0–5): thumb opposition and APB 0/5; FPL 2/5; index flexors reduced; pronator quadratus weak; ulnar-innervated muscles 5/5. Muscle girth: thenar girth 1 cm less than on the left.

2. Sensory assessment. Absent light touch over the radial three-and-a-half digits (median nerve distribution); two-point discrimination more than 10 mm (normal up to 6 mm); Tinel's sign advancing at the scar.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Right-hand dominant but currently uses the left hand; unable to button, write or pick up coins. Outcome measures: MMT (0–5) for opposition and pinch; two-point discrimination (normal up to 6 mm); QuickDASH (0–100); PSFS (0–10).

4. Gait analysis. Not relevant — an isolated right forearm/hand condition.

5. Balance. Not relevant.

6. Hand function. Grasping, releasing and precision handling of the right hand impaired — cannot button, write or pick up coins; no thumb opposition; uses the left hand for daily tasks; no assistive device documented.

7. Coordination. Precision coordination of the right hand impaired (clumsy grip).

8. Investigations

Electrodiagnostic studies and any imaging as per medical records; no reports reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Ochsner's clasping testClasp the handsIndex finger fails to flexHigh median lesion. Result in this patient: not formally documented; index flexors reduced on MMT.
Benediction signAttempt a fistIndex stays extendedLong flexor motor loss. Result in this patient: not formally documented; reduced index flexion is consistent.
Tinel's sign (forearm)Percussion along the nerveTingling into the digitsRegeneration front or neuroma. Result in this patient: positive — advancing at the scar.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Loss of thumb opposition and pinch (opposition and APB 0/5)
  • Weak FPL (2/5) with reduced index flexion and weak pronator quadratus
  • Sensory loss over the radial three-and-a-half digits with trophic changes
  • Thenar wasting (girth 1 cm less)

Functional limitations

  • Cannot button, write or pick up coins

11. Functional diagnosis

Right high median nerve lesion with loss of thumb opposition and pinch, thenar wasting and sensory loss in the median distribution, for which tendon transfer is planned; physiotherapy is directed at pre-operative conditioning and post-operative re-education of the transferred tendons.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pre-operative conditioning — full passive opposition, supple scar, oedema-free hand; independent splint use; precautions taught.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Transfer power 3+/5 with a new opposition pattern by week 12; QuickDASH improved by 25 points; independent ADLs.

13. Treatment plan

Pre-operative (2–3 weeks): opponens splint; passive thumb and wrist ROM 10 reps 4 times daily; sensory re-education and scar massage twice daily; wax bath. Post-operative Phase I (0–3 weeks): below-elbow cast with the thumb held in opposition; active use of free joints; elevation. Phase II (3–6 weeks): guarded re-education — ring-finger flexion produces thumb opposition, 10 reps hourly; gentle passive ROM. Phase III (6–12 weeks): putty strengthening 3 × 15 daily; pinch and dexterity drills; wean the splint by week 10; return to work by week 12.

14. Home programme

Motor imagery, texture discrimination, scar mobilisation.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe the role of myofascial release in trapezitis.

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 4 — myofascial schools of manual therapy

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Mechanism of trapezitis and trigger-point pathophysiology2
Assessment of myofascial trigger points2
MFR techniques and application to upper trapezius3
Progression, dosage and adjuncts2
Evidence and self-management1

aMechanism — why the upper trapezius knots up

Trapezitis is overload of the upper trapezius: sustained low-grade contraction from desk posture, phone-on-shoulder habits, emotional stress and poor workstation ergonomics keeps the muscle in continuous activity, exhausting its local circulation. The resulting myofascial trigger point is a hyperirritable spot in a taut band, explained by the integrated hypothesis: an energy crisis — ischaemia releases sensitising substances that lower the local pain threshold and sustain abnormal acetylcholine release, producing the taut band, which further compresses the local vessels. The patient feels aching at the point plus the classic referral to the temple, angle of jaw or between the scapulae.

bAssessment

Diagnose on palpation: a taut band in the upper trapezius, an exquisite spot, reproduction of the patient's recognised pain, a local twitch response to snapping palpation, and restricted, painful cervical rotation or side-flexion with or without a positive stretch test. Screen for perpetuating factors — sleep, workstation, spectacles, stress — because a trigger point with perpetuating factors never stays released.

cMyofascial release — techniques

MFR works on the fascia-muscle complex by sustained, low-load, gentle pressure and elongation rather than forceful kneading. For the upper trapezius: direct release with gentle thumb or knuckle pressure applied at 90 degrees to the taut band, held until tissue softening (typically 60 to 90 seconds); skin rolling over the cervicothoracic fascia to restore fascial mobility; positional release — find the tender point, move the neck into the position of ease and hold, letting the point quieten; and sustained stretch with the head side-flexed away and gently rotated toward, held for the full release time. Follow every release with active use of the range gained: the muscle must learn the new length.

Fig 8 — Neck circle with the taut band, the trigger point and its referral arrows to temple and jaw. Drawing the referral pattern correctly is the clinical fingerprint of this answer.

dProgression, dosage and adjuncts

Treat in the order that matches the assessment: release the trigger point, lengthen the muscle, then retrain. Two to three sessions per week over three to four weeks with a home programme of heat, self-pressure with a ball, and stretching. Adjuncts that combine well: spray-and-stretch with ethyl chloride or ice, post-isometric relaxation, dry needling for stubborn points, ergonomic correction of the workstation, breathing retraining for stress-related elevation, and strengthening of the mid and lower trapezius so the upper fibres stop doing everyone's work.

eEvidence and conclusion

MFR and sustained-pressure techniques show short-term reductions in pain and improved neck range and disability versus placebo in neck-pain trials, with the strongest effect when combined with exercise; dry needling adds short-term benefit. Conclude: MFR releases the taut band, but only posture correction and lower-trapezius retraining keep it released — treat the fire, then remove the fuel.

Examiner's tip: the sequence "release — lengthen — strengthen" is the spine of this answer. Also write the referral pattern of the upper trapezius (temple, jaw, ipsilateral neck) — examiners ask for it in vivas more often than the techniques themselves.

Sources

  1. Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System / myofascial approaches.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Soft-tissue intervention chapter.
  3. Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics. Mechanosensitivity chapters.

Tennis-ball self-release 60 seconds × 3; doorframe stretch; heat; daily chin tucks and scapular squeezes.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. How do you manage pain in fracture cases based on educational and behavioral strategies?

Read this answer in simple English →

Paper IV Unit 2 — educational and behavioural management of pain

Evaluator's indicative distribution (10)

Content expectedMarks
Pain mechanisms after fracture and why education works2
Educational strategies: pain neuroscience and self-management2
Behavioural techniques: relaxation, pacing, operant methods3
Graded exposure and fear-avoidance management per healing phase2
Evidence and conclusion1

aWhy the fracture patient needs more than a pill

Fracture pain is acute nociceptive pain with an inflammatory phase, then movement-related pain during healing, and — if mishandled — a transition to chronic pain with fear of movement, guarded patterns and disuse. The gate control theory explains the opening: descending anxiety and attention amplify the signal; confidence and understanding close the gate. Educational and behavioural strategies exploit exactly this — they change what the patient does and expects, which changes what the nervous system transmits.

bEducational strategies

Pain-neuroscience education first: explain in the patient's language that pain is an alarm produced by the brain on the basis of danger, not a meter of tissue damage — a healing fracture that is protected by a cast is safe to move. Show the healing timeline (inflammation days 1 to 5, soft callus to about 3 weeks, hard callus to about 3 months) so the patient interprets twinges correctly. Give clear rules: weight-bearing status, dos and don'ts, red flags. Set expectations for mobilisation pain and control pathways, teach relaxation breathing to be used before and during painful procedures such as cast removal and pin-site care, and give the patient a written home plan — knowledge that is not written down does not travel home.

cBehavioural techniques

Relaxation and breathing retraining, progressive muscle relaxation of uninvolved segments, guided imagery and distraction for procedural pain; cognitive restructuring to catch catastrophising thoughts ("the bone is breaking again"); pacing to break the boom-bust cycle of overdoing on good days; operant strategies — the family is taught to reinforce function ("well done for walking to the gate") and not to reinforce pain behaviour (not rushing with a tray every time the patient winces); goal-setting and self-monitoring with a simple diary; and positive reinforcement tied to achievement, not to suffering.

Fig 9 — The Melzack-and-Wall gate with the fracture-specific openers and closers. One diagram links education, relaxation and graded exposure to a single mechanism — that is how a 10-marker reads like a story.

dGraded exposure and phase-wise application

After immobilisation, many patients show fear-avoidance: they equate pain with damage and stop moving. Assess with the Tampa Scale and map their fear hierarchy, then expose them in graded steps — from pain-free isometrics, to assisted range, to weight-bearing, stairs and return to work — each step mastered before the next. Time-contingent rather than pain-contingent scheduling ("walk ten minutes at 8 am daily") prevents the patient being ruled by the pain meter. Combine with goal-setting for functional milestones and progress visible to the patient.

eEvidence and conclusion

Pain neuroscience education reduces pain and disability and fear in musculoskeletal cohorts; behavioural graded activity matches or beats standard physiotherapy for return-to-function after injury. Conclude: in fracture care, the pharmacologist controls the chemistry of pain, but the physiotherapist controls the psychology and behaviour of pain — education that the patient can repeat back is the cheapest analgesic on the ward.

Examiner's tip: the examiner set this question under educational and behavioral strategies, so do NOT spend half the answer on TENS and cryotherapy — one sentence on adjuncts is enough, then build the marks on gate control, pain education, pacing, operant reinforcement and graded exposure.

Sources

  1. Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965.
  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Pain chapters.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Pain management chapter.
